28:I[3873,["$2","$3","$4","$23","$25","$26","$27"],"Assistant"]
29:T4b2,The Battle of Plassey in 1757 marks the beginning of Company dominance in Bengal, and the grant of Diwani in 1765 gave the Company a revenue role in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. Company rule continued for about a century after Plassey. The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred the government of India from the Company to the Crown. Crown rule then lasted from 1858 to 1947. The syllabus node History of India and Indian National Movement covers this whole span, and the Mains grouping under Indian Heritage and Culture, History and Geography of the World and the Society expects the candidate to discuss structure and consequences rather than memorise isolated battles.

The ordering matters. Plassey precedes Diwani, Diwani precedes 1858, and Crown rule follows 1858 until 1947. An option that places the Crown takeover before Plassey, or treats 1858 as the start of British rule, reverses the sequence and is incorrect. The Company phase was not absent rule: it was commercial and territorial power exercised by a chartered company, while the Crown phase was direct state power exercised in the name of the sovereign. Keeping the agent of rule distinct prevents a standard assertion-reason error.2a:T51b,The clearest Odisha-specific anchor in the official OPSC material for this topic is the revolt of Jayi Rajaguru and the Paiks of Odisha against the British East India Company in 1804. Rajaguru, described in the material as royal preceptor to Mukundadeva II, mobilised the Paiks, and he was executed on 6 December 1806 at Midnapore. The sequence is fixed: preceptor role, mobilisation of the Paiks, revolt in 1804, execution in 1806. Questions that place the revolt in the nineteenth-century Crown phase, or that attribute it to a revolt against the British Crown rather than the Company, are incorrect because 1804 falls squarely in the Company phase.

After the British conquest of 1803, the Odia-speaking areas were not governed as one unit. The coastal division of Cuttack, Puri and Balasore was attached to the Bengal Presidency, the southern tracts such as Ganjam (and later Koraput) lay in the Madras Presidency, and Sambalpur in the west was later attached to the Central Provinces. Odisha became a separate province only on 1 April 1936. The Odisha anchor therefore does double duty: it tests a regional fact and it tests phase awareness. A candidate who remembers only Plassey and 1858 but misses the 1804 revolt will lose the Odisha-linked question that the official paper uses to test this topic.2b:T4f9,Gandhi's rise within the Congress was not a matter of a single speech. He presided over the Belgaum session of the Indian National Congress in 1924, while Badruddin Tyabji had become the first Muslim Congress President in 1887. The Congress's own historical account distinguishes two later landmarks: Annie Besant was its first woman President at Calcutta in 1917, and Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman President at Kanpur in 1925. The 2025 OPSC match-the-columns item is therefore only a pattern prompt; its Besant-1925 pairing must not be used to overwrite that chronology. The institutional point also matters: Gandhi initiated campaigns, but the Congress Working Committee shared command. Meeting at Sabarmati from 14 to 16 February 1930, the Working Committee authorised Gandhi to launch Civil Disobedience. Treating Gandhi as acting entirely alone misses how the Congress organisation sustained volunteers, funds and local committees.

The syllabus node for this topic is History of India and Indian National Movement, and the Mains grouping places the Gandhian movement under Indian Heritage and Culture, History and Geography of the World and the Society. For Prelims, the emphasis is factual: what was launched, when, by whom authorised, and what followed.2c:T417,The Civil Disobedience Movement was launched through the Dandi Salt March. Gandhi left Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930 and broke the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930 by raising a fistful of salt from the seashore. The march turned a consumption tax into a national symbol and drew volunteers from across India. The colonial response involved large-scale arrests, with about one hundred thousand persons arrested during the campaign. The movement was suspended after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931.

Three examination distinctions follow from this sequence. First, the march began on 12 March and the salt-law breach followed on 6 April; these events launched the movement, which continued into 1931. Second, the breach was deliberate and public, not an incidental violation. Third, the Pact of 1931 was the suspension point, not the start of negotiations in the abstract. Questions often offer a wrong year for the march, a wrong act for the pact, or a wrong figure for arrests; the PIB account and the chronology provide anchors to reject them.2d:T418,The Quit India Movement of 1942 was the final nation-wide satyagraha campaign of the freedom struggle. Gandhi issued the call of Do or Die. The All India Congress Committee adopted the Quit India resolution on 8 August 1942, and Gandhi was arrested on 9 August 1942. The speed of arrest after the resolution is part of the factual sequence: resolution one day, arrest the next. The campaign was not a repeat of the Dandi march with a new name. Dandi was organised around a specific law breach in 1930; Quit India demanded the immediate withdrawal of British rule in 1942 and was launched when the leadership was removed from the field within hours.

For Prelims, the safest anchors are the call, the resolution date, and the arrest date, kept in that order. An option that places the resolution after the arrest, or treats Do or Die as belonging to 1930, can be rejected on chronology alone. The PIB's National Archives exhibition release states all three details, so these precise claims no longer depend on the year-only Gandhi Smriti chronology.2e:T47c,The mature Harappan phase, dated to about 2600-1900 BCE, is the period associated with developed towns, standardised town planning and long-distance exchange. The civilisation as a whole had earlier and later phases, but Prelims questions usually test the mature dates rather than the full sequence. Charles Masson reported the remains at Harappa in 1826; systematic excavations in the early twentieth century later established the significance of Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro. The name Harappan comes from Harappa, the first site that brought the civilisation to light, not from Mohenjo-Daro or from a claim about relative city size.

More than a thousand Harappan sites have been discovered across a wide region covering parts of present-day India, Pakistan and Afghanistan. PIB uses that count in its description of Dholavira, while NCERT and NIOS map sites from Afghanistan and Sind to Gujarat, Haryana, Rajasthan, Maharashtra and western Uttar Pradesh. This distribution explains how shared weights, brick ratios and town forms occur across many settlements. It does not support assigning every river valley in eastern India to the Harappan world.2f:T625,Mohenjo-Daro was a major and exceptionally well-preserved Harappan city, not the largest known site. Rakhigarhi now holds that largest-known distinction in the cited PIB release. Excavations at Mohenjo-Daro began in 1922, and UNESCO inscribed the Archaeological Ruins at Moenjo-Daro as World Heritage in 1980 under criteria including its testimony to a lost civilisation and its exceptional example of a settlement tradition. The city had a planned grid layout, public baths, an elaborate drainage system and a structure traditionally described as a granary.

Brick descriptions require care rather than a one-word label. NCERT records both sun-dried and baked bricks at Harappan settlements, and UNESCO's full description calls Mohenjo-Daro mostly baked brick even though its short description says unbaked brick. Baked or burnt brick is prominent in the city's structures and water infrastructure, while mud or sun-dried brick is also documented, including in platforms. Therefore both "unbaked brick only" and "baked brick only" are unsafe examination statements.

For Prelims, keep the supported attributes together: major planned city, mixed brick evidence, grid layout, public baths, drainage, granary, excavation from 1922 and UNESCO inscription in 1980. NCERT's approximate 125-hectare figure for Mohenjo-Daro should not be confused with UNESCO's 240-hectare inscribed-property figure, which measures a different boundary. An option that calls Mohenjo-Daro the largest known Harappan city is also incorrect because the cited official evidence identifies Rakhigarhi.30:T42c,The Indus script of the Harappan civilisation remains undeciphered. Both NCERT and NIOS state this explicitly, so an option asserting an accepted decipherment can be eliminated. The 2025 OPSC Prelims match-the-columns item on the language of the Indus Valley Civilisation, which pairs hypotheses associated with a Dravidian hypothesis, S. R. Rao, R. Kinnier-Wilson and Asko Parpola, and Soviet scholars, tests recognition of the scholarly debate rather than knowledge of a deciphered text. A learner should treat language hypotheses as proposals while remembering that no decipherment has been accepted.

The distinction is useful in two-statement questions. A statement that the script has been deciphered is incorrect. A statement that the civilisation is called Harappan because Mohenjo-Daro was its largest city is also incorrect: the name comes from Harappa, and Rakhigarhi rather than Mohenjo-Daro is identified as the largest known settlement in the PIB source. Keeping name, size and script as separate facts prevents the most common conflations in this topic.31:T5e6,Statement questions ask which of the listed statements are correct, or which conclusion follows from the passage. The distinction is the central trap. Correct refers to consistency with the given material. Follows refers to logical consequence: the conclusion must be unavoidable given the premises, not merely plausible or generally true. A conclusion that adds a new fact, reverses a cause, or generalises beyond the scope of the passage does not follow even when it sounds reasonable.

A reliable method is to mark each statement as supported, contradicted, or unsupported. Supported statements can be worded almost verbatim from the passage. Contradicted statements conflict with a clear premise. Unsupported statements may be true elsewhere but have no basis in the passage. Only supported statements count as correct, and only unavoidable consequences count as following. Combining statements I and II is permitted only when each is independently supported and the combination does not add an assumption. Over-assuming is the habit to suppress.

Example pattern: a passage states that a library opens on alternate days and that membership requires a local address. The statement that the library opens daily is contradicted, the statement that non-local visitors cannot hold membership is unsupported without a further premise, and the statement that membership is not automatic on entry follows only if the passage makes address a requirement without exception. The pattern teaches restraint, not speed.32:T590,Series questions present terms in order and ask for the next term or the missing term. The first step is to test the simplest rule that fits the visible terms: differences between consecutive terms, multiplication by a growing factor, alternation between two interleaved series, or digit operations within terms. If the simplest rule fails on a middle term, abandon it quickly rather than forcing later terms to fit. Interleaved series, where odd-positioned and even-positioned terms follow separate rules, are common in Paper II.

Analogy and relationship tasks test mapping. In an analogy, the relation between the first pair must match the relation between the second pair, not merely share a topic. In a relationship task, the categories may be nested, disjoint, or partially overlapping. A Venn-type reading is often decisive: if one category is fully inside another, a third category that overlaps both cannot be drawn as fully separate. Candidates who assign each term its everyday meaning without checking the relation will select a distracting option that shares vocabulary but not structure.

Example pattern: the sequence 2, 6, 12, 20, 30 follows adding 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next term is 42. The distractor 44 arises from assuming constant addition of 6, while 36 arises from halving the growth. The correct choice follows the growth of differences, whereas the distractors follow plausible but inconsistent rules.33:T464,Analytical puzzles give a set of conditions about persons, dates, places or arrangements and ask for the only arrangement that satisfies all of them. The method is to list the conditions, place the most restrictive condition first, and eliminate arrangements that violate any single condition. Care with data sufficiency and relationship logic is essential: avoid assuming that a missing detail is irrelevant, and avoid treating a possible arrangement as the only arrangement. Blood relation and direction tasks test the same discipline on family trees and positions. A symbol map fixed at the start prevents mid-question reinterpretation of the same sign.

Coding tasks test consistent substitution. The learner must infer the code for a word or number from given examples and apply the same rule without adding an extra step. Letter-position shifts, reverse alphabets, and digit sums are frequent families, but the rule must be inferred from the examples rather than borrowed from memory of a different code. If two rules fit the examples, the option set usually breaks the tie: only one rule will produce an offered code.34:T55a,The **Regulating Act of 1773** was Parliament's first attempt to supervise the Company, and it accepted that the Company had political as well as trading functions. It turned the Governor of Bengal into the Governor-General of Bengal, gave him an executive council of four, and placed the Bombay and Madras presidencies under him. Warren Hastings was the first holder. It also provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta, set up in 1774 with a chief justice and three judges, and barred Company servants from private trade and from taking gifts.

The **Amending Act of 1781** (the Act of Settlement) repaired gaps in that scheme. Official acts of the Governor-General, his council and Company servants were taken out of the Supreme Court's reach, as were revenue matters, and the Court was told to apply the personal law of the defendant.

**Pitt's India Act of 1784** split the Company's commercial work from its political work. The Court of Directors kept commerce; a new **Board of Control** in Britain supervised civil, military and revenue government. This arrangement is remembered as **double government**, and the Act was also the first to describe the Company's lands as "British possessions in India". The **Act of 1786** then met Lord Cornwallis's conditions for taking office: he could override his council in special cases and would also be Commander-in-Chief.35:T5b1,| Act | What changed |
|---|---|
| Charter Act 1793 | Overriding power over the council extended to all later Governors-General and Governors; trade monopoly renewed for twenty years; Board of Control salaries charged to Indian revenues |
| Charter Act 1813 | Company's general trade monopoly ended (tea and China trade kept); missionaries allowed; western education to be promoted; local governments could tax |
| Charter Act 1833 | Governor-General of Bengal became **Governor-General of India** (Lord William Bentinck first); all legislative power centralised in him; the Company became a purely administrative body; laws now called Acts, not Regulations |
| Charter Act 1853 | Legislative and executive functions of the council separated for the first time; six legislative councillors added, forming a central legislative council; open competition for the covenanted civil service; local representation from four provincial governments |

The 1833 Act is the high point of **centralisation**: Bombay and Madras lost their law-making power. It also proposed open competition for Company posts without excluding Indians, but the Court of Directors blocked it. That idea was revived in 1853, when the covenanted civil service was opened to competitive entry and the Macaulay Committee was set up in 1854. Unlike earlier charters, the 1853 Act renewed the Company's rule without a fixed term, which signalled that Parliament could end it whenever it chose.36:T633,The **Government of India Act of 1858**, passed after the revolt of 1857, wound up the East India Company and transferred its territories, powers and revenues to the Crown. The Governor-General was now also styled **Viceroy**, the Crown's direct representative; Lord Canning was the first. Double government ended: the Board of Control and the Court of Directors were abolished, and a **Secretary of State for India**, a British cabinet member answerable to Parliament, took full control, assisted by an advisory Council of India of fifteen members. Observers note that the Act changed who controlled India from London far more than how India was governed on the ground.

The **Indian Councils Act of 1861** began associating Indians with law-making. The Viceroy could nominate Indians as non-official members, and in 1862 Lord Canning nominated the Raja of Benaras, the Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao. The Act reversed the trend of 1833 by restoring legislative powers to Bombay and Madras, provided for new councils in Bengal, the North-Western Provinces and Punjab, gave legal recognition to Canning's **portfolio system**, and allowed the Viceroy to issue ordinances valid for six months in an emergency.

The **Indian Councils Act of 1892** enlarged the councils while keeping an official majority, let members discuss the budget and question the executive, and allowed some non-official seats to be filled on the recommendation of bodies such as universities, chambers of commerce and district boards. The word "election" was avoided, but this was election in all but name.37:T6fa,The **Indian Councils Act of 1909** (Morley–Minto Reforms) raised the Central Legislative Council from 16 to 60 members, allowed non-official majorities in the provincial councils (but not at the Centre), and let members ask supplementary questions and move resolutions on the budget. For the first time an Indian joined the Viceroy's executive council: **Satyendra Prasad Sinha**, as Law Member. Most controversially it created **separate electorates** for Muslims, so that Muslim members were chosen only by Muslim voters; Lord Minto is therefore called the father of communal electorate.

The **Government of India Act of 1919** (Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms) followed the declaration of 20 August 1917 that responsible government was the goal, and took effect in 1921.

- Subjects were split into **central and provincial** lists through the Devolution Rules, though the overall structure stayed unitary.
- Provincial subjects were divided into **transferred** (such as education, health and local government, run by ministers answerable to the legislature) and **reserved** (such as police, justice, land revenue and finance, run by the Governor and his executive council). This was **dyarchy**, and it largely failed.
- **Bicameralism and direct elections** appeared at the Centre: a Council of State and a Legislative Assembly.
- Three of the six members of the Viceroy's executive council, other than the Commander-in-Chief, had to be Indians.
- Separate electorates were extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans; franchise was limited by property, tax and education.
- A High Commissioner for India in London, a public service commission (the Central Public Service Commission came in 1926), separate provincial budgets, and a review after ten years.38:T55b,A long statute of 321 sections and 10 schedules, the 1935 Act is the single largest source of the administrative structure the Constitution later adopted.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| All-India Federation | Provinces and princely states as units; three lists — Federal (59 items), Provincial (54), Concurrent (36); residuary powers with the Governor-General. Never came into being because the states did not join |
| Provincial autonomy | Dyarchy ended in the provinces; Governors to act on the advice of ministers responsible to the legislature. Worked from 1937 to 1939 |
| Dyarchy at the Centre | Federal subjects split into reserved and transferred — never implemented |
| Bicameral provinces | Six of eleven: Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam, United Provinces |
| Franchise | About 14 per cent of the population could vote; separate representation also for women and labour |
| New institutions | Reserve Bank of India; Federal, Provincial and Joint Public Service Commissions; Federal Court (1937); Federal Railway Authority; Auditor-General |
| Territorial changes | Burma separated; new provinces of **Orissa** and Sind created |

The Council of India of 1858 was abolished, and the Secretary of State got a team of advisers instead. For an Odisha aspirant, the creation of Orissa as a separate province under this Act is a natural one-mark question.39:T61c,Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced on 20 February 1947 that British rule would end by June 1948. The Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947, accepted by the Congress and the Muslim League, brought partition forward, and the **Indian Independence Act** gave it legal effect.

- India became independent from 15 August 1947, partitioned into the dominions of India and Pakistan, each free to leave the Commonwealth.
- The Viceroy's office ended; each dominion got a Governor-General appointed on the advice of its own cabinet, and the Secretary of State for India was abolished.
- Each Constituent Assembly could frame any constitution and repeal any British law, including this Act, and could legislate meanwhile. Until new constitutions came, the 1935 Act governed both dominions, with modifications.
- British paramountcy over the princely states lapsed; they could join India, join Pakistan or stay independent.
- The Governor-General and provincial Governors became constitutional heads acting on ministerial advice; the British monarch lost the veto and the title Emperor of India.

Lord Mountbatten became the first Governor-General of the Dominion of India and swore in Jawaharlal Nehru as Prime Minister. The Constituent Assembly formed in 1946 also served as the dominion's Parliament. In the **Interim Government of 1946** the members sat as the Viceroy's executive council, with Nehru as its vice-president (External Affairs) and Sardar Patel holding Home; in the **first cabinet of 1947**, Dr B. R. Ambedkar held Law and Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Education.3a:T741,The Assembly was set up in **November 1946** on the lines of the Cabinet Mission Plan. Its design had five elements.

| Element | Rule |
|---|---|
| Total strength | **389** — 296 for British India and 93 for princely states |
| British India split | 292 from the eleven Governors' provinces + 4 from the four Chief Commissioners' provinces (one each: Delhi, Ajmer-Merwara, Coorg, British Baluchistan) |
| Basis of allocation | Seats in proportion to population, roughly one per million |
| Communities | Each province's seats shared among Muslims, Sikhs and General in proportion to their population |
| Method | Members of each community in the provincial assembly elected their own representatives by proportional representation through the single transferable vote; princely-state members were nominated by their rulers |

So the Assembly was **partly elected and partly nominated**, and even the elected part was chosen **indirectly** by provincial legislators who had themselves been elected on the narrow franchise of the 1935 Act.

Elections for the 296 British-Indian seats took place in **July–August 1946**. The Congress won **208**, the Muslim League **73**, and small groups and independents **15**. The princely states kept away, so their 93 seats lay empty at first. Despite the indirect method, the Assembly drew in Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Parsis, Anglo-Indians, Indian Christians, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, including women from these groups — **15 women** in all. Almost every leading figure of the time was a member; the notable exception was Mahatma Gandhi. Among the women, **Malati Chowdhury** represented Orissa.

|---|---|
| Hindus | 163 |
| Muslims | 80 |
| Scheduled Castes | 31 |
| Indian Christians | 6 |
| Backward Tribes | 6 |
| Sikhs | 4 |
| Anglo-Indians | 3 |
| Parsees | 3 |3b:T546,The Assembly first met on **9 December 1946**. The Muslim League boycotted it and pressed for Pakistan, so only 207 members attended. In line with French practice, the oldest member, **Dr Sachchidananda Sinha**, presided as temporary Chairman.

| Date | Office-bearer |
|---|---|
| 11 December 1946 | **Dr Rajendra Prasad** elected permanent Chairman (President) |
| 25 January 1947 | H. C. Mukherjee elected Vice-President |
| 16 July 1947 | V. T. Krishnamachari elected as a second Vice-President |

On **13 December 1946** Nehru moved the **Objectives Resolution**, which set out the philosophy of the future constitution. Its main ideas were these: India would be an independent sovereign republic; British India, the princely states and other willing territories would form a Union; the units would be autonomous and hold residuary powers except those given to the Union; all authority would flow from the people; social, economic and political justice, equality of status and opportunity and a set of freedoms would be guaranteed, subject to law and public morality; minorities, backward and tribal areas and depressed classes would get safeguards; territorial integrity would be preserved; and India would contribute to world peace. The Assembly adopted it unanimously on **22 January 1947**, and a modified form of it became the **Preamble**.3c:T722,Princely-state members began to trickle in: by 28 April 1947 six states (Baroda, Bikaner, Jaipur, Patiala, Rewa, Udaipur) were represented, and after the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947 most others followed, as did League members from the Indian side. The **Indian Independence Act of 1947** then changed the Assembly's position in three ways.

- **Sovereign body:** it could frame whatever constitution it chose and could repeal or alter any British law applying to India.
- **Legislature too:** it became the Dominion Legislature, the first Parliament of free India, meeting on separate days for each role. Rajendra Prasad presided over constitution-making; **G. V. Mavalankar** presided over law-making (he was elected its Speaker when it first sat as a legislature on 17 November 1947). Both roles ran until 26 November 1949.
- **Smaller house:** League members from areas going to Pakistan left, so strength fell from 389 to **299** — the provinces from 296 to 229 and the princely states from 93 to 70. Pakistan got its own Constituent Assembly.

Beyond drafting and legislating, the Assembly also performed several symbolic acts.

| Date | Act |
|---|---|
| 22 July 1947 | Adopted the national flag |
| May 1949 | Ratified India's Commonwealth membership |
| 24 January 1950 | Adopted the national anthem and the national song; elected Rajendra Prasad first President |

The work took **11 sessions** across 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, drew on the constitutions of about 60 countries, devoted 114 days to the draft, and cost about ₹64 lakh. The final session was on 24 January 1950, when members signed the document. The Assembly then carried on as the **provisional Parliament** from 26 January 1950 until the first elected Parliament, formed after the 1951–52 general elections, came into being in May 1952.3d:T644,The Assembly divided its work among eight major committees and many minor ones. The chairmen are a favourite match-the-pair topic.

The date of adoption, **26 November 1949**, is the one recorded in the Preamble. As adopted, the Constitution had a Preamble, **395 Articles and 8 Schedules**; the Preamble itself was passed last. Ambedkar, then Law Minister, steered the draft through the House and is honoured as the **Father** and **chief architect** of the Constitution. Since a government decision of 19 November 2015, 26 November is observed every year as **Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas)**.

Enforcement came in two steps. A small group of provisions — on citizenship, elections, the provisional Parliament, temporary and transitional matters and the short title (Articles 5–9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393) — took effect on 26 November 1949 itself. The rest came into force on **26 January 1950**, the "date of commencement", now Republic Day. That date was picked because on 26 January 1930 the country had celebrated **Purna Swaraj** day following the Lahore Congress of December 1929. On commencement, the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935 (with its amending Acts) were repealed, though the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act 1949 was kept alive.

|---|---|
| 393 | Short title |
| 394 | Commencement |
| 394A | Authoritative Hindi text |
| 395 | Repeals |3f:T46c,The word comes from the Latin **constituere**, "to establish" or "to set up". In current usage a constitution is the set of principles that lays down how a government is organised and how it works, and what rights and duties link the government with the people. It goes by many labels: the fundamental law of the land, the supreme or basic law, the instrument of government, the basic structure of the polity, or the **grundnorm** of the country.

Scholars stress different aspects of the idea.

| Scholar | Emphasis of the definition |
|---|---|
| Gilchrist | The rules that organise government, distribute power among its organs and fix the principles for using that power |
| Gettell | The basic principles that decide the form of the state, including how sovereign power is shared, how functions are exercised and how government relates to the governed |
| K. C. Wheare | The entire system of government — the body of rules that create and regulate it |
| Wade and Phillips | A document with special legal sanctity that sets out the framework and main functions of the organs of the state and the principles they must follow |40:T460,These two classifications overlap heavily — the source itself treats the distinction as roughly the same.

| Basis | Type | Nature | Also called | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Origin | **Evolved** | Grows slowly through conventions, practices, principles and court rulings | Cumulative | Britain |
| Origin | **Enacted** | Deliberately framed by a constituent assembly or council, or issued by a king or parliament, as a document or set of documents | Conventional | USA, India |
| Form | **Written** | Provisions gathered in a document or series of documents, consciously adopted by a constituent body | Documentary, codified | USA, Canada, Japan, France, India |
| Form | **Unwritten** | Most rules found outside any single text — in conventions, charters, statutes and judgments; a product of history | Non-documentary, uncodified | UK, New Zealand, Israel |

Do not confuse the word "conventional" here. An enacted constitution is called conventional because a convention (an assembly) made it, not because it rests on conventions — the British evolved constitution is the one that relies on conventions.41:T656,Having a constitution is not the same as having **constitutionalism**. A dictatorship may have a constitutional document while its rulers remain unchecked. Constitutionalism means, at its heart, **limited government** — the opposite of arbitrary power. A country has it only when its constitution disperses power rather than concentrating it and places further restraints on those who hold it. Even power handed over by a constitutional text, if it is arbitrary, defeats the idea. Constitutional government should therefore be democratic government, ruled by law rather than by despotic, authoritarian or totalitarian will; some writers call such limited government "civilised" government.

| Thinker | Core idea |
|---|---|
| Carl Friedrich | A system of effective checks on government action — rules of fair play that make government responsible |
| J. S. Roucek | Essentially limited government, the reverse of rule by the unrestrained will of rulers |
| K. C. Wheare | Rule-based government limited by the constitution's terms, not merely by what rulers wish or are able to do |
| S. P. Ybema | Government counts as constitutional only when rulers are bound by rules that limit their power |

**Louis Henkin** listed eight elements of constitutionalism:

| # | Element |
|---|---|
| 1 | Popular sovereignty |
| 2 | Rule of law |
| 3 | Democratic, responsible and accountable government |
| 4 | Separation of powers with checks and balances |
| 5 | Independent judiciary |
| 6 | Civilian control of the armed forces |
| 7 | Police bound by law and subject to judicial control |
| 8 | Respect for individual rights |42:T7ab,No written constitution in the world is longer. Compare the original and present shape:

| | Original (1949) | Present |
|---|---|---|
| Articles | 395 | about 470 |
| Parts | 22 | 25 |
| Schedules | 8 | 12 |

Amendments since 1951 have dropped about 20 Articles and one Part (Part VII, on Part-B states, deleted by the 7th Amendment of 1956) and added about 95 Articles, four Parts — **IV-A** and **XIV-A** (42nd Amendment), **IX-A** (74th) and **IX-B** (97th) — and four Schedules (9th to 12th). For comparison, the US Constitution began with just 7 Articles.

Four factors explain the bulk: the size and diversity of the country; the historical pull of the long 1935 Act; the use of a **single constitution for both the Centre and the states**; and the large number of lawyers in the Constituent Assembly. The document therefore contains administrative detail and matters that other democracies leave to ordinary law or convention.

Until 2019, Jammu and Kashmir had its own constitution and special status under Article 370. The Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019, replaced the 1954 Order and applied the whole Constitution there, and the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, split the state into two Union territories — Jammu & Kashmir, and Ladakh.

|---|---|
| 7th | Union List (now 98 subjects, originally 97), State List (59, originally 66), Concurrent List (52, originally 47) |
| 8th | Languages: 14 at first, now 22 — Sindhi (21st Amdt, 1967); Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali (71st, 1992); Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali (92nd, 2003); Oriya renamed **Odia** (96th, 2011) |

| 12th | Municipalities — 18 matters (74th Amdt, 1992) |43:T6e9,Ambedkar said the framers had "ransacked" all the known constitutions of the world. A useful three-way split: the **structural** part came largely from the 1935 Act; the **philosophical** part (Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles) from the American and Irish constitutions respectively; and the **political** part (cabinet government and executive–legislature relations) from Britain. The 1935 Act was the single biggest material source — roughly 250 of its provisions were taken over, and more than half the Constitution closely resembles it.

| Source | Features borrowed |
|---|---|
| Government of India Act, 1935 | Federal scheme, office of Governor, judiciary, public service commissions, emergency provisions, Supreme Court's advisory jurisdiction, administrative details |
| Britain | Parliamentary government, rule of law, legislative procedure, single citizenship, cabinet system, prerogative writs, parliamentary privileges, bicameralism |
| USA | Fundamental rights, independent judiciary, judicial review, impeachment of the President, removal of judges, office of Vice-President |
| Ireland | Directive Principles, nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha, method of electing the President |
| Canada | Federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre, Centre's appointment of Governors |
| Australia | Concurrent List, freedom of trade and commerce, joint sitting of the two Houses |
| Weimar Germany | Suspension of Fundamental Rights during emergency |
| USSR | Fundamental duties; social, economic and political justice in the Preamble |
| France | Republic; liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble |
| South Africa | Amendment procedure; election of Rajya Sabha members |
| Japan | Procedure established by law |44:T4dc,India preferred the British parliamentary model, which rests on co-operation between legislature and executive, to the American presidential model, which rests on their separation. Also called the Westminster model, responsible government or cabinet government, it operates at both the Centre and in the states. Its features in India are: a nominal and a real executive; rule by the majority party; collective responsibility of the executive to the legislature; ministers drawn from the legislature; leadership by the Prime Minister or Chief Minister; and the power to dissolve the lower House. The PM's dominance is such that some call it **"Prime Ministerial government"**.

Two differences from Britain matter: the Indian Parliament is **not sovereign**, and India has an **elected head of state** (a republic), whereas Britain has a hereditary monarch.

On the other side, Indian judicial review is narrower than American, because Article 21 uses **"procedure established by law"** rather than the US **"due process of law"**. So the framers struck a middle course between British **parliamentary sovereignty** and American **judicial supremacy**: the Supreme Court can strike down laws, while Parliament can amend most of the Constitution.45:T79b,| Feature | Fundamental Rights (Part III) | Directive Principles (Part IV) | Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Political democracy; check on executive tyranny and arbitrary laws | Social and economic democracy; a welfare state | Remind citizens of obligations to country, society and fellow citizens |
| Justiciable? | Yes — enforceable through writs | No | No |
| Origin | Original | Original; Ambedkar called them a "novel feature" | Added by the 42nd Amdt (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice; one more by the 86th Amdt (2002) |

There are now **six** Fundamental Rights: equality (Arts 14–18), freedom (19–22), against exploitation (23–24), freedom of religion (25–28), cultural and educational rights (29–30) and constitutional remedies (32). There were seven originally; the 44th Amendment of 1978 removed the right to property (Art 31) and made it a legal right under **Article 300-A** in Part XII. An aggrieved person can go straight to the Supreme Court, which can issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. The rights are not absolute: they carry reasonable restrictions, can be curtailed by a constitutional amendment, and can be suspended in a National Emergency — except **Articles 20 and 21**.

The Directive Principles fall into socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual groups. Though courts cannot enforce them, the Constitution calls them fundamental in governance and makes it the state's duty to apply them in law-making; their real sanction is public opinion. In **Minerva Mills (1980)** the Court held that the Constitution rests on a balance between the Rights and the Directives.

Part IV-A has a single Article, **51-A**, listing **eleven** duties — among them respecting the Constitution, flag and anthem, protecting the country's sovereignty, unity and integrity, promoting common brotherhood, and preserving the composite culture.46:T4cf,India has no official religion. The secular character shows in many provisions.

| Provision | Secular content |
|---|---|
| Preamble | "Secular" added by the 42nd Amdt (1976); liberty of belief, faith and worship |
| Arts 14, 15, 16 | Equality before law; no religious discrimination; equal opportunity in public employment |
| Art 25 | Freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion |
| Art 26 | Denominations may manage their own religious affairs |
| Art 27 | No compulsion to pay taxes for promoting a religion |
| Art 28 | No religious instruction in fully state-maintained institutions |
| Arts 29, 30 | Protection of language, script and culture; minorities' educational institutions |

The Western idea of secularism is **negative** — a wall between church and state — which suits a society with one dominant faith poorly. India, being multi-religious, adopts **positive** secularism: equal respect and equal protection for all religions. The Constitution also ended **communal representation** (religion-based seats used under the 1909, 1919 and 1935 Acts), while allowing temporary reservation for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.47:T404,Elections to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies are held on **universal adult franchise**: every citizen aged 18 or above votes, regardless of caste, race, religion, sex, literacy or wealth. The voting age was cut from 21 to 18 by the **61st Amendment Act of 1988**, effective 1989. Given the country's size, poverty, inequality and illiteracy, this was a bold experiment — many Western countries had extended the vote only slowly (women got it in the USA in 1920, Britain in 1928, France in 1945 and Switzerland only in 1971). It broadens democracy, raises the dignity of ordinary people, upholds equality and gives minorities and weaker sections a voice.

Although India has a dual polity, it has **single citizenship**. An American is a citizen of both the USA and a state, with two sets of rights; an Indian has one citizenship and the same civil and political rights everywhere in the country. Riots and caste, linguistic and ethnic conflicts show, however, that the goal of a fully integrated nation is still unfinished.48:T555,Besides the three organs of government, the Constitution creates independent bodies as bulwarks of democracy, protected by security of tenure, fixed service conditions and charged expenditure.

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| Election Commission | Free and fair elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President |
| Comptroller and Auditor-General | Audits Central and state accounts; guardian of the public purse |
| Union Public Service Commission | Recruits for the All-India and higher Central services; advises the President on disciplinary matters |
| State Public Service Commissions | Recruit for state services; advise the Governor on discipline |

The emergency provisions aim to protect the country's sovereignty, unity, integrity and security and its democratic order.

| Emergency | Ground | Article |
|---|---|---|
| National | War, external aggression or armed rebellion ("armed rebellion" replaced "internal disturbance" through the 44th Amdt, 1978) | 352 |
| State (President's Rule) | Breakdown of constitutional machinery, or failure to follow Central directions | 356, 365 |
| Financial | Threat to India's financial stability or credit | 360 |

In an emergency the Centre becomes all-powerful, turning the federal structure into a unitary one **without any formal amendment** — a feature unique to India.49:T534,| Criticism | Main voices | Response or note |
|---|---|---|
