- The North-Eastern Council (Act of 1971) has eight members and must adopt a unified regional plan.8b:T5e1,The President may proclaim a National Emergency under Article 352 when the security of India, or of any part of it, is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion. The threat need not have materialised; an imminent danger is enough if the President is satisfied it exists. An emergency on the ground of war or external aggression is called an **External Emergency**; one based on armed rebellion is an **Internal Emergency**.

Several amendments shaped this power:

| Amendment | Change |
|---|---|
| 38th (1975) | President may issue separate proclamations on different grounds even while one is already in force; proclamation made immune from judicial review |
| 42nd (1976) | Operation of an emergency may be confined to a specified part of India |
| 44th (1978) | "Armed rebellion" replaced the vague phrase "internal disturbance"; proclamation only on the **written advice of the cabinet**; the bar on judicial review removed |

The cabinet rule answers a specific episode. In 1975 Prime Minister Indira Gandhi advised the President to proclaim emergency without consulting her colleagues, who learnt of it only after the event. After 1978 the cabinet — the Prime Minister and the ministers of cabinet rank — must recommend in writing, so a Prime Minister cannot act alone. In **Minerva Mills (1980)** the Supreme Court confirmed that a proclamation can be questioned in court if it is mala fide, or rests on facts that are wholly extraneous or irrelevant, or is absurd or perverse.8c:T5af,Both Houses must approve the proclamation within **one month**; the window was two months until the 44th Amendment shortened it. If the Lok Sabha is dissolved when the proclamation is issued, or is dissolved within that month without having approved it, the proclamation survives until 30 days after the reconstituted Lok Sabha first sits, provided the Rajya Sabha has approved it meanwhile.

Once approved, the emergency lasts **six months** and can be continued without any upper limit, provided Parliament approves it again every six months. Before 1978 a single approval let it run as long as the government wished. Each approving resolution needs a **special majority** in each House: a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting. That too is a 1978 addition; earlier a simple majority sufficed.

The President may revoke the proclamation at any time by a fresh proclamation, which needs no parliamentary approval. Since 1978 the President **must** revoke it if the Lok Sabha passes a resolution disapproving its continuance. If one-tenth of the Lok Sabha's total membership gives written notice to the Speaker (or to the President when the House is not in session), a special sitting must be held within **14 days** to consider such a resolution.

| | Resolution approving continuance | Resolution disapproving continuance |
|---|---|---|
| Passed by | Both Houses | Lok Sabha alone |
| Majority | Special | Simple |8d:T573,The states keep functioning during a National Emergency, but the Centre gains overriding powers in three spheres.

- **Executive:** in normal times the Union can direct a state only on specified matters; now it can direct a state on any matter. State governments are controlled, not suspended.
- **Legislative:** Parliament may legislate on any State List subject. State legislatures are not suspended, but their laws yield to Parliament's. Such Union laws lapse six months after the emergency ends. The President may also issue ordinances on state subjects when Parliament is not sitting, and Parliament may confer powers and duties on Union officers for matters outside the Union List. The 42nd Amendment extended these executive and legislative effects even to states where the emergency is not in operation.
- **Financial:** the President may alter the constitutional sharing of revenues, reducing or cancelling transfers to the states. The change lasts until the end of the financial year in which the emergency ends, and each such order must be laid before both Houses.

Parliament may also extend the five-year term of the Lok Sabha by law, one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the emergency ceases. The term of a state legislative assembly can be stretched the same way. The **Fifth Lok Sabha (1971–77)** is the example: its life was extended twice, by a year each time.8e:T699,**Article 358** frees the State from the limits of Article 19 the moment a proclamation is made; no separate order is needed. Laws and executive acts that curtail the six freedoms cannot be challenged on that ground while the emergency lasts. When it ends, Article 19 revives and inconsistent laws stop operating, yet nothing done in the meantime can be questioned afterwards.

**Article 359** works differently. It lets the President, by order, suspend the right to move a court for enforcing the Fundamental Rights named in the order. The rights remain in existence; only the remedy is put on hold. The order may cover the whole emergency or a shorter span, the whole country or part of it, and it must be placed before each House.

The 44th Amendment narrowed both. Article 358 now applies only to an emergency declared on the ground of war or external aggression, not armed rebellion. Under Article 359 the enforcement of **Articles 20 and 21** can never be suspended. And under both, only laws connected with the emergency, and executive action taken under such laws, enjoy immunity.

| Point | Article 358 | Article 359 |
|---|---|---|
| Rights affected | Article 19 only | Rights named in the Presidential Order |
| How it operates | Automatic on proclamation | Needs a Presidential Order |
| Kind of emergency | External only | External and internal |
| Period | Whole duration of the emergency | Whole duration or shorter, as the order says |
| Area | Entire country | Entire country or a part |
| Limit | Article 19 suspended entirely | Articles 20 and 21 cannot be touched |

Their common feature: only emergency-related laws, and action under them, are shielded from challenge.8f:T96c,President's Rule under Article 356 can rest on two grounds. Under Article 356 itself, the President may act on being satisfied that a state's government cannot be carried on according to the Constitution — on the Governor's report or even without one. Under **Article 365**, a state's failure to comply with a Union direction allows the President to treat that as such a situation.

Both Houses must approve within **two months**, with the same Lok Sabha-dissolution rule as above. An approved proclamation lasts six months and may be extended, six months at a time, up to **three years**. Each resolution needs only a **simple majority** of members present and voting. Since the 44th Amendment, an extension beyond one year is allowed only if a National Emergency is in force in all of India or in all or part of the state, and the **Election Commission** certifies that assembly elections cannot be held. The President may revoke it at any time without parliamentary approval.

While it lasts, the President dismisses the council of ministers, takes over the state's executive functions and declares that Parliament will exercise the legislature's powers. The Governor runs the state on the President's behalf, aided by the chief secretary or advisers. The assembly is suspended or dissolved; Parliament passes the state's bills and budget, and may delegate law-making to the President, whose laws — **President's Acts** — are usually made after consulting the state's MPs. With the Lok Sabha not in session, the President may authorise spending from the state's Consolidated Fund. Such laws outlast the proclamation until the state legislature changes them. The **High Court** is untouched: its status and powers cannot be taken over or suspended.

| Point | National Emergency | President's Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Ground | Security threatened by war, aggression or armed rebellion | Constitutional breakdown, possibly unrelated to security |
| State government | Continues, Centre gets concurrent power | Executive dismissed, legislature suspended or dissolved |
| Delegation of state law-making | Not allowed | Allowed (President's Acts) |
| Maximum period | None | Three years |
| States affected | Relations with all states change | Only the state concerned |
| Majority for approval | Special | Simple |
| Fundamental Rights | Affected | Not affected |
| Lok Sabha can force revocation | Yes | No |90:T9d7,The first imposition was in **Punjab in 1951**, and by now the provision has been invoked more than 125 times, many of them for political ends. In 1977 the Janata government of Morarji Desai brought nine Congress-ruled states under it, arguing their assemblies no longer reflected the voters; the Congress returned the favour in nine states in 1980. In 1992 three BJP-ruled states — Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan — were taken over for not enforcing the Centre's ban on religious organisations. Ambedkar had hoped the article would stay a "dead letter"; H. V. Kamath later quipped that Ambedkar was gone but the articles were very much alive.

The 38th Amendment had made the President's satisfaction under Article 356 final; the 44th removed that bar. In **S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)** the Supreme Court upheld the 1992 action on the ground that secularism is a basic feature, but rejected the impositions in Nagaland (1988), Karnataka (1989) and Meghalaya (1991). Its main rules:

- The proclamation is open to judicial review; satisfaction must rest on relevant material, and the Centre carries the burden of showing it. Courts examine relevance, not adequacy.
- If the proclamation falls, the court can restore the dismissed ministry and revive the assembly.
- The assembly may only be suspended until Parliament approves; dissolution must wait for that approval.
- Loss of majority is to be tested on the floor of the House.
- A new party at the Centre cannot dismiss state ministries simply because they belong to rivals.
- Article 356 is an exceptional power for rare use; an anti-secular state government can, however, be acted against.

Drawing on the **Sarkaria Commission** report (1988), the Court also listed proper and improper uses.

| Proper use | Improper use |
|---|---|
| Hung assembly after elections | Governor recommends it without exploring an alternative ministry |
| Majority party will not form a ministry and no coalition is possible | Governor judges support himself instead of a floor test |
| Ministry resigns after defeat and nobody else can form one | Ruling party loses badly in Lok Sabha polls (as in 1977, 1980) |
| State disregards a constitutional direction of the Centre | Internal disturbance short of subversion or breakdown |
| Internal subversion or a fomented violent revolt | Maladministration, corruption charges or financial strain |
| Physical breakdown endangering security | No prior warning given, or used to settle intra-party disputes |91:T40d,Article 360 lets the President proclaim a Financial Emergency when the financial stability or credit of India, or of any part of its territory, is threatened. The 38th Amendment's bar on judicial review was again deleted in 1978. Approval by both Houses is needed within **two months**, by simple majority. Once approved, it continues until revoked — no maximum period and no repeated approval.

During it, the Union may direct any state to follow canons of financial propriety and other directions, including cuts in salaries and allowances of state employees and reserving money and financial bills for the President after the legislature passes them. The President may order salary cuts for Union employees and for **judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts**. H. N. Kunzru warned that this threatened state financial autonomy; Ambedkar explained it was modelled on the American **National Recovery Act of 1933**, passed during the Great Depression. No Financial Emergency has ever been declared, not even during the 1991 crisis.92:T42c,Critics feared that the provisions would wreck federalism, concentrate power in the Union executive, make the President a dictator, nullify state finances and empty Fundamental Rights of meaning. H. V. Kamath foresaw the foundation of a totalitarian, police state; K. T. Shah called the chapter one of reaction and retrogression; T. T. Krishnamachari spoke of a constitutional dictatorship. Defenders answered back: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar saw them as the life-breath of the Constitution, and Mahabir Tyagi as a safety valve. Ambedkar himself admitted they could be abused for political purposes.

| Article | Subject |
|---|---|
| 352 | Proclamation of Emergency |
| 353 | Effect of the proclamation |
| 354 | Distribution of revenues during an emergency |
| 355 | Union's duty to protect states |
| 356 | Failure of constitutional machinery in states |
| 357 | Legislative powers under an Article 356 proclamation |
| 358 | Suspension of Article 19 |
| 359 | Suspension of enforcement of Part III rights |
| 359A | Punjab (repealed) |
| 360 | Financial Emergency |93:T419,- Part XVIII, Articles 352–360: National Emergency (352), President's Rule (356), Financial Emergency (360).
- Grounds of 352: war, external aggression, armed rebellion ("internal disturbance" replaced in 1978).
- 352 needs written cabinet advice; approval within one month by special majority; renewal every six months, no ceiling.
- Lok Sabha alone can force revocation of 352 by simple majority; one-tenth members can demand a sitting within 14 days.
- Article 358: Article 19 suspended automatically, external emergency only; Article 359: Presidential Order, never Articles 20 and 21.
- National Emergencies: 1962, 1971, 1975; Shah Commission led to the 44th Amendment.
- 356: approval within two months by simple majority; maximum three years; beyond one year needs National Emergency plus EC certificate.
- First President's Rule: Punjab, 1951; Bommai (1994) made it reviewable and insisted on floor tests.
- 360: approval within two months, runs indefinitely; never declared.
- High Court powers can never be assumed under President's Rule.94:T5a2,The people do not elect the President directly. An **electoral college** does, made up of:

| Included | Excluded |
|---|---|
| Elected members of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha | Nominated members of either House |
| Elected members of state legislative assemblies | Nominated members of assemblies |
| Elected members of the assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry (added by the 70th Amendment, 1992, effective 1995) | All members, elected or nominated, of state legislative councils; nominated members of the Puducherry assembly |

Delhi's assembly has no nominated members. The 104th Amendment of 2019 ended nomination of Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha and assemblies from 25 January 2020. Members of a dissolved assembly lose their vote even if the fresh election has not yet been held.

The Constitution demands **uniformity** among states and **parity** between the states taken together and the Union. Each MLA's vote is therefore weighted: divide the state's population by its number of elected MLAs, then divide by 1,000. Under the 84th Amendment, "population" means the 1971 census figure until data from the first census after 2026 is published. Each MP's vote equals the total value of all MLA votes divided by the number of elected MPs, so the two halves of the college carry nearly equal weight. In the **2022** election, for instance, an MP's vote was worth 700, and the whole college of 4,809 electors carried a value of 10,86,431.95:T6e3,The election uses **proportional representation by single transferable vote**, with a secret ballot. Each elector gets one ballot and may rank as many candidates as there are in the contest. To win, a candidate needs a quota: total valid votes divided by two (one seat plus one), plus one — in effect an absolute majority. First preferences are counted first; if nobody reaches the quota, the lowest candidate is eliminated and that candidate's ballots pass to the next preferences, round after round, until someone does. Critics in the Assembly noted that "proportional representation" is a misnomer for a single vacancy — it is really a preferential or alternative vote — and that each voter in fact expresses several preferences rather than one vote.

The **Supreme Court** decides all disputes about the election, and its word is final. An election cannot be challenged merely because the college had vacancies. If an election is set aside, acts done by the President before the judgment remain valid.

Why indirect? The framers gave three answers. A nominal head with no real power did not need a direct popular mandate, which would sit oddly with parliamentary government. A nationwide poll for a symbolic office would be costly and exhausting. And a college of MPs alone was rejected because a single dominant party in Parliament would always pick its own nominee; including state legislators makes the President a representative of both the Union and the states.

Some election facts worth knowing: **Dr Rajendra Prasad** won in 1952 and 1957 and is the only person to hold two terms; **N. Sanjeeva Reddy** was elected unopposed in 1977; the 1969 contest between **V. V. Giri** and Sanjeeva Reddy was the closest; and **Droupadi Murmu** won in 2022.96:T66b,A candidate must be an Indian citizen, at least **35 years** old, qualified to be elected to the Lok Sabha, and must not hold an office of profit under the Union, a state, a local authority or any other public authority. The sitting President or Vice-President, a Governor, and a Union or state minister are not treated as holding offices of profit for this purpose.

The nomination needs **50 proposers and 50 seconders** from the electoral college, and a deposit of **₹15,000** in the Reserve Bank of India, forfeited if the candidate fails to win one-sixth of the votes polled. Before 1997 the figures were ten each and ₹2,500; they were raised to deter frivolous candidates.

The **Chief Justice of India** (or, failing him, the senior-most available Supreme Court judge) administers the oath. The President swears to execute the office faithfully, to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law, and to serve the well-being of the people. Anyone acting as President takes a similar oath.

Conditions of office: the President cannot be a member of Parliament or a state legislature — a member who is elected vacates that seat on assuming office — and cannot hold any other office of profit. Rashtrapati Bhavan is provided rent-free; emoluments are fixed by Parliament and cannot be cut during the term. Parliament raised the monthly salary from ₹1.5 lakh to ₹5 lakh in 2018. The President is immune from legal liability for official acts and, during the term, from criminal proceedings even for personal acts, and cannot be arrested. Civil proceedings over personal acts are possible after **two months' notice**.97:T7e0,The term is **five years** from the day of assuming office. The President may resign by writing to the **Vice-President**, stays on beyond five years until the successor takes charge, and may be re-elected any number of times (the American President is limited to two terms).

Removal is by **impeachment** for "violation of the Constitution", a phrase the Constitution leaves undefined. The steps:

| Step | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Initiation | Either House; charges signed by one-fourth of its members |
| Notice | 14 days to the President |
| First House | Resolution passed by two-thirds of its **total membership** |
| Second House | Investigates the charges; the President may appear or be represented |
| Removal | Second House also passes by two-thirds of total membership; removal from that date |

Impeachment is quasi-judicial. Note the asymmetry: **nominated MPs take part** in impeachment though not in the election, while **elected MLAs** vote in the election but play no part in impeachment. No President has ever been impeached.

A vacancy arises on expiry of the term, resignation, removal, death, or otherwise — for example on disqualification or a voided election. If the term is ending, the election must be completed before it ends; any delay simply keeps the outgoing President in office, so the Vice-President does not step in. For any other vacancy the election must be held within **six months**, and the new President gets a full five-year term. Meanwhile the **Vice-President** acts as President, and also discharges the functions when the President is absent or ill. If that office too is vacant, the **Chief Justice of India**, or failing that the senior-most available judge, acts. Two Presidents — **Zakir Husain** and **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed** — died in office. After Husain's death in 1969, Vice-President V. V. Giri acted, then resigned to contest, and Chief Justice **M. Hidayatullah** officiated for about a month. Whoever acts enjoys the President's powers and immunities.98:T515,| Sphere | Main powers |
|---|---|
| Executive | All Union executive action in the President's name; rules for authenticating orders and for transaction of business; appoints the Prime Minister and ministers (who serve at pleasure), Attorney General, CAG, Election Commissioners, UPSC members, Governors, Finance Commission; may seek information from the PM and ask that a minister's decision go to the whole council; appoints a backward classes commission and an inter-state council; administers UTs; declares scheduled areas |
| Financial | Prior recommendation for money bills; causes the Budget to be laid; no demand for grants without recommendation; advances from the Contingency Fund of India; constitutes a Finance Commission every five years |
| Judicial | Appoints the Chief Justice and judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts; may seek the Supreme Court's advice on law or fact (Article 143), which is not binding; pardoning power |
| Diplomatic | Treaties concluded in the President's name, subject to Parliament's approval; sends and receives envoys |
| Military | Supreme commander of the defence forces; appoints service chiefs; declares war and concludes peace subject to Parliament |
| Emergency | National Emergency (352), President's Rule (356, 365), Financial Emergency (360) |99:T5e2,The President is a constituent part of Parliament. The office summons and prorogues the Houses, dissolves the Lok Sabha and calls a **joint sitting**, which the Speaker chairs. The President addresses Parliament at the first session after a general election and at the first session each year, and may send messages to either House. If both presiding officers of a House are absent, the President may appoint a member to preside. Twelve members of the Rajya Sabha are nominated for distinction in literature, science, art and social service; two Anglo-Indian nominations to the Lok Sabha existed until the 104th Amendment ended them. Questions of disqualification of MPs are decided by the President **after consulting the Election Commission**.

Prior recommendation is required for several kinds of bills — those drawing on the Consolidated Fund, altering state boundaries or creating states, money bills, taxes in which states are interested, bills changing the meaning of "agricultural income", bills affecting the principles of distributing money to states, and surcharges for Union purposes. A state bill restricting freedom of trade also needs the President's prior sanction. The President lays before Parliament the reports of the CAG, UPSC and Finance Commission, issues ordinances during recess, and makes regulations for the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Ladakh — and for Puducherry only while its assembly is suspended or dissolved.9a:T814,Under **Article 111** the President, faced with a bill passed by Parliament, may assent, withhold assent, or return it (unless it is a money bill) for reconsideration; if Parliament passes it again, with or without changes, assent must follow. The aim is to check hasty or unconstitutional legislation.

| Type of veto | Meaning | Indian President? |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute | Withholding assent; the bill dies | Yes |
| Qualified | Overridable only by a higher majority | No — the US President has it |
| Suspensive | Overridable by re-passing with an ordinary majority | Yes, except for money bills |
| Pocket | Taking no action, with no time limit | Yes |

The **absolute veto** is used mainly for private members' bills, or for government bills when a cabinet falls before assent and its successor advises against them. Dr Rajendra Prasad withheld assent to the **PEPSU Appropriation Bill** in 1954, and R. Venkataraman to a 1991 bill on MPs' salaries and pensions passed without his prior recommendation. The **pocket veto** exists because the Constitution sets no deadline — unlike the ten days allowed in the USA. Zail Singh used it in 1986 on the **Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill**, criticised as curbing press freedom; Venkataraman returned it in 1989 and the new government dropped it. There is **no veto on a constitutional amendment bill**: the 24th Amendment of 1971 made assent compulsory.

For **state bills**, the Governor under Article 200 may assent, withhold, return or reserve the bill for the President. On a reserved bill, the President under Article 201 may assent, withhold, or direct the Governor to return it — but even if the legislature passes it again, the President is not bound to assent, and there is no time limit, so a pocket veto is possible here too.

| Bill | Central | State |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary | Assent, reject or return | Assent, reject or return |
| Money | Assent or reject, not return | Assent or reject, not return |
| Constitutional amendment | Assent only | Cannot be introduced in a state legislature |9b:T662,**Article 123** lets the President issue ordinances, with the force of an Act of Parliament, when Parliament is in recess. Four limits apply.

- An ordinance can be issued only when both Houses, or either of them, are not sitting; one made while both are sitting is void. It is not a parallel law-making power.
- The President must be satisfied that immediate action is needed. In **Cooper (1970)** the Court held that satisfaction can be challenged for mala fides — for instance, proroguing a House just to bypass it. The 38th Amendment shielded it; the 44th removed the shield.
- Its scope equals Parliament's legislative competence, and it faces the same limits, so it cannot abridge Fundamental Rights (Article 13 counts ordinances as "law").
- It must be laid before both Houses on reassembly and lapses **six weeks** after reassembly (counted from the later date if the Houses meet on different days), or sooner if both Houses disapprove. With a maximum gap of six months between sessions, an ordinance can survive at most six months and six weeks without approval. Acts done under a lapsed ordinance stay valid.

The President issues or withdraws ordinances only on ministerial advice. An ordinance may be retrospective, may amend Acts, ordinances or tax laws, but cannot amend the Constitution, and it needs no National Emergency. Lok Sabha rules require a statement explaining the urgency when a replacing bill is introduced. In **D. C. Wadhwa (1986)** the Court, reviewing Bihar's practice of repromulgating ordinances for years, held that repeated repromulgation without legislative action is a fraud on the Constitution.9c:T526,**Article 72** lets the President grant clemency in three classes of case: offences against Union law, sentences by **court martial**, and all **death sentences**. The power is independent of the judiciary; the President does not sit as an appeal court, but can correct judicial error or soften a harsh sentence.

| Form | Effect |
|---|---|
| Pardon | Wipes out sentence and conviction and all disqualifications |
| Commutation | Swaps the punishment for a lighter kind (death to rigorous to simple imprisonment) |
| Remission | Shortens the sentence without changing its nature |
| Respite | Lighter sentence because of a special fact, such as disability or pregnancy |
| Reprieve | Temporary stay, especially of a death sentence, so clemency can be sought |

A Governor has a similar power under **Article 161** for offences against state law, but cannot touch court-martial sentences or pardon a death sentence, though a Governor may suspend, remit or commute one. In **Kehar Singh (1988)** the Court held there is no right to an oral hearing, the President may re-examine evidence, the power is exercised on cabinet advice, no guidelines are needed, and review is limited to decisions that are irrelevant, irrational, mala fide or discriminatory. **Maru Ram (1980)** had already held the advice and review points.9d:T500,India adopted the British model, so the President is a **nominal executive**. Ambedkar compared the office to the English monarch: head of the State, not of the executive; the nation's symbol and seal, bound by ministerial advice, unable to dismiss ministers who hold a majority. Three articles fix the position: **Article 53** vests executive power in the President; **Article 74** provides a council of ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise; **Article 75** makes the council collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

The **42nd Amendment (1976)** made that advice expressly binding. The **44th (1978)** let the President send advice back once for reconsideration, after which the reconsidered advice binds. K. R. Narayanan used this twice: in October 1997 on a recommendation for President's Rule in Uttar Pradesh, which the cabinet then dropped, and in September 1998 for Bihar, imposed only in February 1999 after the cabinet repeated its advice.

There is no constitutional discretion, but there is **situational discretion**: choosing a Prime Minister when no party has a clear majority or a PM dies without an obvious successor, dismissing a council that cannot prove the Lok Sabha's confidence, and dissolving the Lok Sabha when the council has lost its majority.9e:T45a,- Electoral college: elected MPs, elected MLAs, elected members of Delhi and Puducherry assemblies; no nominated members, no MLCs.
- MLA vote = state population (1971) ÷ elected MLAs ÷ 1,000; MP vote = total MLA votes ÷ elected MPs.
- PR by single transferable vote, secret ballot; quota = valid votes ÷ 2, plus 1; disputes go to the Supreme Court.
- Qualifications: citizen, 35 years, eligible for Lok Sabha, no office of profit; 50 proposers + 50 seconders; ₹15,000 deposit.
- Oath by the Chief Justice; resignation to the Vice-President; five-year term, unlimited re-election.
- Impeachment: one-fourth signatures, 14 days' notice, two-thirds of total membership in each House; never used.
- Vacancy election within six months; Vice-President, then Chief Justice, act meanwhile.
- Vetoes: absolute, suspensive and pocket — no qualified veto; none on amendment bills (24th Amendment).
- Ordinance (Art 123): only in recess, lapses six weeks after reassembly; maximum life six months six weeks.
- Pardon (Art 72): Union law, court martial, death sentence; Governor (Art 161) cannot pardon death sentences.9f:T860,Like the President, the Vice-President is chosen indirectly. Ordinary voters do not elect the office holder. The electoral college consists of the members of both Houses of Parliament, and it includes nominated members as well as elected ones. Members of state legislative assemblies take no part. The contrast with the President's college is the point most often asked about:

| Group of voters | Vice-President's electoral college | President's electoral college |
|---|---|---|
| Elected members of Parliament | Included | Included |
| Nominated members of Parliament | Included | Not included |
| Elected members of state assemblies | Not included | Included |

The reasoning behind this difference was explained by Dr B.R. Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly. The President's authority reaches into the administration of the Union and of the states, so state legislators should have a voice in choosing that person. The Vice-President, by contrast, mainly presides over Rajya Sabha and only rarely, and for a short time, steps into the President's shoes. The framers therefore judged a wider college unnecessary for that office.

The method of voting is the same as for the President. Voting uses proportional representation through the single transferable vote, and each ballot is secret. The Supreme Court inquires into and decides every doubt or dispute about the election, and its decision is final. An election cannot be challenged merely because the electoral college was incomplete, that is, because some seats were vacant. If the Court later declares a person's election void, the acts that person performed before that declaration remain valid.

The original Constitution required both Houses to sit together at a joint meeting to elect the Vice-President. The Eleventh Amendment Act of 1961 replaced that cumbersome arrangement with the electoral college described above.

Elections held since 1952 show a pattern. Four were uncontested, in 1952, 1957, 1979 and 1987. Dr S. Radhakrishnan won the first two. In the most recent contest the chapter records, in 2022, Jagdeep Dhankar secured 528 votes against 182 for Margaret Alva.a0:T62c,A person seeking the office must satisfy the following eligibility tests:

| Requirement | What it means |
|---|---|
| Citizenship | The candidate must be a citizen of India |
| Age | The candidate must have completed 35 years |
| Membership test | The candidate must be qualified to be elected to Rajya Sabha |
| Office of profit | The candidate must not hold any office of profit under the Union, a state, a local authority or any other public authority |

Some officeholders are treated differently. A sitting President or Vice-President, a state Governor, and a Union or state minister do not count as holding an office of profit for this purpose, so they may stand. Procedure also matters. A nomination must be proposed by at least 20 electors and seconded by at least 20 electors, and the candidate must lodge a security deposit of ₹15,000 with the Reserve Bank of India.

Before entering office, the Vice-President must make and sign an oath or affirmation. In it the holder promises to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and to discharge the duties of the office faithfully. The President administers the oath, or a person the President appoints for that purpose does so.

The Constitution sets two conditions for holding the office once elected. First, the Vice-President must not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a state legislature house. If a sitting member is elected, that person is treated as having vacated the seat on the day of entering the Vice-President's office. Second, the holder must not take up any other office of profit.a1:T529,The term is five years, counted from the day the Vice-President enters office. The holder may resign at any time by a letter addressed to the President. Removal before the term ends does not need an impeachment. A resolution for removal is passed in Rajya Sabha by a majority of all its members then in office, and the Lok Sabha must agree to it. The motion can be introduced only in Rajya Sabha, and at least 14 days' advance notice must be given before it is moved. The Constitution does not list any ground for removal.

When the five years lapse, the Vice-President may continue in office until a successor takes charge. The office carries no bar on re-election, and a person may be elected any number of times. Dr Radhakrishnan, for example, served two terms.

A vacancy can arise on expiry of the term, on resignation, on removal, on death, or in other ways, such as disqualification or the setting aside of the election. The timing rules differ by cause:

- If the term is about to expire, the election to fill the seat must be held before the term ends.
- If the office falls vacant for any other reason, the election must be held as soon as possible.
- The person elected to fill a vacancy serves a full five-year term from the day of assuming charge.

Krishna Kant was the first Vice-President to die in office.a2:T615,The office has two functions. The first is that the Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha. In that role the powers and duties are similar to those of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

The second is acting as President. When the presidency falls vacant through resignation, impeachment, death or otherwise, the Vice-President performs the President's functions for a maximum of six months, and a new President must be elected within that period. The Vice-President also discharges the President's functions whenever the President is absent, ill or otherwise unable to act, until the President resumes office.

While acting as President, the Vice-President does not chair Rajya Sabha. The Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha performs those duties during that time. Two episodes illustrate the second role. Vice-Presidents V.V. Giri and B.D. Jatti acted as President after the deaths in office of Dr Zakir Husain and Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed. Dr Radhakrishnan discharged presidential functions in 1960, when Dr Rajendra Prasad was touring the Soviet Union, and again in 1961, when Dr Prasad was seriously ill.

The Constitution fixes no separate salary for the Vice-President. The holder draws the pay of the Chairman of Rajya Sabha in the capacity of ex-officio Chairman. During any period of acting as President, however, the Vice-President receives the salary and allowances of the President instead, and not those of the Chairman. Other benefits, such as a furnished residence and medical and travel facilities, are provided under the relevant laws.a3:T432,- Chosen indirectly by an electoral college of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated members; state assembly members do not vote.
- Single transferable vote and secret ballot; the Supreme Court decides disputes and its decision is final.
- Eligibility: Indian citizen, at least 35 years, qualified for Rajya Sabha, and no office of profit.
- Nomination needs 20 proposers and 20 seconders; the security deposit is ₹15,000 with the RBI.
- Term of five years; the holder continues until a successor takes charge, and re-election has no limit.
- Removal: a Rajya Sabha resolution with 14 days' notice, agreed to by Lok Sabha; no impeachment and no listed grounds.
- Ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha; the Deputy Chairman takes over the chair while the Vice-President acts as President.
- Acts as President for at most six months after a vacancy, and during the President's absence or illness.
- Unlike the American Vice-President, does not succeed for the unexpired term.
- The 1961 Eleventh Amendment replaced the joint-sitting method with the electoral college.a4:T810,Article 75 says only that the President appoints the Prime Minister; it lays down no procedure. Convention fills the gap: the President invites the leader of the majority party in the Lok Sabha. The President is not free to pick anyone.

Real choice arises in two situations.

| Situation | What the President does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| No party has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha | Personal discretion; usually invites the leader of the largest party or coalition and asks for a vote of confidence within a month | 1979: President Neelam Sanjiva Reddy named Charan Singh after Morarji Desai's Janata government fell. This was the first use of the discretion |
| The sitting Prime Minister dies and there is no obvious successor | Individual judgement | 1984: after Indira Gandhi's assassination, President Zail Singh appointed Rajiv Gandhi rather than a caretaker; the party later elected him leader |

If the ruling party itself elects a new leader after a death, the President has no option but to appoint that person. After the deaths of Nehru and Shastri, when the leadership was contested, the seniormost minister, Gulzari Lal Nanda, was appointed to act as Prime Minister until the party chose its leader.

**Proving a majority.** In 1980 the Delhi High Court held that the Constitution does not demand that a person prove a majority before being appointed. The President may appoint first and ask for proof within a reasonable time. Charan Singh (1979), V. P. Singh (1989), Chandrasekhar (1990), P. V. Narasimha Rao (1991), A. B. Vajpayee (1996), Deve Gowda (1996), I. K. Gujral (1997) and Vajpayee again (1998) took office this way.

**Membership of a House.** In 1996 the Supreme Court held that a non-member can be made Prime Minister for six months, within which he or she must get into either House or cease to hold the post. The Prime Minister may belong to either House: Indira Gandhi (1966), Deve Gowda (1996) and Manmohan Singh (2004) were Rajya Sabha members. In Britain, by contrast, the Prime Minister must sit in the House of Commons.a5:T57a,The President administers two oaths before the Prime Minister takes charge: the oath of office and the oath of secrecy. Both are in the same form as for any Union minister.

- **Oath of office** — faith and allegiance to the Constitution, upholding India's sovereignty and integrity, faithful discharge of duty, and fairness to all people according to the Constitution and law, free of fear, favour, affection or ill will.
- **Oath of secrecy** — not to reveal, directly or indirectly, any matter brought before or known to the Prime Minister as a Union minister, except as needed for official duty.

**Term.** The term is not fixed; the Prime Minister holds office during the pleasure of the President. That does not allow the President to dismiss the Prime Minister whenever he or she likes. While the Prime Minister commands a Lok Sabha majority, dismissal is not possible; once confidence is lost the Prime Minister must resign or can be dismissed. V. P. Singh (1990) and Deve Gowda (1997) resigned after losing votes in the Lok Sabha.

**Pay.** Parliament fixes the salary and allowances from time to time, under the Salaries and Allowances of Ministers Act, 1952. The Prime Minister draws what a member of Parliament receives, plus a sumptuary allowance, free housing, travel allowance and medical facilities. A 2001 amendment raised the sumptuary allowance from ₹1,500 to ₹3,000 a month.a6:T501,| Relation to | Powers and duties |
|---|---|
| The President | Principal channel of communication with the council (Article 78): conveys all council decisions on Union administration and legislative proposals; supplies whatever information the President asks for; if asked, places before the council a matter a single minister has decided but the council has not considered |
| The President (advice) | Advises on appointing the Attorney General, the Comptroller and Auditor General, the chairman and members of the UPSC, election commissioners, and the chairman and members of the Finance Commission |
| Parliament | Leader of the Lower House; advises on summoning and proroguing sessions; may recommend dissolution of the Lok Sabha at any time; announces government policy on the floor of the House |

**Other roles.** The Prime Minister chairs NITI Aayog (successor to the Planning Commission), the National Integration Council, the Inter-State Council, the National Water Resources Council and some other bodies. Beyond that, the office shapes foreign policy, acts as chief spokesman of the Union government, is crisis manager at the political level during emergencies, meets delegations from different states, leads the ruling party and is the political head of the services.a7:T569,The Constitution has no provision for a caretaker government; it is a situational arrangement and a practical necessity. The term is used for a council of ministers that has resigned, or whose house has been dissolved, and is asked to carry on until a successor takes over. Its main task is to hold free and fair elections.

Such a government is limited to routine administration. It should not announce major policy or start new schemes, except for national security or national interest.

- The Tarkunde Committee (1974–75), an unofficial electoral-reform body set up under Jayaprakash Narayan, said a caretaker government should not launch new policies, promise or begin projects, grant allowances, loans or pay rises, or hold official functions attended by ministers.
- In August 1979, while dissolving the Lok Sabha, President Reddy issued a communique recording the ministers' assurance of fair elections and no significant new policy or spending decisions, with urgent national-interest work excepted.
- The Calcutta High Court (December 1979) noted that the Constitution does not mention a caretaker government, but such an exceptional situation calls for one that only carries on day-to-day administration.
- Two reasons constrain a caretaker Prime Minister: the usual accountability to Parliament is missing, and the government must not use its position for electoral gain.a8:T458,Five Articles give the basic framework. Article 74 sets up the Council and makes it the President's adviser. Article 75 covers the appointment, tenure, responsibility, qualifications, oath and pay of ministers. Articles 77 and 78 deal with the conduct of government business and the Prime Minister's duties, and Article 88 defines what ministers may do in Parliament.

| Article | Subject | Core rule |
|---|---|---|
| 74 | Council of Ministers | A council headed by the Prime Minister aids and advises the President, who acts on that advice |
| 75 | Other provisions on ministers | Appointment, size, tenure, collective responsibility, oath and salary |
| 77 | Conduct of government business | Executive action runs in the President's name; the President frames rules for allocating business among ministers |
| 78 | Duties of the Prime Minister | Keep the President informed of Cabinet decisions and legislative proposals, and furnish information on request |
| 88 | Ministers and the Houses | A minister may speak in either House and its committees, but may vote only in the House to which he or she belongs |a9:T604,Before taking office, a minister takes two oaths, both administered by the President. The oath of office binds the minister to loyalty to the Constitution, to protecting India's sovereignty and integrity, to diligent service, and to treating all people fairly under the Constitution and the law. The oath of secrecy forbids disclosing matters that come to the minister's knowledge in office, except as the duties require.

In 1990 the appointment of Devi Lal as Deputy Prime Minister was challenged, since the Constitution mentions only the Prime Minister and ministers. The Supreme Court upheld his oath. It held that titles such as Deputy Prime Minister, minister of state or deputy minister are descriptive and confer no powers of the Prime Minister, so they do not affect the validity of the oath.

Parliament fixes ministers' salaries and allowances, under the Salaries and Allowances of Ministers Act of 1952. A minister receives the pay of a member of Parliament plus extra benefits such as a sumptuary allowance graded by rank, free accommodation, travel allowance and medical facilities.

The legal position is different from Britain's. There, the Crown's orders are countersigned by a minister, who can be sued if an order breaks the law, because the Crown can do no wrong. In India the Constitution contains no such system. A public act of the President need not be countersigned by a minister, and the courts cannot inquire into the advice ministers give the President. Responsibility in India is therefore political, not legal.aa:T684,Collective responsibility is the central principle of parliamentary government. The Council is answerable to the Lok Sabha as a single team, and the ministers rise or fall together. If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, every minister must resign, including those who sit in Rajya Sabha. The Council can also advise the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha and call fresh elections on the ground that it no longer reflects the electorate's views. The President is not bound to accept that advice once the Council has lost the Lok Sabha's confidence.

Cabinet decisions bind every minister, including those who dissented in the meeting. A minister must defend the decision inside and outside Parliament, and one who cannot must resign. Examples include Dr B.R. Ambedkar, who left over the Hindu Code Bill in 1953; C.D. Deshmukh, who left over the reorganisation of states; and Arif Mohammad Khan, who left over the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act of 1986. Ministers need not resign one by one when the Council falls, because the Prime Minister's resignation carries the whole Council with it.

Individual responsibility works through the President's pleasure. The President can remove a minister even while the Council enjoys Lok Sabha support, but acts only on the Prime Minister's advice. If a minister's performance or views diverge from the Prime Minister's, the Prime Minister can ask that minister to resign or advise the President to dismiss him or her. Ambedkar argued in the Constituent Assembly that collective responsibility depends on a Prime Minister holding such power, which is why the office matters to the system as a whole.ab:T602,The Council has three tiers. Cabinet ministers head the major ministries, such as home, defence, finance and external affairs, and attend Cabinet meetings. Ministers of state either hold independent charge of a ministry or are attached to a cabinet minister, and they work under that minister's overall responsibility. Deputy ministers have no independent charge; they assist cabinet ministers or ministers of state and are not in the Cabinet. A deputy Prime Minister is sometimes named, usually for political reasons. Parliamentary secretaries are a separate category: the Prime Minister, not the President, appoints them, they are outside the Council, and they have no department.

The words "Council of Ministers" and "Cabinet" are often used as if they meant the same thing. The table below separates them.

| Feature | Council of Ministers | Cabinet |
|---|---|---|
| Size | The wider body, with all three tiers | A smaller body of cabinet ministers only |
| Meetings | Does not meet as a body to transact business | Meets regularly, usually about once a week |
| Powers | Holds all powers, but only in theory | Exercises those powers in practice and acts for the Council |
| Constitutional basis | Articles 74 and 75; size left to the Prime Minister within the 15 per cent limit | Not in the original text; the 1978 insertion in Article 352 defines it for emergency purposes but says nothing about its powers |
| Relationship with the Lok Sabha | Collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha | Enforces that collective responsibility |ac:T530,The Cabinet is the highest decision-making authority in the formal system. It formulates the central government's chief policies, supplies its supreme executive direction, coordinates the central administration, and handles emergencies. It also settles major legislative and financial matters, foreign affairs, and senior appointments such as those to constitutional bodies and the top secretariat posts. Commentators have long described the Cabinet as the centre that drives the state, and Ramsay Muir went further for Britain, calling the Cabinet a dictatorship limited only by publicity. The chapter treats that description as applying equally to India.

Beneath the formal Cabinet lies an informal inner circle, often called the "Inner Cabinet" or "Kitchen Cabinet". It consists of the Prime Minister and a few trusted colleagues, and sometimes outsiders such as friends or family. Its advantages are speed, a small group that can meet often, and secrecy on sensitive political questions. Its drawbacks are that it weakens the Cabinet as the highest decision-making body and that it lets people with no formal role influence government, bypassing the legal process. Every Indian Prime Minister has had such a circle, and it was especially powerful under Indira Gandhi. Similar circles exist in the United States and Britain.ad:T75a,Cabinet committees are extra-constitutional. The Constitution does not mention them, but the Rules of Business provide for them. They come in two kinds. Standing committees are permanent, while ad hoc committees are formed for a special problem and disbanded once it is solved. The Emergency Committee formed in 1962 after the Chinese invasion is the usual example of the second kind. The Prime Minister sets up committees as needed, so their number, names and membership change over time. Membership usually consists of cabinet ministers, though non-cabinet ministers can be members or attend as special invitees. The Prime Minister usually chairs the committee, and if he or she is a member, presides over it by necessity. Committees both prepare proposals and take decisions, although the full Cabinet can review what they decide. Their purpose is to lighten the Cabinet's workload, allow closer examination of policy, and improve coordination.

The chapter lists eight functioning committees:

| Committee | Remit |
|---|---|
| Political Affairs | Domestic and foreign policy; the most powerful of the committees, often called the "Super-Cabinet" |
| Economic Affairs | Directs and coordinates government activity in the economic field |
| Appointments Committee of the Cabinet | Higher appointments in the Central Secretariat, public enterprises, banks and financial institutions |
| Parliamentary Affairs | Progress of government business in Parliament |

| Accommodation | Allotment of government housing to MPs, central government employees and other persons and organisations |
| Investment and Growth | Capital inflows, export promotion, import substitution and ease of doing business |
| Employment and Skill Development | Skill building, employability and women's participation in the workforce |ae:T503,- Articles 74 and 75 set up the Council of Ministers; Articles 77, 78 and 88 cover business, the Prime Minister's duties and ministers' rights in Parliament.
- Advice to the President became binding through the 42nd Amendment (1976), and the 44th Amendment (1978) allowed one reconsideration.
- The President appoints the Prime Minister, and other ministers on the Prime Minister's advice; a non-member must get into a House within six months.
- The 91st Amendment (2003) capped the Council at 15 per cent of Lok Sabha strength and barred defectors from appointment.
- Ministers hold office at the President's pleasure, but the President acts only on the Prime Minister's advice.
- The Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; a no-confidence motion removes all ministers, including those in Rajya Sabha.
- India has no system of ministerial legal responsibility, and courts cannot inquire into ministers' advice.
- The Cabinet is the smaller, practical centre of power; the eight functioning committees do much of its detailed work.

- Groups of Ministers are ad hoc, and the Second ARC wanted them used selectively and with time limits.af:T833,Under Article 79, Parliament has three parts: the **President**, the **Council of States** and the **House of the People** (Hindi names Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha adopted in 1954). The President sits in neither House yet is integral to Parliament: no bill becomes law without assent, and the President summons and prorogues the Houses, dissolves the Lok Sabha, addresses them and issues ordinances during recess. This copies Britain's "Crown-in-Parliament"; the American President, by contrast, is no part of Congress.

| | Rajya Sabha | Lok Sabha |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum strength | 250 (238 from states and UTs + 12 nominated) | 550 (530 from states + 20 from UTs) |
| Present strength | 245 (225 states, 8 UTs, 12 nominated) | 543 (524 states, 19 UTs) |
| How chosen | Elected MLAs vote by proportional representation with single transferable vote (STV) | Direct election by adult voters in territorial constituencies |
| Term | Permanent; one-third retire every second year; six-year member terms | Five years from its first meeting, unless dissolved earlier |

Rajya Sabha seats follow population (Fourth Schedule), so Uttar Pradesh has 31 and Tripura one, unlike the two-per-state US Senate. Only three UTs (Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir) are represented there. The 12 nominees bring expertise in art, literature, science and social service without facing election. **Odisha** holds 10 Rajya Sabha and 21 Lok Sabha seats (3 reserved for SCs, 5 for STs).

The **61st Amendment (1988)** lowered the voting age from 21 to 18. Nomination of two Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha, last extended to 2020 by the 95th Amendment, was not renewed by the **104th Amendment (2019)** and lapsed on 25 January 2020.

The six-year Rajya Sabha term comes from the Representation of the People Act, 1951, not the Constitution; lots decided who in the first batch (1952) retired early. The President may dissolve the Lok Sabha before five years, and no court can question it. During a national emergency its life can be extended by law one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the emergency ends.b0:T4fc,Representation is kept uniform twice over: each state gets seats in proportion to population (states under six million excepted), and each state's constituencies carry roughly equal populations. Both are to be readjusted after every census by an authority Parliament sets up; Delimitation Commission Acts came in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002.

| Amendment | Effect |
|---|---|
| 42nd (1976) | Froze seat allocation and boundaries at the 1971 level till 2000 |
| 84th (2001) | Freeze extended to 2026; boundaries and reserved seats may be redrawn on 1991 figures |
| 87th (2003) | That redrawing to use the 2001 census, without changing seats per state |
| 104th (2019) | SC/ST reservation in the Lok Sabha extended to 2030 |

Reserved SC/ST seats are elected by all voters of the constituency; there is no separate electorate, and SC/ST candidates may also contest general seats.

The Lok Sabha uses **first-past-the-post** in single-member constituencies, which can under-represent minorities. India uses STV for the Rajya Sabha, legislative councils, and presidential and vice-presidential elections, but rejected it for the Lok Sabha: it is hard for voters to follow and tends to fragment parties. It is also costly, rules out by-elections and weakens the voter–member link.b1:T820,| | Constitution | Representation of the People Act, 1951 |
|---|---|---|
| Qualifications | Citizen; oath before a person authorised by the Election Commission; age **30** (Rajya Sabha) or **25** (Lok Sabha) | Registered elector in a parliamentary constituency; SC/ST to contest a reserved seat |
| Disqualifications | Office of profit (ministers and exempted posts excepted); unsound mind declared by a court; undischarged insolvent; foreign citizenship or allegiance | Corrupt practices; a sentence of two years or more (preventive detention excluded); unfiled election accounts; government contracts; office in a corporation with 25% government stake; dismissal for corruption; social crimes such as dowry or sati |

Since 2003 a Rajya Sabha candidate need not be an elector of the state concerned; the Supreme Court upheld this in 2006. The **President** decides disqualification disputes, acting on the **Election Commission's** opinion.

Under the **Tenth Schedule**, a member is unseated for leaving the party voluntarily, defying its whip, joining a party after winning as an independent, or (if nominated) joining one after six months. The **Speaker or Chairman** decides these cases, and the **Kihoto Hollohan** judgment (1992) made that decision reviewable by courts.

Seats are also vacated by:

- **double membership** — a person elected to both Houses has 10 days to choose, or loses the Rajya Sabha seat; one also elected to a state legislature loses the parliamentary seat unless the state seat is given up within 14 days;
- **resignation**, effective when the presiding officer accepts it as genuine;
- **absence** from every sitting for 60 days without leave;
- a void election, expulsion, or becoming President, Vice-President or Governor.

When a disqualified person wins, the 1951 Act lets the **High Court** void the election, with appeal to the Supreme Court. No member may vote or claim privileges before the oath; sitting without it costs ₹500 a day. Salaries are set by Parliament; a pension came in 1976, and in 2018 pay became ₹1,00,000 a month.b2:Ta45,The **Speaker** is chosen by the Lok Sabha from its members on a date the President fixes, and does not vacate office on dissolution, staying until the new House meets. Removal needs a resolution backed by a majority of all the then members, after 14 days' notice and with at least 50 members supporting its consideration; during that debate the Speaker cannot preside but may speak and vote in the first instance.

The Speaker's powers come from the Constitution, the Lok Sabha's rules and convention. The Speaker keeps order, is the final interpreter of rules and precedent within the House, adjourns for want of quorum, casts a vote only on a tie, presides at **joint sittings**, may allow a secret sitting, certifies **money bills** with final effect, decides **defection** cases, and chairs the Business Advisory, Rules and General Purposes Committees. Independence rests on removal only by effective majority, pay charged on the Consolidated Fund, protection from criticism except on a substantive motion, and seventh rank in precedence beside the Chief Justice. Unlike Britain, the Speaker does not resign from the party.

| Office | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Deputy Speaker | Elected after the Speaker on a date the Speaker fixes; not subordinate to the Speaker; heads any committee joined; often from the opposition |
| Panel of chairpersons | Up to ten named by the Speaker; cannot preside if the offices are **vacant** (a member appointed by the President acts) |
| Speaker pro tem | Named by the President, usually the senior-most member; swears in members and conducts the Speaker's election |
| Chairman, Rajya Sabha | The Vice-President ex officio; not a member of the House; cannot vote while own removal is debated; no Chairman's pay while acting as President |
| Deputy Chairman | Elected by the Rajya Sabha; acts when the chair is vacant or the Vice-President acts as President |

The Chairman lacks two Speaker powers: certifying money bills and presiding at joint sittings. The offices began in 1921 as President and Deputy President of the Central Legislative Assembly; **Vithalbhai J. Patel** (1925) was the first Indian and elected holder. **G. V. Mavalankar** and **Ananthasayanam Ayyangar** were the first Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

The **Leader of the House** is the Prime Minister if in the Lok Sabha, or a nominated minister. A Leader of the Opposition was first recognised in 1969 and given statutory status in 1977; recognition needs one-tenth of the House. **Whips** rest purely on convention; the government's chief whip is the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs in the Lok Sabha.b3:T5a7,The President summons the Houses, and the gap between sessions cannot exceed **six months**. Usually there are three: Budget (February–May), Monsoon (July–September) and Winter (November–December).

| | Adjournment | Prorogation | Dissolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| By | Presiding officer | President | President, or expiry |
| Ends | A sitting | The session | The Lok Sabha itself |
| Pending bills | Survive | Survive (notices lapse) | Mostly lapse |

On dissolution, a bill lapses if pending in the Lok Sabha or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha. It survives if pending only in the Rajya Sabha, if a joint sitting was notified before dissolution, or if it awaits the President's assent or has come back from the President for reconsideration.

**Quorum** is one-tenth including the presiding officer: 55 in the Lok Sabha, 25 in the Rajya Sabha. Decisions go by majority of those present and voting, the presiding officer having only a casting vote. Divisions use the automatic recorder, "Aye"/"No" slips, or (now obsolete) lobbies. Business is in Hindi or English, with interpretation from Eighth Schedule languages; the Official Languages Act, 1963 kept English after 1965. **Ministers and the Attorney General** may speak in either House, at joint sittings and in their committees, but that right carries no vote. A **lame-duck session** is one held by an outgoing Lok Sabha after its successor is elected, as in 1957 and 1962.b4:T677,**Question hour** opens each sitting. Starred questions get oral answers with supplementaries; unstarred ones get written answers without; short-notice questions, on under ten days' notice, are answered orally. **Zero hour**, which follows, is not in the rules; it is an Indian innovation dating from 1962.

Closure motions end debate: simple, by compartments, **kangaroo** (only key clauses debated) and **guillotine** (leftover clauses voted when time expires).

| Device | Point to remember |
|---|---|
| Calling attention | Seeks a minister's statement on an urgent matter; Indian innovation of 1954, and in the rules |
| Adjournment motion | Interrupts business for a definite, urgent, recent matter; needs 50 members; implies censure, so **not used in the Rajya Sabha**; debate at least 2½ hours |
| No-confidence motion | Tests the ministry's majority (Art. 75); needs 50 members |
| Motion of thanks | On the President's address; defeat means defeat of the government |
| Point of order | Raised when rules are breached; suspends proceedings, no debate |
| Half-an-hour / short duration discussion | No formal motion or vote; up to three and two days a week respectively |
| Special mention | Rajya Sabha residual device; Lok Sabha's version is Rule 377 |

| Censure motion | No-confidence motion |
|---|---|
| Must state reasons | Needs no reasons |
| Against one minister, several or all | Against the whole council only |
| Ministry need not resign | Ministry must resign |

A **resolution** is always a substantive motion; private members' resolutions are taken on alternate Fridays, and statutory ones arise under the Constitution or an Act.b5:T9d0,Government (public) bills are moved by ministers on seven days' notice, and their defeat may topple the ministry; private members' bills need a month's notice and their defeat changes nothing. An **ordinary bill** goes through a **first reading** (introduction, no debate), a **second reading** (general discussion, committee stage, clause-by-clause consideration — the decisive stage), a **third reading** (accept or reject the whole, no amendments), the same steps in the **other House**, and **assent**. The President may assent, withhold assent, or return the bill once; if repassed, assent must follow, so the veto is only suspensive.

A **money bill** (Article 110) deals *only* with taxation, Union borrowing, the Consolidated and Contingency Funds, appropriation, charged expenditure, receipts and audit. Fines, licence or service fees and local taxes do not make a bill a money bill. The **Speaker's** certificate on this is final against courts, both Houses and the President.

| | Ordinary bill | Money bill |
|---|---|---|
| Introduced | Either House, by any member | Lok Sabha only, by a minister, on the President's recommendation |
| Rajya Sabha | Can amend or reject; may hold it six months | Only recommends; must return within **14 days** |
| Deadlock | Joint sitting possible | Not possible |
| President | Assent, withhold or return | Assent or withhold; cannot return |

Every money bill is a financial bill, but not vice versa. A **financial bill (I)** (Art. 117(1)) mixes Article 110 matters with general law; like a money bill it starts only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation, but the Rajya Sabha may amend or reject it. A **financial bill (II)** (Art. 117(3)) involves spending from the Consolidated Fund with no Article 110 matter; it can start in either House, and the President's recommendation is needed at the **consideration** stage, not introduction.

A **joint sitting** (Article 108) settles deadlock on ordinary or financial bills — when the other House rejects a bill, final disagreement on amendments persists, or six months pass — never on money or amendment bills. It cannot be held on a bill that has lapsed, though one notified before dissolution survives. The **Speaker** presides, then the Deputy Speaker, then the Deputy Chairman; the Chairman never does. Lok Sabha rules apply and a simple majority passes the bill. Only three: **Dowry Prohibition (1960)**, **Banking Service Commission (Repeal) (1977)** and **Prevention of Terrorism (2002)**.b6:T963,The Constitution never says "budget"; Article 112 calls it the **annual financial statement** for the year 1 April–31 March. The railway budget, separated in 1924 after the Acworth Committee, was merged back in **2017**.

| Article | Rule |
|---|---|
| 112 | Statement laid before both Houses; charged and voted spending shown apart |
| 113 | Demands only on the President's recommendation; only the Lok Sabha votes them and may cut but not raise them; charged items discussed, not voted |
| 114 | No withdrawal without an appropriation law |
| 116 | Vote on account, vote of credit, exceptional grants |
| 117 | Tax bills only on the President's recommendation and never in the Rajya Sabha |
| 265 | No tax without authority of law |

**Charged expenditure** includes the President's emoluments; pay of the presiding officers of both Houses; Supreme Court judges' salaries and pensions; High Court judges' **pensions**; the CAG and UPSC; debt charges; and court decrees.

The budget passes in six stages: presentation (on **1 February** since 2017, with no debate that day), general discussion (no cut motions or vote), scrutiny by the **24 departmental standing committees**, Lok Sabha voting on demands, the appropriation bill, and the finance bill. **Cut motions** come in three forms: policy cut (demand reduced to ₹1), economy cut (a specified sum) and token cut (₹100, to air a grievance). On the last day the Speaker puts all remaining demands to vote together — the **guillotine**.

A **vote on account**, usually two months' spending at about one-sixth of the total, bridges the gap until the Appropriation Act; it now accompanies the interim budget of an election year. Under the 1931 Provisional Collection of Taxes Act the finance bill must be enacted within **75 days**.

Other grants: **supplementary** (voted sum falls short), **additional** (new service), **excess** (overspending, voted after the year once the **Public Accounts Committee** approves), **vote of credit** (a "blank cheque" for an unforeseen demand), **exceptional** and **token** (funded by reappropriation).

The **Consolidated Fund** (Art. 266) takes all revenue and loans and needs a law for withdrawals; the **Public Account** (Art. 266) holds deposits and is run by executive action; the **Contingency Fund** (Art. 267) is at the President's disposal for unforeseen spending, held by the finance secretary.b7:T4ab,Privileges protect each House, its committees and members, and extend to ministers and the Attorney General, but **not to the President**.

| Collective | Individual |
|---|---|
| Publish proceedings and bar others (the 44th Amendment let the press publish true reports, except of secret sittings) | No arrest during a session and 40 days either side — **civil** cases only |
| Secret sittings; own rules; punish breach or contempt | Freedom of speech in the House and its committees |
| No court inquiry into proceedings; no arrest within the precincts without the presiding officer's leave | Exemption from jury service and from testifying during a session |

Every breach of privilege is a contempt, but not every contempt is a breach. Article 105 first linked unlisted privileges to the British House of Commons; the 44th Amendment (1978) dropped that reference without changing substance. Privileges remain uncodified.

India's Parliament is not sovereign in Dicey's British sense. It is bound by a **written Constitution**, the **federal** division of powers, **judicial review**, and justiciable **Fundamental Rights** under Article 13 — closer to the US Congress than to Westminster.b8:Ta8e,Three standing committees handle public money. They have much in common: each is elected every year from among MPs by proportional representation through the single transferable vote, each has a one-year term, and a minister cannot be a member of any of them. The table compares their main features.

| Feature | Public Accounts Committee | Estimates Committee | Committee on Public Undertakings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Origin | First set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act of 1919 | First post-independence committee formed in 1950 on the recommendation of John Mathai | Created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee |
| Members | 22 (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha) | 30, all from the Lok Sabha | 22 (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha) after 1974 |
| Chairman | Chosen from among members by the Speaker; since 1967 by convention from the Opposition | Appointed by the Speaker; generally from the ruling party | Appointed by the Speaker from among members |

The Public Accounts Committee is the most important of the three. It examines the CAG's three audit reports on appropriation accounts, finance accounts and public undertakings. It looks beyond legal compliance to economy, prudence and propriety, and it aims to expose waste, loss, extravagance and corruption. The CAG works closely with it as an adviser. Because the Committee studies expenditure already incurred, it cannot intervene in day-to-day administration, cannot disallow expenditure, and cannot issue orders. Only Parliament can decide on its findings.

The Estimates Committee is often called a continuous economy committee, because it suggests ways to achieve economy, efficiency and administrative reform within the policy behind the estimates. It may suggest alternative policies, but it cannot question the policy Parliament has laid down. It has no CAG-style expert support, and it covers a rotating set of ministries each year.

The Committee on Public Undertakings examines the business of public enterprises from the standpoint of autonomy and efficiency, asking whether they are run on sound business and commercial lines. It may not look into major government policy, day-to-day administration, or matters that a special statute reserves to a machinery of its own. Its members are not technical experts, which limits its reach.b9:T8c8,Seventeen Department-Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) were set up in 1993 on the recommendation of the Rules Committee of the Lok Sabha. Seven more followed in 2004, bringing the total to 24. Their main aim is to make the executive, the Council of Ministers, more accountable to Parliament, especially in financial matters, and to help Parliament debate the budget more effectively. Together the 24 committees cover every ministry and department of the Central government. Eight are attached to Rajya Sabha and sixteen to the Lok Sabha.

Each DRSC has 31 members, 21 from the Lok Sabha nominated by the Speaker and 10 from the Rajya Sabha nominated by the Chairman. A minister cannot be nominated. If a member is appointed a minister later, that person stops being a member of the committee. The term is one year from the date of constitution.

Their functions are four. They consider the demands for grants of the ministries they cover before the House votes on them, but their reports may not suggest cut motions. They examine bills referred to them. They consider the annual reports of ministries. And they consider long-term national policy documents placed before the Houses. They must not take up day-to-day administration, and they should not generally take up matters already before another parliamentary committee. Their recommendations are advisory.

The procedure for demands for grants is fixed. After the general budget debate, the Houses adjourn for a set period. The committees consider the demands during that period, report within it without seeking more time, and produce a separate report for each ministry. For bills, a committee considers the general principles and the clauses of a bill that has been introduced and referred to it.

The chapter lists several merits of the system. Its proceedings are free of party bias, its procedure is more flexible than the House's, and it gives parliamentary control a closer and more continuous character. It allows members to learn how government works, lets committees call experts and public opinion, and gives opposition parties and Rajya Sabha a larger role in financial control. Ministries within the DRSCs' purview have largely accepted their recommendations and acted on them.ba:T6e6,Several standing committees check the conduct of members and the executive. It maintains the link between India's Parliament and the parliaments of the world, through exchanges of delegations, goodwill missions, correspondence and documents. It works in two capacities: as India's National Group of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) and as the principal Indian branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association (CPA).

Membership is open to every MP. Former MPs can join as associate members, but associates have limited rights. They cannot be represented at IPU and CPA meetings and conferences, and they do not get the travel concessions some CPA branches offer to members. A member or former member can also become a life member on payment of a fixed life subscription.

The presidency of the IPG goes by office to the Lok Sabha's presiding officer. Two vice-presidencies follow automatically: one for the Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker and one for the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman. The Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha also serves ex officio as the group's Secretary-General. The Rajya Sabha Chairman, that is, the Vice-President of India, does not hold the presidency of the IPG.

Its stated aims are to promote personal contact among Indian MPs, to study issues likely to come before Parliament through seminars and publications, to arrange lectures by MPs and eminent persons on political, defence, economic, social and educational problems, and to arrange visits abroad to build contacts with other parliaments. It arranges addresses by visiting heads of state and government, publishes a quarterly newsletter, and since 1995 has given an annual Outstanding Parliamentarian award, whose nominations are finalised by a five-member committee set up by the Speaker. Only members who have been in the IPG for at least six months at the time of forming a delegation may be included in an Indian parliamentary delegation abroad.bd:T50f,The Inter-Parliamentary Union is an international body of sovereign parliaments, which at present numbers 179. IPG members have also held office in IPU bodies, such as committees, rapporteurships and drafting committees, which lets India press its views in IPU meetings.

The Commonwealth Parliamentary Association counts roughly 17,000 legislators and staff, who sit in some 180 bodies at national, state, provincial and territorial level across 53 Commonwealth countries. Its aim is to deepen knowledge of parliamentary democracy and to promote cooperation among its members.
