Judges are appointed by the President. For the Chief Justice, the President consults such Supreme Court and high court judges as are considered necessary. For every other judge, consulting the Chief Justice is compulsory, along with other judges as needed. What "consultation" really means has been settled by a series of Supreme Court rulings, called the Judges cases.

| Case | Year | What it held |
|---|---|---|
| First Judges case (S.P. Gupta) | 1981 | Consultation is only an exchange of views, not concurrence |
| Second Judges case (Advocates-on-Record Association) | 1993 | Consultation means concurrence; the CJI's advice binds the President, after consulting two senior colleagues; the senior-most judge must become CJI |
| Third Judges case (Presidential Reference) | 1998 | The CJI must consult a collegium of the four senior-most judges; a recommendation made without proper consultation does not bind the government |
| Fourth Judges case | 2015 | The 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act were struck down as hurting judicial independence; the collegium returned |

The 99th Amendment (2014) and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act (2014) had tried to replace the collegium with a commission (Articles 124A to 124C). The 2015 verdict voided both. On the top post, the convention of promoting the senior-most judge held from 1950 to 1973, when A.N. Ray was chosen over three seniors (Shelat, Hegde, Grover) who had decided Kesavananda Bharati against the government; they resigned. In 1977 M.U. Beg was preferred over H.R. Khanna. The 1993 ruling closed this discretion.c0:T4c2,Only the President can remove a judge, and only after both Houses, in the same session, pass an address supported by a special majority: a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two-thirds of those present and voting. There are two grounds, proved misbehaviour and incapacity. The word "impeachment" is not used in the Constitution for judges; it appears only for the President, though it is commonly used for judges too.

The Judges Enquiry Act, 1968 lays down the steps:

1. A notice of motion signed by 100 Lok Sabha members or 50 Rajya Sabha members goes to the Speaker or Chairman.
2. The presiding officer may admit or reject it.
3. If admitted, a three-member committee investigates: a Supreme Court judge (or the CJI), a high court Chief Justice and a distinguished jurist.
4. If the committee finds guilt or incapacity, the House may take up the motion.
5. After passage by special majority in each House, the address goes to the President, who orders removal.

No Supreme Court judge has ever been removed. The first case was that of Justice V. Ramaswami (1991–1993). The committee held him guilty of misbehaviour, but the motion failed in the Lok Sabha because the Congress abstained.c1:T443,| Arrangement | Article | Who appoints | Condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acting Chief Justice | 126 | President | CJI post vacant, or CJI absent or unable to work |
| Ad hoc judge | 127 | CJI, after consulting the high court's Chief Justice and with the President's prior consent | Quorum of permanent judges is lacking; the person must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge |
| Retired judge | 128 | CJI, with the consent of the President and of the person | Retired Supreme Court or qualified high court judge sits for a limited period; enjoys the powers of a judge but is not otherwise treated as one |

Delhi is the seat of the Court, but the CJI, with presidential approval, may name other places. This is a discretionary power, so no court can direct that it be used. With the President's approval the Court frames its own rules of procedure. Constitutional cases and Article 143 references go to a bench of at least five judges; other matters are heard by single judges or division benches. Judgments are delivered in open court, by majority, and dissenting opinions are permitted.c2:T4d3,As guardian of the Constitution and protector of fundamental rights, the Court must be shielded from pressure by the executive and the legislature. The Constitution does so through the following safeguards.

- **Mode of appointment:** the executive acts only after consulting the judiciary itself.
- **Security of tenure:** removal only by the prescribed process and grounds, so judges do not serve at the President's pleasure.
- **Fixed service conditions:** pay and privileges cannot be reduced, save in a financial emergency.
- **Charged expenditure:** salaries, pensions and administrative costs fall on the Consolidated Fund of India, so Parliament may discuss but not vote on them.
- **No discussion of conduct:** neither Parliament nor a state legislature may debate a judge's conduct, except during a removal motion.
- **Ban on post-retirement practice:** retired judges cannot plead before any court or authority in India.
- **Contempt power:** the Court can punish those who lower its authority.
- **Own staff:** the CJI appoints officers and servants and fixes their service conditions without executive interference.
- **Protected jurisdiction:** Parliament cannot cut down the Court's jurisdiction, though it may widen it.c3:T7ac,Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar of the Drafting Committee remarked that no other Supreme Court in the world has more powers.

**Original jurisdiction (Article 131).** It is exclusive in disputes between the Centre and states, or among states. Exclusive means no other court may hear the dispute, and original means it is heard first, not on appeal. The dispute must involve a legal right, so purely political questions are out, and a private person cannot sue the Centre or a state under this head. Four matters fall outside it: disputes arising from pre-Constitution treaties, agreements and sanads that still operate (or that bar the jurisdiction), inter-state river water disputes (under the 1956 Act), matters sent to the Finance Commission, and certain adjustments of expenses and pensions between the Centre and states. The first suit (1961) was West Bengal's challenge to the Coal Bearing Areas Act of 1957, which the Court dismissed.

**Writ jurisdiction (Article 32).** Any citizen whose fundamental rights are violated may go straight to the Supreme Court for habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto or certiorari. This power is shared with high courts, so it is concurrent, unlike the exclusive federal jurisdiction. The Supreme Court issues writs only for fundamental rights, while a high court can do so for other purposes as well, so the high court's writ power is wider. Parliament may extend the Supreme Court's writ power to other purposes.

**Advisory jurisdiction (Article 143).** The President may refer two kinds of matter. For a question of law or fact of public importance, the Court may decline to answer. For a dispute arising from a pre-Constitution treaty or sanad, it must answer. Either way, the opinion is advisory and does not bind the President. Fifteen references have been made so far, from the Delhi Laws Act (1951) to the 2G spectrum matter (2012); others include Berubari Union (1960) and the Rama Janma Bhumi case (1993).c4:Ta69,The Court mainly hears appeals from high courts, under four heads.

| Head | When an appeal lies |
|---|---|
| Constitutional | High court certifies that a substantial question of law on interpreting the Constitution is involved |
| Civil | High court certifies a substantial question of law of general importance that the Supreme Court should decide. The old ₹20,000 money limit went in 1972 (30th Amendment) |
| Criminal | As of right, without certificate, where the high court reversed an acquittal and awarded death, or took a case to itself and imposed death; the 1970 law added life imprisonment or ten years. Otherwise on a high court certificate. No appeal as of right if the high court reversed a conviction and acquitted |
| Special leave (Article 136) | Discretionary leave against any judgment of any court or tribunal except a military one; may be sought against interim or final orders, in any kind of matter |

**Court of record (Article 129).** Its proceedings are preserved as evidence and precedent, and it can punish contempt, including contempt of high courts, subordinate courts and tribunals (as held in 1991). The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, drawn from the H.N. Sanyal committee (1963), divides contempt into civil (wilful disobedience of orders) and criminal (scandalising the court, prejudicing proceedings, obstructing justice). Fair criticism, innocent publication and fair reports are not contempt. Punishment is up to six months' simple imprisonment, a fine up to ₹2,000, or both, and proceedings must begin within a year. Village courts such as Nyaya Panchayats lie outside the Act.

**Judicial review.** The Court can declare Central and state laws and executive orders invalid if they violate the Constitution.

**Review and curative petitions (Article 137).** A review petition is filed within thirty days before the same bench, on grounds such as new evidence, an error on the face of the record or any sufficient reason. Even after dismissal, a curative petition is possible on narrow grounds such as breach of natural justice, a gross miscarriage of justice, abuse of process or bias.

**Other powers.** The Court alone decides disputes over the election of the President and Vice-President. On a presidential reference it inquires into misbehaviour by the UPSC chairman and members or their state counterparts, and its advice binds the President. It may withdraw cases from high courts or transfer them between high courts, its law binds all courts (Article 141), and it supervises all courts and tribunals. Parliament can enlarge its powers on Union List matters, and the Centre and states can do so by special agreement.c5:T552,Judicial review means that courts can examine the constitutionality of legislation and of executive orders, whether made by the Centre or by a state. A provision found to be ultra vires, that is, beyond constitutional power, is declared illegal and void. Once it is struck down, the government cannot enforce it.

Justice Syed Shah Mohamed Quadri classified judicial review into three categories:

| Category | What is reviewed |
|---|---|
| Constitutional amendments | Whether an amendment itself respects the Constitution's basic features |
| Legislation and subordinate legislation | Laws of Parliament and of state legislatures, along with rules and regulations made under them |
| Administrative action | Decisions and orders of the Union, state governments and other authorities |

The Supreme Court's landmark rulings show the range of the power. In the Golaknath case (1967) the Court considered whether Parliament could amend the Fundamental Rights. The Bank Nationalisation case (1970) and the Privy Purses case (1970) tested government measures against property and other rights. The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) established the basic structure doctrine, and the Minerva Mills case (1980) applied it. In 2015 the Court declared the 99th Constitutional Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014 unconstitutional and void.c6:T596,The phrase "judicial review" does not appear in the Constitution, but many articles confer the power. They fall into three groups.

| Group | Articles | What they provide |
|---|---|---|
| Fundamental Rights | 13, 32, 226 | Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void (Art. 13); the Supreme Court enforces Fundamental Rights through writs (Art. 32); the High Courts may issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose (Art. 226) |
| Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court | 131 to 136, 143 | Original jurisdiction in centre-state and inter-state disputes (131); appeals in constitutional, civil and criminal cases (132 to 134); the certificate for appeal from High Courts (134A, added in 1978); jurisdiction under pre-constitution law (135); special leave to appeal (136); advisory opinion of the President's reference (143) |
| High Court superintendence | 227 | Superintendence over all courts and tribunals within the High Court's territory, except military courts |
| Division of powers | 245, 246, 251, 254, 372 | Territorial extent and subject matter of laws, with the Union, State and Concurrent Lists; central law prevails in conflict with state law; pre-constitution laws continue in force (372) |

Three points are often tested. Article 32 covers only Fundamental Rights, while Article 226 is wider. Article 136 excludes military tribunals and courts martial. Article 227 excludes military courts as well.c7:T4a6,A law or executive order may be challenged in the Supreme Court or a High Court on three grounds. It may infringe a Fundamental Right in Part III. It may lie outside the competence of the authority that made it. Or it may be repugnant to a constitutional provision.

The scope of judicial review in India is narrower than in the United States. The American Constitution contains a due process clause, which allows courts to strike down laws both for substance and for unreasonableness of procedure. The Indian Constitution uses "procedure established by law", and the Supreme Court asks only whether the authority acted within its powers. It does not ask whether the law is reasonable, suitable or wise as policy. Critics of the American system have called its court a third chamber of the legislature, or a super-legislature.

India follows neither model fully. It has borrowed American judicial supremacy, but only to a limited extent, and it does not accept British parliamentary supremacy either. Parliament's sovereignty is limited by a written Constitution, federalism with a division of powers, Fundamental Rights and judicial review. The result is a synthesis of the two principles.c8:T7a8,Article 31B, added with the Ninth Schedule by the First Amendment Act of 1951, protects the laws listed in that schedule from challenge on the ground that they violate Fundamental Rights. When the schedule began it held 13 laws. It now holds 282. Most of the state laws deal with land reform and the abolition of zamindari, while the central laws cover other matters.

The protection was progressively narrowed by the courts:

- **Kesavananda Bharati (1973):** laws in the Ninth Schedule remain open to challenge if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution.
- **Waman Rao (1980):** laws placed in the schedule after 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda judgment, survive only if they do not damage the basic structure.
- **I.R. Coelho (2007):** there is no blanket immunity. Laws added after 24 April 1973 can be challenged if they violate Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21, or the basic structure. A law is tested by the direct impact and effect test, sometimes called the rights test. Under it, the form of the amendment matters less than what it does to rights.

Coelho also held that a law already upheld cannot be challenged again on the same principles, and that transactions completed under such a law cannot be reopened. A law struck down for violating Part III, if later added to the schedule, can still be challenged.

The schedule has grown in stages, and Table 27.1 summarises the additions:

| Period | Amendments and totals |
|---|---|
| Before 24 April 1973 | First (1951): 13 laws; Fourth (1955): 7; Seventh (1964): 44; Twenty-Ninth (1972): 2. Total 66 |
| After 24 April 1973 | Thirty-Fourth (1974): 20; Thirty-Ninth (1975): 38; Fortieth (1976): 64; Forty-Seventh (1984): 14; Sixty-Sixth (1990): 55; Seventy-Sixth (1994): 1; Seventy-Eighth (1995): 27. Total 219 |
| Overall | Entries numbered up to 284, but three entries (87, 92 and 130) were dropped and one was numbered 257A, so the actual count is 282 |c9:T50e,- The Constitution confers judicial review; the phrase itself does not appear in it, and the basic structure doctrine protects it from amendment.
- Judicial review is the power to declare laws and executive orders of the Centre and states void if they are ultra vires.
- Quadri's three categories: amendments, legislation and subordinate legislation, and administrative action.
- Three grounds: violation of Part III, lack of competence, and repugnancy to constitutional provisions.
- Article 13 voids inconsistent laws; Article 32 gives Supreme Court writs for Fundamental Rights; Article 226 gives High Court writs for those rights and any other purpose.
- Indian courts ask whether a law is within the authority's power, not whether it is reasonable; this is narrower than the American due process approach.
- India's position is a synthesis of American judicial supremacy and British parliamentary supremacy, limited by the written Constitution and federalism.
- Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule came in by the First Amendment (1951), and the schedule now holds 282 laws.

Since the mid-twentieth century, a version of judicial review has been nicknamed judicial activism, especially in the United States. The table separates the two:

| Point | Judicial review | Judicial activism |
|---|---|---|
| Core task | Tests a law against constitutional parameters, then upholds or strikes it down | Reshapes the law to suit changing social and economic conditions |
| Purpose | Keeps the law within the Constitution | Makes the Constitution's ideals real in practice |
| Judge's role | Interprets | Takes part in policymaking and brings personal policy preferences in |
| Typical tool | Ruling on validity | Directions to authorities and expanded standing |

The chapter adds a useful caution. At its broadest, activism covers any occasion on which a court strikes down a validly enacted law, so critics often say the terms are mixed up. Where the expansion comes from PIL, the widened standing has pushed the court's jurisdiction further than before, and critics use the word activism for that enlarged role.cb:T4ca,Dr B.L. Wadehra lists several causes. When the legislature and the executive fail to discharge their duties, public confidence in the Constitution and in democracy wears away, and citizens look to the courts for protection. Judges who welcome social reform are willing to widen PIL and loosen the rules on locus standi. Where the legislature has not legislated, the court may fill the gap. The Constitution itself gives the judiciary room to play an active role.

Subhash Kashyap describes situations in which the courts may have to cross into the field of the other organs. These include a legislature that does not perform its functions, and a hung legislature whose weak government cannot take any decision that could displease a caste, community or other group. Politicians who fear losing power may send public issues to the courts so as to delay hard choices or to pass the blame to them. Courts may also be needed where the other organs fail to protect basic rights, such as a decent life or a healthy environment. Kashyap warns that a strong, authoritarian government may misuse the courts for its own ends, as was attempted during the Emergency, and that courts themselves may be drawn towards populism and publicity.cc:T7c8,The jurist Upendra Baxi mapped the social groups that have driven activism. The main types are summarised below:

| Group type | Chief concern |
|---|---|
| Civil rights and people's rights groups | Civil and political rights; social and economic rights against state repression |
| Consumer and bonded-labour groups | Accountability in the economy; ending wage slavery |
| Environmental groups | Pollution and environmental degradation |
| Child rights and custodial rights groups | Child labour, literacy, juveniles, prisoners and preventive detainees |
| Poverty and indigenous rights groups | Famine relief, urban poverty, forest dwellers and Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas |
| Women's rights groups | Gender equality, violence against women, dowry deaths |
| Bar, media and lawyer groups | Autonomy of the judiciary and the press; causes taken up by lawyers |
| Opponents of large irrigation projects and individual petitioners | Challenges to mega projects; freelance activism |

Baxi also catalogued the fears that activism creates among judges. He asked whether courts exceed their role, whether they have the expertise, whether their workload can be borne, whether their authority is weakened when orders are ignored, whether an excess of PIL helps democracy, and what a judge's standing will be after retirement. These fears are set out below:

| Fear | The question it raises |
|---|---|
| Ideological | Are courts taking over the powers of the legislature, executive or autonomous bodies? |
| Epistemic | Do judges have enough knowledge of economics, science and other technical fields? |
| Management | Can the courts handle the extra work when pending cases are already so many? |
| Legitimation | Will orders that the executive can ignore erode the authority and faith placed in courts? |
| Democratic | Is a flood of PIL strengthening democracy or draining its potential? |
| Biographic | What place will a judge have in national affairs after retirement if they overdo PIL? |cd:T6a1,In the United States, activism and judicial restraint are rival philosophies. Those who favour restraint hold that judges should only say what the law is. Law-making belongs to legislators and executives, and judges should keep their own political values out of their opinions. They also hold that the original intent of the framers can be known and should guide the courts.

The doctrine of restraint rests on six assumptions in the American setting. The court is non-elective and so less democratic than the elected branches. The power of judicial review is not expressly granted by the Constitution, so its origin is open to question. Separation of powers must be respected. Federalism requires courts to defer to state governments. Courts depend on Congress for jurisdiction and resources, and on public acceptance for their effectiveness, so they should not overstep without weighing the risk. And courts, as custodians of legal tradition, should keep clear of politics. The chapter notes that all these assumptions except the one on judicial review hold good in India as well.

In December 2007 the Supreme Court called for judicial restraint. It said that courts must not take over legislative or executive functions, and that judges who do so act unconstitutionally. The Bench warned that activism must not become adventurism, and that courts should avoid embarrassing administrators, who have expertise the courts lack. It reasoned that if legislatures or executives fail, the remedy lies with citizens, through their votes and peaceful protest, and not with judges. Taking over those functions would upset the balance of power and expose judges to closer monitoring by elected officials.ce:T48b,- Judicial activism: a proactive judiciary protecting rights and promoting justice. Also called judicial dynamism; the opposite of judicial restraint.
- Term first used in 1947 by Arthur Schlesinger Jr.; in India the doctrine took shape in the mid-1970s.
- Two aspects: directions to government through PIL, and a wider reading of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
- Judicial review tests a law against the Constitution; activism moulds the law to changing social needs.
- Wadehra's causes: collapse of responsible government, public reliance on courts, judicial enthusiasm, legislative vacuum.
- Kashyap's causes: a weak hung government, politicians passing hard choices to courts, misuse by an authoritarian government.
- Baxi's typology of activist groups, and his six fears: ideological, epistemic, management, legitimation, democratic and biographic.
- US restraint rests on six assumptions; five hold in India, but not the one on the origin of judicial review.
- Activism widens locus standi through PIL, and critics call that expansion judicial overreach.
- The December 2007 Supreme Court bench warned against judicial adventurism and placed the remedy with voters.cf:T470,Ordinary litigation is adversarial. One party claims relief against another, and the other resists. PIL works differently, and the table below sets out the main contrasts that the chapter draws:

| Aspect | Ordinary litigation | Public Interest Litigation |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Enforces one person's right against another | Promotes and vindicates public interest |
| Relationship | Adversarial dispute between two sides | Cooperation between petitioner, State or public authority and the court |
| Role of the court | Largely passive, decides the dispute before it | Assertive and creative; takes a positive attitude to the acts in question |
| Procedure | Fixed rules of pleading and procedure | Flexibility, though still within judicial tenets |
| Subject | Individual rights | Violations affecting large numbers of poor or disadvantaged people |
| Outcome | Adjudicates individual rights | Does not decide individual rights in the traditional sense |

The chapter also calls PIL a strategic arm of the legal aid movement. Its aim is to bring justice within the reach of the poor, a group that has little visibility in society.d0:T4dd,In 1988 the Supreme Court laid down guidelines for entertaining letters and petitions as PIL. These were revised in 1993 and 2003. Under them, the following categories are ordinarily entertained:

| Entertained as PIL | Not entertained as PIL |
|---|---|
| Bonded labour and neglected children | Landlord and tenant disputes |
| Non-payment of minimum wages and exploitation of casual workers | Service matters, including pension and gratuity |
| Jail complaints: harassment, premature release, death in jail, speedy trial | Complaints against Central or State departments and local bodies, except the first ten categories |
| Police refusal to register a case, harassment or custodial death | Admission to medical and other educational institutions |
| Atrocities on women, including bride-burning, rape and dowry-related killings | Petitions for early hearing of cases pending in the High Courts and subordinate courts |
| Harassment of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and backward classes | |
| Environmental pollution, ecological balance, food adulteration, forests and wildlife | |
| Petitions from riot victims and family pension | |

The lesson is that PIL is about wide public harms, not about individual service or property disputes.d1:T442,Several principles govern how a PIL is handled. Any interested person may petition under Articles 32 and 226 on behalf of disadvantaged people who cannot reach the court. The court treats a letter or a telegram as a PIL where it raises a public issue of enforcing the rights of many people, and it relaxes procedural and pleading rules in such cases. Where large-scale injustice is involved, the court invokes Articles 14 and 21 and international human-rights conventions on fair trial.

The Supreme Court also set limits. A dispute between two groups that is purely a matter of private law cannot be brought as PIL. The court will not ordinarily enter into policy, and it must not transgress the bounds of its jurisdiction. It may, however, use a commission or other bodies to investigate facts, and in special cases it may even direct the management of a public institution. The High Courts have narrower power: they lack a power akin to the complete-justice power of Article 142, and ordinarily they should not entertain a PIL that challenges the validity of a statute or statutory rule.d2:T401,The Supreme Court has warned that PIL is not a cure for every wrong. It was meant to protect the basic rights of the weak, and abuse has grown in recent times. The Court has also named the distorted forms it wants to stop: publicity, politics, private, money-driven and middle-class interest litigation. It therefore set guidelines to encourage genuine PIL and discourage the rest:

- Genuine and bona fide petitions are to be encouraged, and petitions for extraneous reasons curbed.
- Each High Court should frame its own rules rather than leave every judge to devise a procedure.
- The court should check the petitioner's credentials and be prima facie satisfied that the contents are correct.
- Substantial public interest must be involved before the petition is entertained, and larger public harm, urgency and gravity should get priority.
- There must be no personal gain, private motive or oblique motive behind the petition.
- Busybodies filing for ulterior motives should be discouraged, including by exemplary costs.d3:T423,The Governor is not chosen by voters or by an electoral college. The President appoints by a warrant under hand and seal, so in effect the Governor is the Centre's nominee. In the Hargovind Pant case (1979), however, the Supreme Court held that the post is not employment under the Central government; it is an independent constitutional office, neither controlled by nor subordinate to the Centre.

The Draft Constitution proposed direct election on adult suffrage. The Constituent Assembly dropped this American model and adopted the Canadian one, in which the Centre appoints the provincial head. The reasons recorded include:

- election fits badly with a parliamentary state where the Governor is only a nominal head, and costly arrangements would serve no purpose;
- a popularly elected Governor could clash with the Chief Minister, would belong to a party instead of being neutral, and might encourage separatist tendencies;
- the Chief Minister might push a weak party loyalist as candidate;
- nomination lets the Centre keep its hold over the states.d4:T69e,Only two qualifications are laid down: Indian citizenship and a minimum age of 35.

The **Sarkaria Commission** (1983–88) wanted more care in selection. A Governor should be eminent in some field, come from outside the state, be detached from local politics and not have been heavily active in politics lately. A politician of the Centre's ruling party should not be sent to a state run by another party. It proposed writing consultation with the Chief Minister into Article 155, and suggested that the Prime Minister may informally consult the Vice-President and the Lok Sabha Speaker.

**Oath.** The Governor promises to execute the office faithfully, to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law, and to devote himself or herself to the people's service and well-being. It is administered by the Chief Justice of the state High Court, or the seniormost judge present. Anyone discharging the Governor's functions takes the same oath.

| Condition | Rule |
|---|---|
| Membership of legislature | Not allowed; a sitting member who is appointed is deemed to vacate the seat on taking office |
| Other office of profit | Barred |
| Residence | Raj Bhavan, without paying rent |
| Emoluments | Fixed by Parliament; cannot be reduced during the term |
| Two states | Pay shared between the states in a proportion the President decides |
| Salary | Raised in 2018 from ₹1.10 lakh to ₹3.50 lakh per month |

**Immunities.** The Governor has personal immunity for official acts. During the term, no criminal proceedings can be started, even for personal acts, and arrest or imprisonment is barred. Civil proceedings over personal acts are possible only after two months' notice.d5:T4b5,The Governor serves five years from entering office, but at the pleasure of the President, and may resign by writing to the President. In the Surya Narain case (1981) the Supreme Court held that the President's pleasure cannot be questioned in court, so the Governor has no security of tenure and can be removed at any time. The Constitution lists no grounds for removal.

That is why changes of government at the Centre often bring changes of Governors. In 1989 the National Front government under V. P. Singh asked all Governors to resign, because the Congress had appointed them; some were replaced and some stayed. In 1991 the Narasimha Rao government changed fourteen Governors appointed by the V. P. Singh and Chandra Sekhar governments.

- The President may transfer a Governor to another state for the remaining term.
- A Governor whose term has ended can be reappointed in the same or another state.
- A Governor continues beyond five years until the successor takes charge, so the state is never without one.
- For contingencies the Constitution does not cover, such as a Governor's death, the President may make arrangements; the Chief Justice of the High Court can be asked to act temporarily.d6:T52c,The Governor has executive, legislative, financial and judicial powers similar to the President's, but no diplomatic, military or emergency powers. Executive powers include:

- All executive action of the state is taken formally in the Governor's name; the Governor makes rules for authenticating orders, for convenient transaction of business and for allocating business among ministers.
- Appoints the Chief Minister and, on his or her advice, the other ministers, who hold office at the Governor's pleasure. Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha must have a Tribal Welfare minister; the 94th Amendment (2006) removed Bihar from this list.
- Appoints the Advocate General (pleasure of the Governor, remuneration fixed by the Governor) and the State Election Commissioner, who can be removed only like a High Court judge.
- Appoints the chairman and members of the State Public Service Commission, though only the President can remove them.
- Can ask the Chief Minister for information on administration and legislative proposals, and can require a minister's individual decision to be placed before the council.
- Can recommend President's Rule; during that rule the Governor wields wide executive power as the President's agent.
- Acts as chancellor of the state's universities and appoints vice-chancellors.d7:T8a1,The Governor is an integral part of the state legislature and can:

- summon and prorogue it, and dissolve the legislative assembly;
- address it at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year, and send messages on pending bills or otherwise;
- appoint a member to preside when the offices of both Speaker and Deputy Speaker, or both Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the council, are vacant;
- nominate one-sixth of the legislative council from people with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service;
- decide disqualification of members in consultation with the Election Commission;
- lay the reports of the State Finance Commission, the State Public Service Commission and the Comptroller and Auditor General before the legislature.

Until 2020 the Governor also nominated one Anglo-Indian member to the assembly; the 104th Amendment (2019) ended this.

**Assent to bills.** On receiving a bill passed by the legislature, the Governor has four choices: assent, withhold assent, return it for reconsideration (not a money bill), or reserve it for the President. If the legislature passes the returned bill again, with or without changes, the Governor must assent. Reservation is compulsory where the bill would endanger the position of the High Court. Soli Sorabji listed further grounds: a bill contrary to the Constitution or the Directive Principles, against the larger interest of the country, of grave national importance, or about compulsory acquisition of property under Article 31A.

**Ordinances (Article 213).** When the legislature is not in session, the Governor may issue ordinances; the legislature must approve them within six weeks of reassembling, and the Governor may withdraw one at any time. The text calls this the Governor's most important legislative power. In D. C. Wadhwa (1986) the Supreme Court found that Bihar's Governor had issued 256 ordinances between 1967 and 1981, many repromulgated again and again for one to fourteen years. Repeated repromulgation of the same text, without trying to pass a bill, violates the Constitution and the ordinance can be struck down.d8:T4fb,| Point | President | Governor |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary bill | Assent, withhold or return; only a suspensive veto | Assent, withhold, return, or reserve for the President |
| Reserved bill | Can return it once; if passed again, not bound to assent, may withhold | Has no further role once reserved; the President's assent alone is needed |
| Money bill | Assent or withhold; cannot return | Assent, withhold or reserve; cannot return |
| Ordinance | When Parliament, or either House, is not in session | When the assembly, or either House of a bicameral legislature, is not in session |
| Ordinance scope | Subjects on which Parliament can legislate | Subjects on which the state legislature can legislate |
| Instructions | None needed | Needs the President's instructions in three cases: where a bill would need prior presidential sanction, where he would reserve such a bill, or where the Act would be invalid without presidential assent |
| Disapproval | Both Houses pass resolutions | Assembly resolution, agreed to by the council if there is one |
| Pardon: law | Offences against Central law | Offences against state law |
| Pardon: death sentence | Can pardon | Cannot pardon; can only suspend, remit or commute |
| Pardon: court-martial | Can act | No such power |d9:T881,Three Articles fix the position. **Article 154** vests the state's executive power in the Governor, exercisable directly or through subordinate officers. **Article 163** sets up a council with the Chief Minister at its head to aid and advise the Governor, except where the Governor must act in his or her discretion. **Article 164** makes the council collectively responsible to the legislative assembly, the basis of parliamentary government in the state.

The Governor differs from the President in two ways. The Constitution contemplates discretion for the Governor but not the President. And since the 42nd Amendment (1976), ministerial advice binds the President, while no such rule exists for the Governor. If a dispute arises over whether something falls within discretion, the Governor's decision is final and cannot be questioned in court.

**Constitutional discretion:**

- reserving a bill for the President;
- recommending President's Rule;
- acting as administrator of an adjoining union territory given as additional charge;
- fixing the royalty from mineral licences payable by Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram to an autonomous tribal district council.

**Situational discretion** arises from circumstances: choosing a Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority or when the incumbent dies with no obvious successor; dismissing a council that cannot prove confidence; and dissolving the assembly when the council has lost its majority.

**Special responsibilities.** Under presidential directions the Governor consults the ministers but finally acts in discretion in these cases:

| State | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Maharashtra | Separate development boards for Vidarbha and Marathwada |
| Gujarat | Separate development boards for Saurashtra and Kutch |
| Nagaland | Law and order while disturbance continues in the Naga Hills–Tuensang area |
| Assam | Administration of tribal areas |
| Manipur | Administration of hill areas |
| Sikkim | Peace and social and economic advancement of different sections |
| Arunachal Pradesh | Law and order |
| Karnataka | Separate development board for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region (98th Amendment, 2012) |da:T86b,The Constitution lays down no detailed procedure. Article 164 says only that the Governor appoints the Chief Minister. The Governor does not have a free choice, because convention requires him to call the leader of the majority party in the Legislative Assembly. When no party has a clear majority, the Governor exercises personal discretion. He usually calls the leader of the largest party or coalition and asks for a vote of confidence within a month.

Some further points are useful for revision:

- If a Chief Minister dies with no obvious successor, the Governor may have to judge who should be appointed. Where the ruling party elects a new leader after a death, the Governor has no real choice.
- The Governor may appoint first and ask the new Chief Minister to prove majority within a reasonable time. Proof of majority is not required beforehand.
- A person who is not a legislator may be appointed Chief Minister, but must get elected to a House within six months, failing which he ceases to hold the office.
- The Chief Minister may sit in either House, though the Legislative Assembly has supplied most holders. Members of the Legislative Council have also been appointed.

The Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State Relations (1983–88) guided the Governor in a no-majority situation. It ranked the options as follows:

| Order | Who is called to form the government |
|---|---|
| 1 | An absolute majority party, whose leader must be asked automatically |
| 2 | A pre-election alliance |
| 3 | The largest single party, claiming support from others and independents |
| 4 | A post-election coalition in which all partners join the government |
| 5 | A post-election alliance in which some parties govern and others support from outside |

The Commission also said the Governor's task is to ensure that a government is formed, not to build one that pursues policies he approves. A Chief Minister who is not the leader of an absolute-majority party should seek a vote of confidence within 30 days. Where rival claims to majority support arise, the Governor should not decide them privately, but should have them tested on the floor of the House.db:T582,The Chief Minister's powers can be grouped by relationship. The table brings them together:

| Relationship | Powers and duties |
|---|---|
| Council of ministers | The Governor appoints only those whom he recommends; allocates and reshuffles portfolios; can ask a minister to resign or advise the Governor to dismiss one; presides over council meetings; coordinates all ministers |
| Governor | Principal channel of communication between the Governor and the council; must report council decisions and proposals for legislation and provide information when asked; advises on key appointments such as the Advocate-General, state public service commission members and the state election commissioner |
| State legislature | Advises the Governor on summoning and proroguing sessions; can recommend dissolution of the Assembly at any time; announces government policy on the floor |
| Other roles | Chairman of the State Planning Board; rotating vice-chairman of a zonal council; member of the Inter-State Council and the NITI Aayog; chief spokesman; crisis manager; leader of the party in power; political head of the services |

The Chief Minister's resignation or death dissolves the council as a whole. Another minister's resignation or death only creates a vacancy. The Governor's discretionary powers reduce the Chief Minister's influence to a degree, but the office remains central to state administration.dc:T584,Two Articles, 163 and 164, set the framework in broad terms. The other provisions that matter are Article 166, which governs how government business is conducted; Article 167, which sets the Chief Minister's duty to inform the Governor; and Article 177, which gives ministers the right to speak in the Houses without the right to vote there, unless they are members:

| Article | Subject-matter |
|---|---|
| 163 | Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister to aid and advise the Governor |
| 164 | Appointment, tenure, responsibility, oath and salary of ministers |
| 166 | Conduct of government business; executive action is taken in the Governor's name |
| 167 | Duty of the Chief Minister to inform the Governor and place matters before the council |
| 177 | Right of ministers to speak and take part in House proceedings, but not to vote unless a member |

On advice, Article 163 provides that the Governor acts on the council's advice except where he must act in his discretion. The Governor's decision on whether a matter is discretionary is final. The advice given by ministers cannot be enquired into in any court. In the Shamsher Singh case (1974) the Supreme Court held that outside discretionary spheres the Governor must act on the council's aid and advice, and where the Constitution requires the Governor's satisfaction, that satisfaction is the council's, not the Governor's personal view.dd:T508,The Constitution does not fix the size of the council or the rank of its members, so the Chief Minister decides these according to the needs of the time. The council has three ranks: cabinet ministers, ministers of state and deputy ministers. Cabinet ministers head the major departments and attend the cabinet. Ministers of state may hold independent charge or work under a cabinet minister, but do not attend the cabinet unless invited. Deputy ministers have no independent charge and assist cabinet ministers. A deputy Chief Minister may be appointed, usually for local political reasons.

The cabinet is the core of the council. It is the highest decision-making body in the state, the chief policy-making and coordinating body, and the supreme executive. It also acts as an advisory body to the Governor, deals with major legislative and financial matters, controls higher appointments, and handles emergencies.

The cabinet works through cabinet committees, which may be standing or ad hoc. The Chief Minister sets them up as needed, so their number and composition change over time. They prepare proposals and take decisions, but the cabinet can review those decisions. A final point for exams: states have departments, not ministries. The term ministry is used only at the Centre.de:T54b,State legislatures are not uniform. Most states have a single House, the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha), and in them the legislature consists of the Governor and the Assembly. Six states are bicameral: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra and Karnataka. There the legislature is the Governor plus the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad, the upper House or house of elders) and the Assembly (the lower, popular House). The Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Council was abolished by the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act 2019.

**Article 169** lets Parliament create or abolish a Council if the Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority: a majority of its total membership and at least two-thirds of members present and voting. Parliament then acts by an ordinary law with a simple majority, and this law is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368. The Constituent Assembly doubted the second chamber as unrepresentative, slow and costly, so each state is left free to choose.

| State | History of its Council |
|---|---|
| West Bengal and Punjab | Abolished in 1969 |
| Andhra Pradesh | Created 1957, abolished 1985, revived under the 2005 Act (effective 2007) |
| Tamil Nadu | Abolished 1986; Act of 2010 to recreate it never came into force, as the Assembly asked in 2011 to drop the proposal |df:T502,Assembly members are directly elected on adult franchise. Strength may range from 60 to 500 depending on population. Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim and Goa have a lower minimum of 30, and Mizoram and Nagaland have 40 and 46. Some members in Sikkim and Nagaland are elected indirectly.

- **Anglo-Indian nominee:** the Governor's nomination of one member ended on 25 January 2020, as the 104th Amendment of 2019 did not extend it.
- **Constituencies:** each state is divided into territorial constituencies with a uniform population-to-seat ratio, using the last published census.
- **Readjustment:** after each census the number of seats and the constituency boundaries are readjusted in the manner Parliament decides. Delimitation Commission Acts came in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002. The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze seat totals and constituencies at the 1971 level until 2000, and the 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze until 2026 to reward population control. The 87th Amendment (2003) moved the basis for delimiting constituencies from the 1991 to the 2001 census, without changing the total seats.
- **SC and ST seats:** reserved in proportion to population. Originally for ten years, the reservation has been extended repeatedly, and the 104th Amendment now carries it to 2030.e0:T573,Members of the Council are indirectly elected. Its maximum strength is one-third of the Assembly's and its minimum is 40, a rule that keeps the directly elected House dominant. Parliament fixes actual numbers.

| Share of Council | Chosen by |
|---|---|
| One-third | Members of local bodies such as municipalities and district boards |
| One-twelfth | Graduates of three years' standing living in the state |
| One-twelfth | Teachers of three years' standing, secondary school level or above |
| One-third | Assembly members, from persons who are not Assembly members |
| Remainder (one-sixth) | Nominated by the Governor for expertise in literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service |

So five-sixths of members are indirectly elected and one-sixth are nominated. Election follows proportional representation by single transferable vote. Parliament may change this scheme, but has never done so.

The **Assembly** is not a permanent House. Its term is five years from its first meeting, and the Governor can dissolve it earlier. During a national emergency Parliament may lengthen the term by one year at a time, but never beyond six months after the emergency ends. The **Council** is a continuing House that cannot be dissolved. One-third of its members retire every second year, so each member serves six years, and retired members can be re-elected or renominated.e1:T827,A member must be an Indian citizen, make an oath or affirmation before the person authorised by the Election Commission, be at least 25 for the Assembly or 30 for the Council, and satisfy Parliament's other conditions. Under the Representation of the People Act 1951, a candidate must be an elector in an Assembly constituency of the state. A Governor's nominee to the Council must reside in the state. A person contesting a reserved seat must belong to the relevant SC or ST, though such persons may also contest general seats.

Constitutional **disqualifications** are holding an office of profit under the Union or state government (ministers and exempted offices aside), being of unsound mind as declared by a court, being an undischarged insolvent, lacking citizenship or voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship, and any disqualification under a law of Parliament. The 1951 Act adds conviction with imprisonment of two years or more, corrupt practices, failure to lodge election accounts, interest in government contracts, and dismissal for corruption or disloyalty. Preventive detention is not a disqualification. The Governor decides on these questions after obtaining the Election Commission's opinion.

Defection under the Tenth Schedule is decided differently: by the Speaker of the Assembly or the Chairman of the Council, not by the Governor. In *Kihoto Hollohan* (1992) the Supreme Court held that this decision is subject to judicial review.

Before taking a seat, each member takes an oath before the Governor or his nominee. Without it a member cannot vote or take part and gets no privileges, and sitting or voting without the oath, or knowing oneself disqualified, draws a penalty of ₹500 per day.

A seat falls vacant on:

- election to both Houses (one seat is vacated under state law);
- disqualification;
- resignation in writing to the Speaker or Chairman, effective when accepted;
- absence from all meetings for sixty days without permission;
- the election being declared void, expulsion, election as President or Vice-President, or appointment as Governor.e2:T4bd,The Assembly has a Speaker and Deputy Speaker, the Council a Chairman and Deputy Chairman, and each House also has a panel of presiding members. Their salaries are fixed by the state legislature and charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State, so they are not voted on annually. Each is elected by the House from among its members.

| Office | Leaves office on | Resignation addressed to |
|---|---|---|
| Speaker | Ceasing to be a member, resignation, or removal | Deputy Speaker |
| Deputy Speaker | Same three grounds | Speaker |
| Chairman | Same three grounds | Deputy Chairman |
| Deputy Chairman | Same three grounds | Chairman |

Removal requires a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members (an effective majority), moved after 14 days' notice.

The **Speaker** keeps order, interprets the rules and precedents within the House, votes only to break a tie, may permit a secret sitting, decides defection cases, appoints committee chairmen, and chairs the Business Advisory, Rules and General Purposes Committees. The Speaker alone certifies a Money Bill, and that decision is final; the Council's Chairman lacks this power. Deputies act when the office is vacant or the principal is absent.e3:T581,The Governor summons each House. No more than six months may separate two sessions, so the legislature meets at least twice a year. An **adjournment** pauses a sitting for hours, days or weeks, and **adjournment sine die** ends it without a fixed date; both are done by the presiding officer. **Prorogation** ends the session and is done by the Governor, who may do so even while the House sits. **Dissolution** ends the life of an Assembly. The Council cannot be dissolved.

On dissolution of the Assembly the fate of bills is as follows.

| Bill | Fate |
|---|---|
| Pending in the Assembly | Lapses |
| Passed by the Assembly, pending in the Council | Lapses |
| Pending in the Council, not passed by the Assembly | Does not lapse |
| Awaiting the assent of Governor or President | Does not lapse |
| Returned by the President for reconsideration | Does not lapse |

Quorum is ten members or one-tenth of the House including the presiding officer, whichever is greater. Decisions are by a majority of members present and voting, excluding the presiding officer, who votes only to break a tie. Business is conducted in the state's official language, Hindi or English, though the presiding officer may allow the mother tongue. Every minister and the Advocate General may speak in either House and its committees without a vote, and a minister may take part even in a House of which he or she is not a member.e4:T564,An ordinary bill may start in either House and be moved by a minister or a private member. It goes through three readings in the originating House and then to the other. In a unicameral state, a bill passed by the Assembly goes directly to the Governor.

When the Assembly sends a bill to the Council, the Council may pass it as is, pass it with amendments, reject it, or sit on it. If it rejects the bill, proposes amendments the Assembly refuses, or takes no action for three months, the Assembly may pass the bill again and send it back. If the Council again rejects it, amends it unacceptably or does not pass it within one month, the bill is deemed passed in the Assembly's second version. The Council can therefore delay an ordinary bill by four months at most (three plus one). The Constitution has no joint sitting for state legislatures. A bill that began in the Council and is rejected by the Assembly dies.

The Governor has four options: give assent, withhold assent, return the bill for reconsideration, or reserve it for the President. If a returned bill is passed again, the Governor must assent, so the veto is suspensive only. When a bill is reserved, the President may assent, withhold assent or return it, and the Houses must reconsider it within six months. The Constitution does not say whether the President must assent after a returned bill is passed again.e5:T4ac,A Money Bill cannot originate in the Council. It is introduced only in the Assembly, on the Governor's recommendation, and only by a minister. The Council can neither reject nor amend it. It must send the bill back within 14 days, with or without recommendations. The Assembly may accept or reject any or all of those recommendations. If the Council does not return it within 14 days, the bill is deemed passed in the form the Assembly adopted. The Governor can assent, withhold assent or reserve a Money Bill, but cannot return it. The President, if it is reserved, can assent or withhold assent but also cannot return it.

The Sarkaria Commission sorted bills reserved for the President into three classes. Some **must** be reserved: bills that derogate from High Court powers (Article 200), water or electricity tax bills attracting Article 288, and bills under Article 360 in a financial emergency. Some **may** be reserved for a purpose: bills seeking immunity from Articles 14 and 19 (Articles 31A and 31C), Concurrent List bills meant to prevail over Union law (Article 254), and bills restricting trade that need sanction (Article 304). The rest are reserved at the Governor's discretion.e6:T6e9,| Point | Parliament | State legislature |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary-bill deadlock | Other House rejects, amends unacceptably or sits six months | Council does so for three months |
| Resolution | Joint sitting summoned by the President | No joint sitting; Assembly passes the bill again |
| Money Bill recommended by | President | Governor |

The Council equals the Assembly in a few matters: ordinary bills (though the Assembly prevails on disagreement), approving the Governor's ordinances, drawing ministers including the Chief Minister from it, and considering reports of the State Finance Commission, State Public Service Commission and CAG. It is unequal in many more. It cannot introduce, amend or reject a Money Bill, and the Speaker decides what is a Money Bill. It can discuss the budget but not vote on demands for grants. It cannot remove the ministry, because ministers answer only to the Assembly. It takes no part in electing the President or Rajya Sabha members, and has no effective say in ratifying constitutional amendments. Parliament can abolish it on the Assembly's resolution.

The Council is thus weaker than the Rajya Sabha, which has equal powers with the Lok Sabha apart from money matters and control over the government. Three reasons are given. The Rajya Sabha represents the states and so serves a federal purpose, which a Council does not. The Council is heterogeneous (local bodies, graduates, teachers, nominees), while the Rajya Sabha is mainly elected, with only 12 of 250 members nominated. And the subordinate role fits the British model, where the House of Lords can delay an ordinary bill by one year and a money bill by one month. Critics call it a costly ornament; supporters say it checks hasty legislation and admits experts.e7:T486,Privileges are the special rights and immunities of Houses, committees and members that protect their independence and dignity. They extend to ministers and the Advocate General when they speak in the House, but not to the Governor, though he or she is part of the legislature.

**Collective privileges** include publishing proceedings and barring others from doing so, holding secret sittings, making its own rules, punishing members and outsiders for breach of privilege or contempt (reprimand, admonition or imprisonment; suspension or expulsion for members), holding inquiries and summoning witnesses, barring courts from inquiring into its proceedings, and preventing arrests or legal process within its precincts without the presiding officer's permission.

**Individual privileges** include: freedom from arrest in civil cases (not criminal or preventive detention cases) during a session and for 40 days before and after it; freedom of speech in the House, with no court liability for anything said or voted, subject to the Constitution and the House rules; and exemption from jury service and from appearing as witness while the House is in session.e8:T43a,- Articles 168–212 govern the state legislature; six states have a Council.
- Article 169: Parliament creates or abolishes a Council on the Assembly's special-majority resolution, by ordinary law.
- Assembly strength 60–500, directly elected; Council at most one-third of the Assembly and at least 40, indirectly elected.
- Council: one-third local bodies, one-twelfth graduates, one-twelfth teachers, one-third Assembly, one-sixth Governor's nominees.
- Assembly lasts five years; Council is permanent with one-third retiring every second year.
- Minimum age is 25 for the Assembly and 30 for the Council; Tenth Schedule cases go to the Speaker or Chairman.
- Presiding officers are removed by an effective majority after 14 days' notice; the Speaker alone certifies Money Bills.
- The Council can delay an ordinary bill by four months at most, and a Money Bill by 14 days; no joint sitting exists.
- Governor's options on ordinary bills: assent, withhold, return, reserve; he cannot return a Money Bill.
- Members are immune from civil arrest 40 days either side of a session.e9:T6d4,The modern High Court began in 1862, when Calcutta, Bombay and Madras each received one under the Indian High Courts Act of 1861. Allahabad followed in 1866. Every province of British India eventually had its own, and after 1950 the provincial court simply became the High Court of the matching state.

Article 214 requires a High Court for each state. The Seventh Amendment Act of 1956 went further and allowed Parliament to set up a common High Court for two or more states, or for states together with a union territory (Article 231). The territorial jurisdiction of a High Court matches the territory of its state, and a common High Court covers the whole area of each unit it serves.

The country now has 25 High Courts. The number rose from 18 to 21 with the three new states of 2000, to 24 when separate courts were created for Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura in 2013, and to 25 when Andhra Pradesh received its own in 2019. Delhi has had a separate court since 1966, while Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh share one. Other union territories fall under neighbouring state courts. Parliament may extend a High Court's jurisdiction to a union territory or withdraw it (Article 230).

| High Court | Established | Territory | Principal seat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Allahabad | 1866 | Uttar Pradesh | Prayagraj, with a bench at Lucknow |
| Bombay | 1862 | Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu | Mumbai |
| Calcutta | 1862 | West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands | Kolkata |
| Madras | 1862 | Tamil Nadu and Puducherry | Chennai |
| Delhi | 1966 | National Capital Territory of Delhi | New Delhi |
| Gauhati | 1948 | Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh | Guwahati |
| Andhra Pradesh | 2019 | Andhra Pradesh | Amaravati |ea:T61b,A High Court consists of a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President thinks fit to appoint. The Constitution does not fix the strength of any court. The President sets it from time to time according to the court's workload.

Judges are appointed by the President, but the Constitution requires consultation before each appointment. The table below records who must be consulted for each post:

| Post | Appointed by | Must be consulted |
|---|---|---|
| Chief Justice of a High Court | President | Chief Justice of India and the state governor |
| Other judges | President | Chief Justice of India, the state governor and the High Court's own Chief Justice |
| Judges of a common High Court | President | Governors of all the states concerned |

The Supreme Court's decisions shaped this process. In the Second Judges case of 1993, the Court held that a High Court judge cannot be appointed unless it accords with the opinion of the Chief Justice of India. In the Third Judges case of 1998, it held that the Chief Justice of India's personal opinion does not by itself amount to consultation; he must act through a collegium of senior Supreme Court judges.

The 99th Constitutional Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, both of 2014, tried to replace the collegium with the National Judicial Appointments Commission. In the Fourth Judges case of 2015, the Supreme Court struck down both as unconstitutional and void, holding that the new body would weaken judicial independence. The collegium system therefore operated again.eb:T487,A person qualifies for a High Court judgeship if he or she is an Indian citizen and meets one of two tests. The first is ten years of holding judicial office in India. The second is ten years as an advocate of a High Court, or of two or more High Courts in succession. The Constitution sets no minimum age. It also differs from the Supreme Court rules in one respect: it does not allow a distinguished jurist to be appointed straight to a High Court bench.

Before taking office, a new judge makes an oath or affirmation before the state governor or a person the governor nominates. The judge swears to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution, to uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India, to perform the duties without fear or favour, affection or ill-will, and to uphold the Constitution and the laws.

Parliament fixes the salaries, allowances, privileges, leave and pension of High Court judges. Once a judge is appointed, these terms cannot be changed to the judge's disadvantage, except during a financial emergency. Judges also receive a sumptuary allowance, free accommodation and facilities such as medical care, a car and a telephone.ec:T756,The Constitution does not fix a term of office. A judge holds office until the age of 62, a limit raised from 60 by the 15th Amendment of 1963. If a dispute arises about a judge's age, the President decides after consulting the Chief Justice of India, and that decision is final. A judge may resign by writing to the President. The office is also vacated on appointment to the Supreme Court or on transfer to another High Court.

A judge can be removed only in the manner the Constitution prescribes. The President orders removal after an address is presented by Parliament in the same session, and the address must pass each House by a special majority, meaning a majority of the House's total membership and a two-thirds majority of the members present and voting. The only grounds are proved misbehaviour or incapacity, the same as for a Supreme Court judge.

The Judges (Inquiry) Act of 1968 governs the impeachment procedure in steps. A removal motion signed by 100 members of the Lok Sabha or 50 members of the Rajya Sabha goes to the Speaker or Chairman, who may admit or reject it. If it is admitted, a three-member committee investigates, consisting of a Supreme Court judge or Chief Justice, a High Court Chief Justice and a distinguished jurist. If the committee finds misbehaviour or incapacity, each House considers the motion, and the address then goes to the President. The text notes that no High Court judge has been impeached so far.

The President may transfer a judge from one High Court to another after consulting the Chief Justice of India, and the judge receives a compensatory allowance on transfer. The Supreme Court has said that transfers must be an exceptional step taken in the public interest and never as punishment (1977). In 1994 it held that transfers are open to judicial review, although only the judge who was moved can challenge the order.ed:T44c,Three temporary arrangements keep a High Court working when its strength falls short:

- **Acting Chief Justice (Article 223):** the President may appoint a judge as acting Chief Justice when the post is vacant, when the Chief Justice is temporarily absent, or when he or she cannot perform the duties.
- **Additional judges (Article 224):** for a period not exceeding two years, when the court's business has temporarily grown or arrears have built up.
- **Acting judges (Article 224):** when a judge other than the Chief Justice is unable to sit, or is temporarily made acting Chief Justice. The acting judge serves until the regular judge returns.

Neither an additional judge nor an acting judge may hold office after reaching 62.

Under Article 224A, the Chief Justice of a High Court may ask a retired judge of that court, or of another High Court, to sit for a temporary period. The request needs the President's prior consent and the retired judge's consent. The retired judge then has the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of a judge of that court, but is not treated as one of its judges.ee:T599,A High Court must be free from pressure by the executive and the legislature if it is to do justice without fear or favour. The Constitution supplies several safeguards:

| Safeguard | What it protects against |
|---|---|
| Appointment after consulting the judiciary | Executive control over who sits on the bench |
| Security of tenure | Removal at the pleasure of the executive; removal is possible only through the impeachment route |
| Fixed service conditions | Reduction of pay or benefits after appointment, except in a financial emergency |
| Charge on the state's Consolidated Fund | Parliamentary vote over judges' salaries and administrative costs (they can be discussed but not voted) |
| Pension charged on the Consolidated Fund of India | Dependence on the state government for retirement benefits |
| No discussion of a judge's conduct | Legislative debate, except while an impeachment motion is before Parliament |
| Bar on practice after retirement | Favours shown in the hope of future work; retired permanent judges may plead only before the Supreme Court and other High Courts |
| Power to punish contempt | Criticism that undermines the court's authority |
| Control over its own staff | Executive interference in recruitment and service conditions of court officers |
| Jurisdiction protected by the Constitution | Curtailment of the powers the Constitution grants, by either Parliament or a state legislature |ef:Tabd,The Constitution does not list every power of a High Court in detail. It states that the court keeps the jurisdiction it had before the Constitution began, and it adds revenue matters, which earlier courts did not hear. Other provisions give it writ jurisdiction, superintendence and consultative functions. Its powers today come from the Constitution, the Letters Patent, Acts of Parliament and of the state legislature, the Indian Penal Code (1860), the Criminal Procedure Code (1973) and the Civil Procedure Code (1908).

**Original jurisdiction** means hearing a dispute at its first stage, rather than on appeal. It covers election disputes for Parliament and the state legislatures, revenue matters, enforcement of fundamental rights, and cases transferred from a subordinate court that raise a constitutional question. The High Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, Madras and Delhi also hear higher-value civil suits in the first instance. Their original criminal jurisdiction, which the three presidency courts once had, was abolished by the Criminal Procedure Code of 1973.

**Writ jurisdiction** comes from Article 226. A High Court may issue habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition and quo warranto. It may do so for enforcing fundamental rights and for any other purpose, which in practice includes enforcing an ordinary legal right. It can reach any person, authority or government inside its territory, and also outside it when the cause of action arose within its territory.

The Supreme Court's writ power under Article 32 is concurrent with this one, so an aggrieved citizen may approach either court when a fundamental right is violated. The High Court's power is wider, because the Supreme Court issues writs only to enforce fundamental rights. In the Chandra Kumar case of 1997, the Supreme Court held that the writ jurisdiction of both courts forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution, so no amendment can oust it.

**Appellate jurisdiction** is the High Court's main role. It hears appeals against subordinate courts within its territory, and in both civil and criminal matters. The civil side works as follows:

- A first appeal lies against a district or subordinate court's decree, on questions of both fact and law, where the amount involved is above the prescribed limit.
- A second appeal lies only on a question of law.
- In some High Courts, an appeal from a single judge's decision goes to a division bench of the same court.

On the criminal side, a sessions court's sentence of imprisonment for more than seven years is appealable to the High Court. A death sentence passed by a sessions court must be confirmed by the High Court before it can be carried out, whether or not the convicted person appeals.f0:T7bb,Under Article 227, the High Court superintends every court and tribunal in its territory, except military courts and tribunals. It may call for returns, make rules and prescribe forms for their practice and proceedings, prescribe the books and accounts they must keep, and fix the fees payable to sheriffs, clerks, officers and legal practitioners.

This power is broad. It covers courts that are not under its appeal jurisdiction, extends to judicial as well as administrative matters, is revisional in character, and may be used on the court's own motion. Because it is extraordinary, the High Court uses it sparingly. The usual grounds are excess of jurisdiction, gross violation of natural justice, error of law, disregard of the law laid down by a superior court, perverse findings and manifest injustice.

Separately from superintendence, the High Court has administrative control over the subordinate judiciary under Article 235. The Governor consults the High Court on posting, promotion and appointment of district judges. The High Court itself handles the posting, promotion, leave, transfer and discipline of the judicial service below the rank of district judge. It may also withdraw a pending subordinate-court case that raises a substantial constitutional question, decide it, or send it back with its ruling. Its law binds every subordinate court in its territory.

As a court of record, the High Court's judgments and proceedings are kept for permanent record, and they carry evidentiary value in any subordinate court. The Constitution does not define contempt, but the Contempt of Courts Act of 1971 does, and it treats contempt as civil or criminal. A High Court may punish contempt of itself and of subordinate courts, except where the act is an offence under the Indian Penal Code. The Constitution gives the Supreme Court an express review power, but a High Court can also review and correct its own orders as an inherent feature of being a court of record.f1:T433,- The High Court is the top court of a state, below the Supreme Court and above the subordinate courts.
- Each state has one (Article 214); a common High Court for several states or UTs is allowed under Article 231.
- Twenty-five High Courts exist today; Delhi has its own since 1966.
- Judges are appointed by the President after consultation; the Chief Justice of India is always among those consulted.
- Qualification: ten years of judicial office or ten years as an advocate; no minimum age.
- Tenure runs to 62; removal requires proved misbehaviour or incapacity, a special-majority address and an inquiry under the 1968 Act.
- Writ powers under Article 226 are wider than the Supreme Court's Article 32 writs, which cover only fundamental rights.
- Superintendence under Article 227 reaches all courts and tribunals, except military ones, and is used sparingly.
- A sessions court's death sentence needs High Court confirmation, whether or not there is an appeal.
- Judicial review rests on Articles 13 and 226; the 42nd Amendment curtailed it and the 43rd restored it.f2:T69a,The Constitution protects the lower judiciary from executive control in several ways. The table below summarises the articles:

| Article | Subject |
|---|---|
| 233 | Appointment, posting and promotion of district judges |
| 233A | Validation of certain district judges' appointments and their judgments (added by the 20th Amendment of 1966) |
| 234 | Recruitment of persons other than district judges to the judicial service |
| 235 | Control over subordinate courts, vested in the High Court |
| 236 | Definitions of "district judge" and "judicial service" |
| 237 | Extension of these provisions to certain classes of magistrates |

A district judge is appointed, posted and promoted by the state governor in consultation with the High Court. To qualify, a candidate must not already be in the central or state government service, must have practised as an advocate or pleader for seven years, and must be recommended by the High Court. Other judicial service posts are filled by the governor after consulting the State Public Service Commission and the High Court. In practice the Commission runs a competitive examination for the judicial service.

The High Court controls the district and subordinate courts. It decides the posting, promotion and leave of judicial officers who hold posts below district judge, and it handles their discipline.

The term "district judge" is wide. It covers city civil court judges, additional and joint district judges, assistant district judges, chief judges of small causes courts, chief presidency magistrates, sessions judges and their additional and assistant colleagues. The governor may also apply these provisions to any class of magistrates.f3:T701,Each state lays down the organisation, jurisdiction and names of its subordinate courts, so the arrangements vary somewhat between states. Broadly, there are three tiers of civil and criminal courts below the High Court:

| Tier | Civil side | Criminal side |
|---|---|---|
| Top of the district | District judge | Sessions judge |
| Middle | Subordinate judge (civil judge, senior division) | Chief judicial magistrate |
| Lowest | Munsiff (civil judge, junior division) | Judicial magistrate |

The district judge is the highest judicial authority in the district. The same officer is called a district judge when deciding civil cases and a sessions judge for criminal cases. He or she has original and appellate powers in both fields, and also supervises all subordinate courts in the district. Appeals from the district judge go to the High Court. A sessions judge may impose any sentence, including life imprisonment and death, but a death sentence needs confirmation by the High Court even when no appeal is filed.

A subordinate judge on the civil side has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction over suits. The chief judicial magistrate tries criminal cases carrying up to seven years' imprisonment. At the bottom, a munsiff hears civil cases involving small sums, and a judicial magistrate tries offences punishable by up to three years.

Metropolitan cities have their own variants: city civil courts on the civil side and metropolitan magistrates on the criminal side. Some states and former presidency towns also have small causes courts, which decide small civil claims summarily. Their decisions are final, but the High Court may revise them. A few states have panchayat courts, known by various names such as Nyaya Panchayat or Gram Kutchery, which try petty civil and criminal cases.f4:T614,Article 39A directs the state to secure that the legal system promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity and to provide free legal aid, so that no citizen is denied justice because of economic or other disabilities. The Legal Services Authorities Act of 1987, which came into force on 9 November 1995, gave this a nationwide network.
