The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) sits at the top. It monitors and evaluates legal aid programmes and lays down the policies and principles that the other bodies follow. Below it are State Legal Services Authorities, a High Court Legal Services Committee in each High Court, and District Legal Services Authorities and Taluk Legal Services Committees in most districts and taluks. The Supreme Court has its own committee for the Supreme Court's programme.

These bodies provide free and competent legal services, organise Lok Adalats, and run legal awareness camps in rural areas. Free services include paying court fees and process fees, supplying a lawyer, obtaining certified copies of orders, and preparing appeals and paper books, including their printing and translation.

The eligible groups are women and children, members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, industrial workmen, victims of mass disasters, violence, floods, drought, earthquakes or industrial accidents, persons with disabilities, persons in custody, and victims of human trafficking or beggary. Persons whose annual income is below ₹1 lakh qualify; the limit in the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee is ₹5 lakh.f5:Tc2f,A Lok Adalat is a forum where disputes are compromised or settled amicably. It may take up a case already pending in a court or a dispute that has not yet reached one. The name means "people's court". The Supreme Court in P.T. Thomas (2005) described it as an alternative dispute resolution device with roots in Gandhian ideas. Proceedings have no winners or losers, and the forum relies on conciliation, negotiation and practical common sense.

The first Lok Adalat camp in independent India was held in Gujarat in 1982. It worked well but had no statutory force for its decisions. The Legal Services Authorities Act of 1987 gave it that status.

Under the Act, the State, District, Taluk, High Court and Supreme Court legal services bodies may organise Lok Adalats, at the times and places they choose. A typical bench has a judicial officer as chairman, with an advocate and a social worker as members.

The jurisdiction covers two kinds of dispute: a case pending before any court, and a matter that falls within a court's jurisdiction but has not been brought before it. Offences that cannot be compounded under any law are excluded. A pending case reaches a Lok Adalat in three ways: the parties agree, one party applies to the court, or the court considers the matter suitable. A pre-litigation dispute may be referred on the application of any party.

A Lok Adalat has the powers of a civil court on several matters. It can summon and examine witnesses on oath, order discovery and production of documents, receive evidence on affidavit, and call for public records. It sets its own procedure. Its proceedings count as judicial proceedings under the Indian Penal Code, and it is treated as a civil court for the Criminal Procedure Code.

An award of a Lok Adalat has the effect of a civil court's decree or another court's order. It is final, binds all parties, and cannot be appealed.

The Act and the practice recognise three kinds of Lok Adalat, as the table shows:

| Type | Features |
|---|---|
| National Lok Adalat | Held on one day across the country, in all courts from the Supreme Court down to taluk level; from 2015 it has also been held each month on a specific subject |
| State Lok Adalat | Also called regular Lok Adalats; includes continuous, daily, mobile (in a multi-utility van) and mega Lok Adalats held on one day in all courts of a state |
| Permanent Lok Adalat | Handles public utility services; discussed in the next section |

National and State Lok Adalats settle pre-litigation and pending matters such as cheque-bounce cases under the Negotiable Instruments Act, bank recovery, labour disputes, service matters, compoundable criminal cases and motor accident claims.

The benefits are straightforward. No court fee is charged, and any fee already paid is refunded when the dispute is settled. Procedure is flexible, so the Civil Procedure Code and the Evidence Act are not applied strictly, and parties can speak to the bench directly through their counsel. The Law Commission of India has also noted that such settlement is less costly and quicker, and keeps relationships intact.f6:T45f,The Legal Services Authorities Act was amended in 2002 to create Permanent Lok Adalats for public utility services. Their main features are:

- The bench has a chairman who is, or has been, a district judge, an additional district judge or a judicial officer of higher rank, plus two members with adequate experience of public utility services.
- Jurisdiction covers passenger and goods transport by air, road and water; postal, telegraph and telephone services; supply of power, light or water; public conservancy and sanitation; hospital and dispensary services; and insurance.
- The original pecuniary limit was ₹10 lakh. The Central Government may raise it, and in 2015 it was raised to ₹1 crore.
- A party may apply before any court case begins. Once an application is made, neither party may approach a court on the same dispute.
- If the bench sees a basis for settlement, it proposes terms. If the parties accept, an award follows; if not, the bench decides the dispute on its merits.
- Awards are final and binding and are passed by a majority of the bench. Offences that cannot be compounded are excluded.f7:T65a,The Family Courts Act of 1984 set up specialised courts to promote conciliation and speedy settlement of disputes about marriage and family affairs. The Law Commission's 59th Report (1974) urged a radically different approach to family disputes, and a 1976 amendment to the Code of Civil Procedure added a special procedure for them. Courts, however, kept treating family disputes as ordinary adversarial civil matters, and the Government concluded that separate courts were needed.

The Act aims at four things: expertise through a court devoted only to family matters, a mechanism for conciliation, an inexpensive remedy, and an informal atmosphere with flexible procedure.

The Act's main features are:

- State Governments set up Family Courts in consultation with the High Court. A court is compulsory in every city or town with a population above one million, and optional elsewhere.
- Exclusive jurisdiction covers matrimonial relief (nullity, judicial separation, divorce, restitution of conjugal rights, and validity of marriage), property of the spouses, legitimacy, guardianship and custody of minors, and maintenance of wife, children and parents.
- The court must first try to reconcile the parties. At this stage the proceedings are informal and rigid rules do not apply.
- Counsellors, social welfare agencies and medical experts may be involved during conciliation.
- A party has no automatic right to be represented by a lawyer, although the court may seek help from a legal expert as amicus curiae.
- Evidence and procedure are simplified, and there is only one right of appeal, which lies to the High Court.f8:T71a,The Gram Nyayalayas Act of 2008 provides village-level courts so that justice is available close to home and is not denied to anyone by social or economic disability. The Act follows the recommendations of the Law Commission's 114th Report and draws on Article 39A.

The main features are:

- A Gram Nyayalaya is a court of Judicial Magistrate of the First Class. Its presiding officer, the Nyayadhikari, is a judicial officer appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court, with the same salary and powers as a First Class Magistrate.
- A court is set up for each intermediate-level Panchayat, or for a group of contiguous Panchayats where there is no intermediate tier.
- Its seat is at the headquarters of the intermediate Panchayat, but it is mobile and goes to villages to hear cases.
- It exercises both criminal and civil powers over matters listed in the Act's two schedules, which the Centre and the states may amend within their competence.
- Criminal trials follow summary procedure. The court is not bound by the Indian Evidence Act but follows natural justice and any rules made by the High Court.
- It tries to bring about conciliation, using appointed conciliators, and an accused person may apply for plea bargaining.
- Appeals in criminal cases lie to the Court of Session, and civil appeals lie to the District Court. Both must be decided within six months of filing.

The Act does not make Gram Nyayalayas compulsory. Many states have instead created regular taluka-level courts, and police reluctance, a lukewarm response from the Bar and overlapping jurisdiction with regular courts have slowed their operation. The Conference of Chief Justices and Chief Ministers in April 2013 left the choice to each state and High Court, with a focus on talukas that lack regular courts.f9:T5f8,The Commercial Courts Act of 2015 created Commercial Courts, Commercial Appellate Courts, and Commercial Divisions and Commercial Appellate Divisions in the High Courts. They decide commercial disputes of a specified value. The Act defines a commercial dispute broadly, covering disputes arising from ordinary transactions of merchants, bankers, financiers and traders, including mercantile documents, joint ventures and partnership agreements, intellectual property and insurance.

The Act's main features are:

- A State Government may set up Commercial Courts at district level. Where a High Court has ordinary original civil jurisdiction, the courts are set up at district judge level instead.
- Commercial Appellate Courts at district judge level hear appeals from the lower commercial courts, outside the areas where High Courts have ordinary original civil jurisdiction.
- The Chief Justice of a High Court with ordinary original civil jurisdiction may constitute a Commercial Division to hear high-value commercial suits filed in that High Court.
- A Commercial Appellate Division, constituted by the Chief Justice, hears appeals against orders of district-level commercial courts and of the Commercial Division.
- The specified value must be at least ₹3 lakh, or any higher figure the Centre notifies. In 2018 it was reduced from ₹1 crore to ₹3 lakh.
- Pre-institution mediation is compulsory before a suit that does not seek urgent interim relief. The Centre may empower Legal Services Authorities to conduct it.fa:T48c,- Articles 233 to 237 govern the lower judiciary: the governor appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court, and the High Court controls the subordinate judiciary.
- A district judge is a sessions judge for criminal work; a death sentence needs High Court confirmation.
- The Legal Services Authorities Act of 1987 created NALSA and the state, district and taluk legal aid bodies that provide free legal services.
- Lok Adalat awards are final, binding and treated as decrees; no appeal lies against them.
- Lok Adalats cannot settle offences that are not compoundable under any law.
- Permanent Lok Adalats (2002) hear disputes in public utility services, such as transport, power, postal and insurance services.
- Family Courts (1984) must reconcile parties first, and their only appeal lies to the High Court.
- Gram Nyayalayas (2008) are village-level courts; the Act does not make them compulsory.
- Gram Nyayalaya criminal appeals go to the Court of Session and civil appeals to the District Court, each within six months.
- Commercial Courts (2015) take commercial disputes of at least ₹3 lakh, and pre-institution mediation is compulsory.fb:T8a5,The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was set up in 1985, with its principal bench at New Delhi. It now has nineteen regular benches, seventeen of them at the seats of High Courts and the other two at Jaipur and Lucknow. Benches also hold circuit sittings at other High Court seats. The benches are not all named after their cities, so the territory each one covers matters. A selection:

| Bench | Territory covered |
|---|---|
| Principal Bench, New Delhi | National Capital Territory of Delhi |
| Allahabad Bench | Uttar Pradesh, excluding the districts under the Lucknow Bench, and Uttarakhand |
| Cuttack Bench | Odisha |
| Hyderabad Bench | Andhra Pradesh and Telangana |
| Calcutta Bench | West Bengal, Sikkim and Andaman and Nicobar Islands |
| Guwahati Bench | Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Tripura, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh |

The CAT has original jurisdiction over recruitment and service matters of the public servants it covers. That includes the All-India Services, the central civil services, civil posts under the Centre, and civilian employees of the defence services. Members of the defence forces are not covered, nor are officers and servants of the Supreme Court or the secretarial staff of Parliament.

Its composition has changed over time. The CAT originally had a Chairman, a Vice-Chairman and Members. The Administrative Tribunals (Amendment) Act of 2006 removed the Vice-Chairman, so the Tribunal now has only a Chairman and Members. Members are drawn from both judicial and administrative backgrounds. A person under fifty cannot be appointed Chairman or Member. Under the Tribunals Reforms Act of 2021, the term is four years, or until the age of 70 for the Chairman and 67 for Members, whichever comes first.

Appointments are made by the Central Government on the recommendation of a search-cum-selection committee. The committee is chaired by the Chief Justice of India, or by a Supreme Court judge the Chief Justice nominates.

The CAT is not bound by the Civil Procedure Code of 1908. It follows the principles of natural justice, which keeps its procedure flexible. The applicant pays a nominal fee of ₹50 and may argue the case personally or through a lawyer.fc:T648,The National Commission has three kinds of jurisdiction. Its pecuniary jurisdiction covers complaints where the value of the goods or services paid for exceeds a stated threshold; the threshold was originally above ten crore rupees and was lowered in 2021 to above two crore rupees. Its appellate jurisdiction covers appeals against orders of any State Commission, which must be filed within 30 days of the order. A late appeal may still be admitted on showing sufficient cause. It also hears appeals against orders of the Central Consumer Protection Authority, within 30 days of receiving that order.

Its revisional jurisdiction lets it call for the records of any consumer dispute pending before, or decided by, a State Commission. This applies in three situations: the State Commission exercised a power that the law did not give it; it failed to exercise a power that the law did give it; or it acted illegally or with a material irregularity.

Beyond these, the National Commission can declare an unfair contract term null and void. It can review its own order for an error apparent on the face of the record, either on its own motion or on a party's application made within 30 days. It can set aside an order passed ex parte when the aggrieved party applies. It can also transfer a complaint from a District Commission in one state to a District Commission in another state, or from one State Commission to another, on a complainant's application or on its own motion. Appeals against its orders lie with the Supreme Court, within 30 days, again with a power to admit late appeals on sufficient cause.fd:T42d,Each State Commission has a President and not less than four members. The maximum number of members is prescribed in consultation with the central government. The central government lays down the qualifications, mode of recruitment, term and removal; the state government sets salaries and allowances.

The State Commission hears complaints where the consideration paid lies above one crore rupees and up to ten crore rupees, originally. The 2021 revision narrowed this band to above fifty lakh rupees and up to two crore rupees. It hears appeals against District Commission orders within 45 days, a longer period than the 30 days that applies to the National Commission. It may also call for and correct the records of District Commissions in the same way as the National Commission does. In addition, it can strike down unfair contract terms, review its own orders for an error apparent on the record within 30 days, and transfer a complaint between District Commissions within its state. It exercises administrative control over the District Commissions in its area.fe:T456,- The 2019 Act repealed the 1986 Act and keeps three tiers: District, State and National consumer commissions.
- State governments create District and State Commissions; the central government creates the National Commission.
- The National Commission has a President and four to eleven members under the 2020 rules, with at least one woman.
- Members of the National Commission are appointed on the advice of a selection committee chaired by the Chief Justice of India or a nominated Supreme Court judge.

- The National Commission supervises the State Commissions and investigates allegations against their members, without disturbing their quasi-judicial freedom.ff:T5f3,In January 1957 the Government of India appointed a committee under Balwantrai G. Mehta to study the Community Development Programme (1952) and the National Extension Service (1953). Reporting in November 1957, it proposed "democratic decentralisation", later known as Panchayati Raj.

- **Three tiers:** gram panchayat (village), panchayat samiti (block), zila parishad (district), linked by indirect elections.
- **Membership:** the village body directly elected; samiti and parishad indirectly elected.
- **Roles:** the samiti is the executive body; the parishad is advisory, coordinating and supervisory, with the Collector as chairman.
- **Substance:** all planning and development handed over, with real transfer of power and adequate resources.

The National Development Council accepted these ideas in January 1958 but let states choose their own patterns, provided the basic principles were common. Rajasthan was first: the Prime Minister inaugurated the scheme at Nagaur on 2 October 1959, and Andhra Pradesh followed the same year. States then diverged on tiers, tenure, composition and finance.

| Pattern | Example | Feature |
|---|---|---|
| Three-tier | Rajasthan | Samiti powerful because the block is the planning unit |
| Two-tier | Tamil Nadu | Only two levels |
| Four-tier | West Bengal | An extra level |
| Maharashtra–Gujarat | Maharashtra, Gujarat | Zila parishad powerful because the district is the planning unit |

Some states also set up nyaya panchayats to try petty civil and criminal cases.100:T6d4,Many study teams examined particular aspects after 1960 (for example the Santhanam committees on finances and elections, and the Diwakar team on the Gram Sabha). Five committees shaped the road to constitutionalisation.

| Committee | Year | Core ideas |
|---|---|---|
| Ashok Mehta | 1977–78 (Janata government) | 132 recommendations; replace three tiers with two (zila parishad and mandal panchayat of 15,000–20,000 people); district as the base unit; compulsory taxation powers; social audit; elections within six months after supersession; seats for SCs and STs by population; constitutional recognition. Rao report also differed from the Hanumantha Rao (1984) report, which preferred separate district planning bodies with the Collector as coordinator.101:T4be,- **Gram Sabha (Article 243A):** all registered voters of the panchayat area; it performs the functions the state legislature gives it.
- **Three tiers:** village, intermediate and district. A state with a population not above 20 lakh need not create the intermediate tier.
- **Elections:** every member at all levels is directly elected. Chairpersons at the intermediate and district levels are chosen indirectly, from among the elected members; the village chairperson is chosen as the state law decides. All members, including chairpersons, vote in meetings.
- **Reservation for SCs and STs:** seats in proportion to their population in the panchayat area, at all three levels, plus reservation of chairperson posts as the state decides.
- **Reservation for women:** at least one-third of seats (including those within SC and ST quotas) and at least one-third of chairperson posts at every level.
- **Backward classes:** reservation is optional and left to the state legislature.

Ten states have Fifth Schedule areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, **Odisha** and Rajasthan. The Act aims at self-rule for tribal people, makes the Gram Sabha the centre of village affairs, fits administration to traditional practice, protects tribal customs, and stops higher-level panchayats from taking over lower-level powers.

- **Customary law:** state legislation must respect custom, religious practice and traditional management of community resources.
- **Gram Sabha role:** it approves development plans before the panchayat takes them up, identifies beneficiaries of poverty alleviation schemes, and certifies fund use.
- **Reservation:** seats are proportional to population but STs get at least half, and all chairperson posts at every level go to STs. The state may nominate unrepresented STs to intermediate and district panchayats up to one-tenth of elected members.
- **Land and projects:** the Gram Sabha or panchayat must be consulted before land acquisition and resettlement; minor water bodies are managed by panchayats.
- **Minor minerals:** recommendation of the Gram Sabha or panchayat is mandatory for prospecting licences and mining leases, and prior recommendation for auctions of concessions.
- **Specific powers:** enforce or restrict intoxicants, own minor forest produce, prevent land alienation and restore unlawfully alienated tribal land, manage village markets, control money-lending to STs, supervise social-sector institutions, and control local plans including tribal sub-plans.
- **Model:** the Sixth Schedule pattern is to be followed for district-level arrangements. Inconsistent laws lapsed one year after assent.104:T53f,Panchayats draw funds from Union grants (Central Finance Commission, Article 280), State Finance Commission devolution (Article 243-I), state loans and grants, Centrally Sponsored Schemes and their own tax and non-tax revenue. The Second Administrative Reforms Commission found that own revenue is thin, dependence on grants is heavy, and much of the grant money is tied to schemes. Village panchayats hold most tax powers (property, profession, land, vehicles, entertainment, water, lighting); the higher tiers rely on tolls, fees and non-tax items. The result is responsibility without matching resources.

Reasons commonly given for weak performance:

- inadequate devolution of the "3Fs": functions, funds and functionaries;
- bureaucratic control that makes sarpanches run to block offices;
- tied funds that do not suit local needs;
- over-dependence on government money, which reduces demand for social audit;
- reluctance to levy taxes on one's own neighbours;
- Gram Sabha powers left unspecified in many state Acts;
- parallel bodies and missions that bypass panchayats;
- poor infrastructure, no full-time secretary, and poorly trained, often semi-literate representatives.

The first municipal corporation was set up at Madras in 1688, under a charter issued in December 1687. Corporations followed at Bombay and Calcutta in 1726. Lord Mayo's Resolution of 1870 on financial decentralisation encouraged self-government institutions. Lord Ripon's Resolution of 1882 is treated as the Magna Carta of local self-government, and Ripon is called its father in India. The Royal Commission on Decentralisation, appointed in 1907 and reporting in 1909 under C. E. H. Hobhouse, took the matter further.

Under the 1919 Act, local self-government became a transferred subject under an Indian minister in the provinces. In 1924 the central legislature passed the Cantonments Act, and under the 1935 Act local government was declared a provincial subject.

After independence, the Central government appointed a series of committees and commissions to improve urban bodies. Their chairmen and years are listed below.

Correa |107:T57b,Every state must have three kinds of municipality: a nagar panchayat, for a transitional area that is moving from rural to urban; a municipal council, for a smaller urban area; and a municipal corporation, for a larger urban area. There is one exception. Where an industrial establishment provides municipal services in an area, the Governor may declare that area an industrial township, and no municipality is then constituted.

The Governor decides which category an area falls into. The criteria are the population, the density of population, the revenue raised for local administration, the share of employment in non-agricultural activity, the area's economic importance, and any other factor the Governor considers relevant.

Every member of a municipality is elected directly by the people of the municipal area. The area is divided into territorial constituencies called wards. The state legislature decides how the chairperson is chosen, and it may also provide for the following persons to sit in a municipality. Persons with special knowledge or experience of municipal administration may sit, but without a vote in meetings. Members of the Lok Sabha and of the state assembly whose constituencies lie wholly or partly in the area may sit, as may Rajya Sabha and state council members registered as electors there. Chairpersons of committees, other than ward committees, may also be included.108:T587,A municipality has a five-year term from its first meeting. It may be dissolved earlier, but a fresh election must be completed before the five years expire, or, after a dissolution, within six months of it. If the balance of the term left after dissolution is less than six months, no fresh election is needed for that remainder. A municipality constituted after an early dissolution serves only for the balance of the original term, so it does not get a full five years.

Two safeguards apply to dissolution. The municipality must be given a reasonable opportunity to be heard first. And no amendment of any law can cause a dissolution before the five-year term ends.

A person is disqualified from membership if disqualified under the election law for the state legislature, or under a state law. Age is not a bar once a person has reached 21, even if he or she is under 25. The state legislature decides which authority settles disqualification disputes.

Superintendence, direction and control of electoral rolls and of all municipal elections belong to the State Election Commission. The state legislature may legislate on every other matter connected with those elections. Courts may not question any law on the delimitation of constituencies or the allotment of seats. An election may be challenged only by an election petition, filed before the authority and in the manner the state legislature prescribes.109:T466,The state legislature may give municipalities the powers they need to work as self-government institutions. These may include the power to prepare plans for economic development and social justice, and to implement schemes entrusted to them, covering the eighteen matters in the Twelfth Schedule.

On finance, the state legislature may authorise a municipality to levy and collect taxes, duties, tolls and fees. It may assign to municipalities taxes the state collects, provide grants-in-aid from the state's Consolidated Fund, and create funds into which municipal money is paid. Each state's finance commission reviews municipal finances every five years and reports to the Governor on sharing revenue, which taxes may be assigned, grants and measures to strengthen municipal finances. The Governor lays that report, with an action-taken memorandum, before the state legislature. The Central Finance Commission then suggests how the state's Consolidated Fund can be augmented to support municipalities, based on the state commission's report. The state legislature also regulates how municipal accounts are kept and audited.10a:T6b0,The Part applies to Union Territories. The President may apply it to a Union Territory with exceptions and modifications. In 2001 the President directed that the district and metropolitan planning provisions (Articles 243ZD and 243ZE) would not apply to the National Capital Territory of Delhi.

Each state must set up a district planning committee to consolidate the plans of panchayats and municipalities in the district and prepare a draft development plan for the whole district. Four-fifths of its members must be elected by the elected members of the district panchayat and of the municipalities, in proportion to the rural and urban populations. In preparing the plan, the committee must consider common matters between rural and urban bodies, such as spatial planning, water sharing and environmental conservation, and the resources available. A metropolitan area, with a population of ten lakh or more, must have a metropolitan planning committee. Two-thirds of its members are elected by municipal councillors and panchayat chairpersons in proportion to the population of each. It must also consider the plans of the local bodies, the national and state priorities and the investments made by central and state agencies.

The Part does not apply to scheduled and tribal areas, and it does not affect the functions of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council in West Bengal. Parliament may nevertheless extend the Part to scheduled areas, with exceptions it specifies. Existing municipal laws continued for one year from 1 June 1993, and the states had to adopt the new system within that period. Municipalities existing at commencement continue until their term ends, unless the state dissolves them earlier.10b:Tfd0,India has eight kinds of urban local body: the municipal corporation, the municipality, the notified area committee, the town area committee, the cantonment board, the township, the port trust and the special purpose agency. The first four are created by state law, though the ones in Union Territories come from Parliament. Each of the eight has a different origin and character, and examiners often test the differences.

**Municipal corporation.** These run large cities, and each state creates them by an act of the state legislature, or a common act for all corporations in the state. A corporation has three authorities: a council, standing committees and a commissioner. The council is the deliberative and legislative wing, made up of elected councillors and a few nominated persons with municipal experience. It is headed by a mayor, who serves a one-year renewable term in most states and is largely a ceremonial head who presides over council meetings. Standing committees handle public works, education, health, taxation and finance, because the full council is too large to work directly. The commissioner, appointed by the state government and usually an IAS officer, is the chief executive who carries out the decisions.

**Municipality.** These run towns and smaller cities, under names such as municipal council, municipal board or city municipality. Like a corporation, a municipality has a council, standing committees and a chief executive officer. Its president or chairman presides over council meetings and, unlike the mayor, holds real executive power, making him or her the pivot of municipal administration. The chief executive officer, appointed by the state government, runs daily administration.

**Notified area committee.** Created by a gazette notification, this body serves a fast-growing industrial town, or a place not yet meeting the conditions for a municipality but important to the state. Its powers are close to those of a municipality, but every member, including the chairman, is nominated by the state government. It is therefore neither elected nor a statutory body in the strict sense.

**Town area committee.** This semi-municipal body administers a small town with a limited set of functions, such as drainage, roads, street lighting and conservancy. A separate state act creates it, and it may be wholly elected, wholly nominated, or partly both.

**Cantonment board.** This body serves the civilian population of a cantonment, the delimited area where troops are permanently stationed. It is set up under the Cantonments Act, 2006, which replaced the 1924 Act, and it is both created and administered by the Central government through the defence ministry. The chapter records 62 cantonment boards, grouped into four categories by civil population: above 50,000; 10,000 to 50,000; 2,500 to 10,000; and below 2,500. Its military officer commanding the station is the ex-officio president, and a vice-president is elected from among the elected members. Its executive officer is appointed by the President of India and belongs to a central cadre.

**Township.** Large public enterprises set up townships to provide civic amenities to staff living in colonies near their plants. An administrator appointed by the enterprise runs it, and it has no elected members. It is an extension of the enterprise's bureaucracy.

**Port trust.** Port areas such as Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai have port trusts, created by an Act of Parliament. They manage and protect the port and provide civic amenities. The membership is partly elected and partly nominated, and the chairman is an official.

**Special purpose agency.** These bodies are function-based rather than area-based. Examples include town improvement trusts, urban development authorities, water and sewerage boards, housing boards, pollution control boards, electricity boards and city transport boards. They are created either by a state statute or by an executive resolution. They are autonomous, and they are not subordinate to the municipal bodies.10c:T5fa,Personnel arrangements take one of three forms. Under a separate personnel system, each local body recruits and controls its own staff, and they cannot move to other bodies; this is the most common system and upholds local autonomy. Under a unified system, the state government appoints and controls municipal staff through state-wide cadres that can be transferred between local bodies; it is found in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, among others. Under an integrated system, municipal staff are members of the state services and can move between local bodies and state departments; Odisha, Bihar, Karnataka, Punjab and Haryana follow it. Several national training bodies serve municipal staff, including the All-India Institute of Local Self-Government, the National Institute of Urban Affairs and the Human Settlement Management Institute.

Urban bodies have five sources of income. Tax revenue includes property tax, the most important tax, along with entertainment, advertisement, professional, water and market taxes and various cesses. Non-tax revenue includes rent, fees and fines, and user charges for water, sanitation and sewerage. Grants come from the Central and state governments for development and reform schemes. Devolution is the transfer of funds from the state, made on the state finance commission's recommendations. Loans come from the state government and financial institutions for capital spending, and borrowing from other institutions needs the state's approval.10d:T4c5,- Eight urban bodies: municipal corporation, municipality, notified area committee, town area committee, cantonment board, township, port trust, special purpose agency.

Each territory was created for one of four broad reasons. Delhi and Chandigarh were political and administrative choices, Puducherry and the merged Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu reflect cultural distinctiveness, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep were valued for strategic reasons. A fourth group, Mizoram, Manipur, Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh, was given union territory status to give special care to backward and tribal peoples before they became states.

In 2019 the old state of Jammu and Kashmir was split into two. The government argued that Ladakh, a large but thinly peopled region with difficult terrain, needed its own status and would have no legislature. Jammu and Kashmir, facing cross-border terrorism, was given a legislature of its own. In 2020 the two small territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu were merged. The reasons offered were shared officers, duplicated secretariats and departments, and the policy of "Minimum Government, Maximum Governance".110:T693,Only three union territories have an elected legislature and a council of ministers headed by a chief minister: Puducherry (since 1963, 30 members), Delhi (since 1992, 70 members) and Jammu and Kashmir (since 2019, 83 members). The other five have no such institutions. Having a local legislature does not reduce the supreme control of the President and Parliament.

Parliament may legislate for any union territory on any subject of the three lists, including the State List, and this power continues even where a local assembly exists. The local assemblies have narrower reach. Puducherry's may legislate on State and Concurrent List subjects. Delhi's excludes public order, police and land, and Jammu and Kashmir's excludes public order and police.

The President may make regulations for the peace, progress and good government of four territories: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Ladakh. For Puducherry the President may do so only when its assembly is suspended or dissolved. A regulation has the force of an Act of Parliament and can repeal or amend such an Act in its application to that territory.

Parliament can set up a high court for a union territory or attach it to a neighbouring state's high court. Delhi is the only union territory with its own high court, which dates from 1966. Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu falls under the Bombay High Court, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands under the Calcutta High Court, Chandigarh under the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Lakshadweep under the Kerala High Court and Puducherry under the Madras High Court. Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh share one high court.111:T616,The Sixty-ninth Amendment Act of 1991, in force from 1 February 1992, gave Delhi special status under Article 239AA. It became the National Capital Territory of Delhi, its administrator became a Lieutenant Governor, and it received an assembly and a council of ministers.

- **Assembly:** 70 members, directly elected, with elections conducted by the Election Commission. It can legislate on the State and Concurrent Lists except public order, police and land. Parliament's laws prevail over its laws.
- **Council of ministers:** limited to ten per cent of the assembly, so at most seven: a chief minister and six other ministers. The President appoints the chief minister, and the others on his advice. They hold office at the President's pleasure and are collectively responsible to the assembly.
- **Lieutenant Governor:** acts on ministerial advice except where he must use his own discretion. If he disagrees with his ministers, the matter goes to the President, whose decision he follows.
- **Failure of machinery:** when the arrangements cannot work, the President may suspend them under Article 239AB and provide for the administration. The power resembles the President's rule under Article 356 in the states, and may be triggered by the Lieutenant Governor's report or otherwise.
- **Ordinances:** the Lieutenant Governor may promulgate them during the assembly's recess, but the assembly must approve each within six weeks of reassembling. He cannot do so when the assembly is dissolved or suspended, and he needs the President's prior permission.112:T49c,- Article 1: three categories of territory; today 28 states, 8 union territories and no acquired territory.
- Union territories were formed as a category in 1956 through the Seventh Amendment and the States Reorganisation Act.
- The eight UTs: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Delhi and Lakshadweep (1956), Puducherry (1962), Chandigarh (1966), Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh (2019), and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu (2020).
- Articles 239 to 241 in Part VIII; the administrator is the President's agent, not a head of state.
- Lieutenant Governors run Delhi, Puducherry, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh; administrators run the other three.
- Legislatures exist in Puducherry (1963), Delhi (1992) and Jammu and Kashmir (2019) only.
- Delhi: 70-member assembly; excludes public order, police and land; council of ministers capped at seven.
- Article 239AB allows the President to suspend Delhi's arrangements; Delhi ordinances need approval within six weeks.
- Parliament legislates on all three lists for UTs; only Delhi has its own high court among UTs (since 1966).
- Five UTs without a legislature have an HMAC or AAC for development discussion.113:T557,The Fifth Schedule works through the state government, with the Governor holding special responsibility and the Centre able to give directions. The Sixth Schedule creates a form of tribal self-rule through elected councils. The table below sets out the contrast.

| Point | Fifth Schedule | Sixth Schedule |
|---|---|---|
| Where it applies | Scheduled areas in any state other than the four north-eastern ones | Tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram |
| Main emphasis | Protection and administration by the state, with Union oversight | Self-rule and preservation of democratic traditions |
| Local units | Scheduled areas, each with a Tribes Advisory Council | Autonomous districts and regions, each with its own councils |
| Lawmaking locally | Governor's regulations, subject to the President's assent | District and regional council laws, subject to the Governor's assent |
| Articles | Article 244 and Article 339 | Article 244, with Article 244A on an autonomous state formed from Assam's tribal areas |

The Sixth Schedule areas are not separate from the state's executive. They stay under the state's executive authority, but their councils carry real local powers. The chapter notes that these communities had governed themselves until the British brought them under control in the nineteenth century, which explains the stress on self-rule.114:T74f,Under the Sixth Schedule, the tribal areas of the four north-eastern states are constituted as autonomous districts. They stay within the executive authority of their states. Their administration rests on the following features:

- The Governor can organise and reorganise autonomous districts, enlarge or shrink them, rename them or redraw their boundaries. Where several tribes live in one district, he may divide it into autonomous regions.
- Each autonomous district has a district council of 30 members: 26 elected on adult franchise for five years, and four nominated by the Governor, who serve at his pleasure. Each autonomous region has its own regional council.
- The councils make laws on matters such as land, forests, canal water, shifting cultivation, village administration, inheritance, marriage and divorce and social customs. Those laws need the Governor's assent.
- Councils may set up village councils or courts for suits between tribes and hear appeals from them. The Governor specifies how far the High Court's jurisdiction over those cases extends.
- A district council can run primary schools, dispensaries, markets, ferries, fisheries and roads. It can also regulate money-lending and trade by non-tribals, again with the Governor's assent.
- The councils assess and collect land revenue and impose certain taxes.
- Acts of Parliament and of the state legislature do not apply to these areas, or apply only with modifications.
- The Governor can appoint a commission to inquire into the administration of these areas, and may dissolve a council on that commission's recommendation.

The power of direction over these Acts varies by state. In Assam it rests with the Governor for both Parliament's and the state's Acts. In Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram the President directs on Acts of Parliament and the Governor on Acts of the state legislature.115:T46d,- Article 244, Part X: Fifth Schedule for scheduled areas in most states; Sixth Schedule for tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
- The Fifth Schedule is often called a constitution within the Constitution; it aims at protecting tribal culture and land.
- The President declares scheduled areas after consulting the Governor; ten states have them.
- The Governor reports annually to the President and can make regulations on land transfer and money-lending.
- A Tribes Advisory Council has 20 members, three-quarters of them tribal MLAs.
- Article 339: the President must appoint a commission at least once ten years after the Constitution began; the first was 1960 and the second 2002.
- Sixth Schedule tribal areas are autonomous districts that stay under the state's executive authority.
- A district council has 30 members: 26 elected, 4 nominated by the Governor; five-year elected terms.
- District and regional council laws need the Governor's assent; councils may collect land revenue and certain taxes.
- Ten Sixth Schedule tribal areas: three each in Assam and Meghalaya, one in Tripura, three in Mizoram.116:T575,Article 324 provides that the Commission has a Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and as many other election commissioners as the President may fix from time to time. Both the CEC and the other commissioners are appointed by the President. If other commissioners are appointed, the CEC acts as chairman. The President may also appoint regional commissioners, after consulting the Commission, to assist it. Service conditions and tenure are determined by the President, subject to any law of Parliament.

The body's size has changed over time.

| Period | Position |
|---|---|
| 1950 to 15 October 1989 | Single-member body: only the CEC |
| 16 October 1989 | Two more commissioners appointed because the voting age had been lowered from 21 to 18 (61st Amendment, 1988); a three-member body |
| January 1990 | The two posts abolished; back to a single member |
| October 1993 | Two commissioners appointed again; a three-member body since then |

The Election Commission (Conditions of Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 1991 adds the following. The CEC and the two commissioners have equal powers and receive pay, allowances and perquisites like those of a Supreme Court judge. Differences of opinion are settled by majority vote of the Commission. The term is six years or until age 65, whichever comes first, and any member can resign by writing to the President.117:T4fc,Its authority over elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President falls into three groups.

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| Administrative | Fix constituency boundaries under the Delimitation Commission Acts; prepare and revise electoral rolls and register voters; announce election dates and scrutinise nominations; supervise the election machinery; request staff from the President or Governor; cancel polls in case of rigging, booth capturing or violence; prepare a roster for party broadcasts on radio and TV |
| Advisory | Advise the President on disqualification of MPs; advise the Governor on disqualification of state legislators; advise the President whether elections can be held in a state under President's Rule so that an Emergency can be extended beyond one year |
| Quasi-judicial | Settle disputes about recognition of political parties and allotment of symbols; appoint officers to enquire into disputes about electoral arrangements |

Other functions include recognising political parties, giving them national or state status according to poll performance, allotting symbols, and framing the code of conduct for parties and candidates. Parliament passed Delimitation Commission Acts in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002.118:T504,The President may remove the chairman or a member on three grounds: insolvency, paid employment outside the office during the term, and unfitness of mind or body as judged by the President. Removal for misbehaviour follows a different route. The President must refer the case to the Supreme Court. If the Court inquires, finds the charge proved and advises removal, the President must follow that advice. While the inquiry runs, the President may suspend the officer.

Misbehaviour is defined narrowly. It arises when the chairman or a member is concerned or interested in a government contract or agreement, or shares in its profit or benefit, other than as a member of an incorporated company with others.

Several safeguards protect independence:

- security of tenure, since removal is only on constitutional grounds;
- service conditions cannot be altered to the officer's disadvantage after appointment;
- salaries, allowances, pensions and staff costs are charged on the Consolidated Fund and not voted by Parliament;
- a former chairman cannot take any further government employment; and
- no officer can serve a second term.

A former member, by contrast, may become the chairman of the UPSC or of a State Public Service Commission, but cannot take any other government post.119:T5c5,The UPSC conducts examinations for the All-India Services, the Central Services and the public services of the centrally administered territories. It can help two or more states frame and run joint recruitment schemes where candidates with special qualifications are needed. On a state governor's request, and with the President's approval, it may serve any of that state's needs.

It must be consulted, and must advise, on:

- methods of recruitment to civil services and posts;
- principles for appointments, promotions and transfers between services, and the suitability of candidates for them;
- disciplinary matters affecting civil servants of the Union, including memorials and petitions on them;
- claims to reimburse legal expenses for acts done in official duty; and
- claims to pension for injuries suffered in service, and the amount awarded.

Parliament can add further functions, or extend its personnel jurisdiction to bodies such as corporations and public institutions. The UPSC submits an annual report to the President, who places it before both Houses with a memorandum explaining where government did not accept the Commission's advice and why.

Two Supreme Court rulings shape practice. Failure to consult the UPSC does not invalidate the government's decision, so the consultation provision is directory rather than mandatory. A selection by the UPSC confers no right to the post, though the government must act fairly and without arbitrariness or malice.11a:T4b4,The safeguards mirror the UPSC's. Security of tenure, unalterable service conditions and expenses charged on the state's Consolidated Fund all protect the commission. Post-retirement rules differ, though. A former SPSC chairman may be appointed chairman or member of the UPSC, or chairman of any SPSC, but no other government post. A former SPSC member may become chairman or member of the UPSC, or chairman of that or any other SPSC, and still cannot take other employment. In both cases a second term is barred.

An SPSC performs, for state services, the functions the UPSC performs for central services. It conducts examinations for state services and must be consulted on recruitment methods, the principles for appointments, promotions and transfers, disciplinary matters including memorials, legal-expense claims and pension claims for injuries. The Governor may refer any other matter to it. Additional functions can be conferred by a state law, which can also bring a local authority, corporate body or public institution within its jurisdiction.

The SPSC presents an annual report to the Governor, who places it before both Houses of the state legislature, with a memorandum on rejected advice.11b:T431,- Articles 315 to 323 in Part XIV govern the UPSC and the SPSCs; the Joint SPSC is statutory.
- The UPSC is appointed by the President; each SPSC by its Governor; the President alone removes both.
- Tenure: six years or 65 for the UPSC; six years or 62 for an SPSC (raised from 60 in 1976).
- At least half of each body's members need ten years' government service; no other qualifications are set.
- A member may act as chairman during a vacancy or absence; the acting chairman serves until the chairman returns or a new one takes over.
- Misbehaviour removal needs a Supreme Court inquiry and its advice is binding on the President.
- Both bodies are consulted but their advice is not binding; the UPSC is exempt from consultation only through regulations.
- Reservation matters and SC/ST claims lie outside both bodies' jurisdiction.
- A former UPSC chairman cannot take other government employment, but a governorship is a constitutional office, not employment.
- The Department of Personnel and Training is the personnel agency; the UPSC is only the recruiting agency.11c:T45a,Article 280 provides for a Finance Commission, which the Constitution describes as a quasi-judicial body. The President constitutes it every fifth year, or earlier if the President considers that necessary. The chapter's table lists fifteen commissions, the latest being the Fifteenth Commission chaired by N.K. Singh.

The commission has a chairman and four other members, all appointed by the President. They hold office for the period the President specifies in the order of appointment, and they may be reappointed. The Constitution leaves Parliament to decide the members' qualifications and the way they are selected, and Parliament has done so. The chairman must have experience in public affairs. The four other members are drawn from a fixed set of categories:

| Category | Who qualifies |
|---|---|
| Judicial | A high court judge, or a person qualified to be one |
| Accounts | A person with specialised knowledge of government finance and accounts |
| Administration | A person with wide experience in financial matters and administration |
| Economics | A person with special knowledge of economics |11d:T52f,The commission makes recommendations to the President on four kinds of matter. The first is the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Centre and the states, and the allocation of each state's share among the states. The second is the principles that should govern grants-in-aid from the Centre to the states, paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India. The third is the measures needed to augment a state's Consolidated Fund so that the panchayats and municipalities in that state can be supported, on the basis of the recommendations of the State Finance Commission. The fourth is any other matter that the President refers to it in the interests of sound finance.

The third function was added by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts of 1992. Those amendments gave constitutional status to panchayats and municipalities, and this role followed from that change.

Before 1960 the commission also recommended grants to Assam, Bihar, Odisha and West Bengal. These grants replaced a share of the export duty on jute and jute products and were meant to last for ten years from the commencement of the Constitution.

After the commission reports, the President lays the report before both Houses of Parliament, together with an explanatory memorandum on what action has been taken on each recommendation.11e:T709,The Council recommends to the Centre and the states on a set of core matters. Those matters include the taxes, cesses and surcharges of the Centre, the states and local bodies that will merge into GST, and the goods and services to be taxed or exempted. The Council also recommends the model GST laws, the principles of levy, the apportionment of tax on inter-state supplies, the place-of-supply rules, and the turnover threshold below which a dealer is exempted. It sets rates, including floor rates with bands, and it may recommend a special rate for a fixed period to raise revenue after a natural calamity or disaster. It also makes special provisions for Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Jammu and Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.

Three further functions stand out. First, the Council recommends the date from which GST applies to petroleum crude, high-speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel. Second, if a dispute arises over its recommendations or their implementation, the Council must establish a mechanism to adjudicate it. That mechanism covers disputes between the Centre and one or more states, disputes between the Centre and states on one side and other states on the other, and disputes between two or more states. Third, the Council recommends compensation to the states for loss of revenue caused by GST. This recommendation runs for five years, and Parliament then determines the compensation. Parliament enacted the Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act in 2017.

The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, later split the former state into two union territories, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, which is why the list in the Council's special provisions refers to the territory.11f:T495,- Article 280: the President constitutes a Finance Commission every fifth year, or earlier if needed; it is quasi-judicial.
- Finance Commission: one chairman and four members, appointed by the President, with qualifications set by Parliament.
- Four heads of recommendation: tax-proceeds sharing, grants-in-aid principles, augmenting funds for local bodies, and any reference by the President.
- Recommendations are advisory; the Union decides, and a state has no legal right to the money.
- Planning Commission overlapped with the Finance Commission until 2014; NITI Aayog replaced it in 2015.
- 101st Amendment (2016) inserted Article 279-A; the President's order came on 15 September 2016.

- Quorum is one-half of members; decisions need three-fourths of weighted votes, with the Union at one-third and states at two-thirds.
- The Council must set up a mechanism for disputes between the Centre and states, or between states.
- Compensation to states for GST revenue loss is recommended for five years, and Parliament determines it under a 2017 law.120:T485,The original Article 338 did not create a commission at all. It provided for a Special Officer for SCs and STs, who was to investigate the constitutional safeguards for both groups and report on them to the President. The arrangement then grew in steps, and the table below sets out each change.

| Year | Change |
|---|---|
| Original Constitution | Article 338 creates a Special Officer, also designated the Commissioner for SCs and STs |
| 1978 | A government resolution sets up a multi-member commission. It is not statutory, and the Commissioner post survives alongside it |
| 1987 | Another resolution revises its functions and renames it the National Commission for SCs and STs |
| 1990 | The 65th Amendment makes it a constitutional, multi-member body. The Act took effect only in 1992 |
| 2003 | The 89th Amendment splits it into the SC commission (Article 338) and the ST commission (Article 338A) |
| 2004 | The separate National Commission for SCs begins its work |

The 1978 and 1987 bodies rested on executive resolutions. Only the 1990 change placed the commission in the Constitution itself, which is why that step matters most for the exam.121:T4da,The story of the backward classes commission starts in court. In the Indra Sawhney case of 1992, widely known as the Mandal judgment, the Supreme Court told the Centre to create a permanent statutory body. Its task would be to examine complaints that a class had been wrongly included in, wrongly left out of, or wrongly excluded from the backward class lists. The National Commission for Backward Classes was set up in 1993 under a statute of that year.

The 102nd Amendment Act of 2018 changed its footing. It inserted Article 338B, which lifted the commission to constitutional status on a par with the SC and ST bodies, and a separate repeal Act of 2018 removed the 1993 statute. The same amendment added Article 342A, under which the President specifies the socially and educationally backward classes, and it enlarged the commission's functions to protect those classes more effectively.

The 105th Amendment Act of 2021 relaxed one link between the states and the commission. State governments no longer need to consult it when they prepare and keep their own lists of socially and educationally backward classes for their own purposes. The Centre and the states must still consult it on major policy matters that affect these classes.122:T406,- Articles 338 (SCs), 338A (STs) and 338B (backward classes) set up three constitutional commissions. The women, minorities, human rights and child rights bodies are statutory.
- 1978: a non-statutory commission by resolution. 1987: renamed the NCSC and STs. 1990: constitutional, in force 1992.
- 2003 (89th Amendment): split into two bodies. The separate NCSC and NCST began in 2004.
- 1999: the Ministry of Tribal Affairs was created. 2005: eight extra functions specified for the NCST.
- 1992 Indra Sawhney directive, then a statutory backward classes commission in 1993.
- 2018 (102nd Amendment): Articles 338B and 342A added. The NCSC lost its OBC role.
- 2021 (105th Amendment): states need not consult the NCBC on their own SEBC lists.

State reports go through the Governor (SCs and STs) or the state government (backward classes).123:T6c1,Article 149 empowers Parliament to set the CAG's duties and powers for the accounts of the Union, the states and other bodies. Parliament did so through the CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971. The table below lists the audit areas that follow from the Constitution and that Act.

| Audit area | What the CAG audits |
|---|---|
| Consolidated Funds | Expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, of each state, and of each union territory that has a legislature |
| Contingency and Public Accounts | Transactions of the Contingency Fund and Public Account of India, and the equivalent state funds and accounts |
| Commercial accounts | Trading, manufacturing, profit and loss accounts, balance sheets and subsidiary accounts kept by government departments |
| Substantially funded bodies | Receipts and expenditure of any body or authority mainly financed from central or state revenues |
| Grants and loans | Accounts of bodies that receive grants and loans for specific purposes |
| Revenue | All receipts of the Centre and the states, and whether the system of assessing and collecting revenue is effective |
| Stores and stock | Stores and stock held in every office and department |
| Government companies | Accounts of government companies, under the Companies Act |
| Statutory corporations | Corporations whose statutes provide for audit by the CAG |
| On request | Any other body, when the President or a Governor asks, for example local bodies |

To carry out this work, the CAG may inspect any office or department subject to audit, examine transactions and question the person in charge, call for any records or papers from the audited entity, and decide the extent and manner of the audit.124:T660,The CAG submits three audit reports to the President. The first is on appropriation accounts, which compare actual spending with the amounts that Parliament sanctioned through the Appropriation Act. The second is on finance accounts, which show the annual receipts and disbursements of the Union. The third is on public undertakings. The President lays all three before both Houses of Parliament, and the Public Accounts Committee then examines them and reports its findings. This chain is how the executive remains accountable to Parliament for financial administration.

Audit work falls into three kinds, and each is distinct in what it asks and whether it is compulsory.

| Kind of audit | Question it answers | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Legal and regulatory | Was the money legally available for the purpose, and does spending match the authority that governs it? | Compulsory |
| Propriety | Was the spending wise, faithful and economical, or was it wasteful or extravagant? | Discretionary |
| Performance | Were the social and economic objectives met, at what cost, and were the schemes run economically? | Within scope since a 2006 Finance Ministry memorandum |

The CAG's freedom differs by the type of transaction. For expenditure, the CAG decides the scope of audit and frames its own audit codes and manuals. For receipts, stores and stock, the CAG must work within rules that the executive government approves. Secret service spending is a limit on the audit: the CAG cannot call for its particulars and must accept a certificate from the competent administrative authority that the money was spent under its authority.125:T4d1,In performing official duties, the Attorney General has the right of audience in every court in India. The officer may speak and take part in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament, in a joint sitting, and in any parliamentary committee on which he is named a member. This right carries no vote. The Attorney General also enjoys the privileges and immunities of a Member of Parliament. Articles 88 and 105 govern these rights.

To avoid any complication or conflict of duty, several limits apply to the office. The Attorney General should not advise or hold a brief against the Government of India, nor advise or appear in a case where he has been called upon to act for the government. He should not defend an accused person in a criminal prosecution without the government's permission, and he should not accept a directorship in a company or corporation without that permission. Advice to a ministry, department, statutory body or public sector undertaking must arrive through the Ministry of Law and Justice, Department of Legal Affairs.

The Attorney General is not a full-time government counsel. He is not a government servant, and he is not barred from private legal practice, so long as the limits above are respected.126:T4ab,- Article 76: the Attorney General of India is the highest law officer of the Union and is appointed by the President.
- Union qualification: as for a Supreme Court judge, so an eminent jurist can qualify. State qualification: as for a High Court judge, with no eminent-jurist route.

- The President is elected by an electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs; the Vice-President by MPs.

The Regional Councils are a point of confusion. They are not permanent organs. They meet to deal with an issue that affects more than one state, and they are chaired by the Chairperson or a nominee. The Governing Council, by contrast, is a standing body of all states and the listed Union Territories.130:T655,The objectives run from policy to governance. They include building a shared national vision with the active involvement of states, fostering cooperative federalism on a continuous basis, and designing credible plans that start at the village level and rise to higher tiers. Two objectives deserve separate attention. One requires that national security interests be built into economic strategy where the body is specifically asked to do so. The other directs attention to sections of society at risk of not benefitting from economic progress.

The principles run as follows, with the guiding idea of each set out in brief:

- **Antyodaya:** service to the poor and marginalised, drawn from Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay's idea.
- **Inclusion:** redressing identity-based inequality by gender, region, religion, caste or class.
- **Village:** bringing villages into the development process.
- **Demographic dividend:** skilling and productive livelihoods for the people.
- **People's participation:** a participative citizenry as the driver of good governance.
- **Governance:** moving the focus from outlay to output to outcome.
- **Sustainability:** keeping sustainability at the core of planning.

The chapter also lists seven pillars of effective governance, covering pro-people and pro-active government, participation, the empowerment of women, inclusion with special attention to SCs, STs, OBCs and minorities, equal opportunity for youth, and transparency through technology. The principles and pillars are not interchangeable: the principles guide the work, while the pillars describe the kind of governance sought.131:T534,The organisation's work is split into two hubs. The Team India Hub carries forward cooperative federalism and designs policy and programme frameworks, and it co-ordinates engagement with the states. The Knowledge and Innovation Hub maintains a resource centre, a repository of research on good governance, and partnerships with universities, think tanks and non-governmental organisations. Functionally, the work falls under four heads: policy and programme framework; co-operative and competitive federalism; monitoring and evaluation; and think-tank, knowledge and innovation.

Cooperative federalism is pursued through structured engagement. Steps taken include meetings between the Prime Minister or Cabinet Ministers and all Chief Ministers, subgroups of Chief Ministers on national issues, the Aspirational Districts Programme for backward districts, model laws on land leasing and agriculture marketing, and separate interventions for the North-East, the Himalayan states and the islands.

Competitive federalism works by ranking. Transparent indices, such as the State Health Index, the India Innovation Index and the Export Competitiveness Index, encourage states to improve, and the body publishes monthly delta rankings for Aspirational Districts. The rankings are paired with hand-holding support rather than punishment.132:T6bc,The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by an executive resolution on the advice of the Advisory Planning Board of 1946. Like NITI Aayog, it was neither constitutional nor statutory, but its role was far more directive. It was a staff agency, so it advised rather than executed, and responsibility for decisions stayed with the Union and state governments. Yet its recommendations carried great weight, and critics called it a 'Super Cabinet' and a 'Parallel Cabinet'. The Commission was wholly Centre-constituted, and no state was represented in it.

| Aspect | Planning Commission | NITI Aayog |
|---|---|---|
| Established | March 1950 | 1 January 2015 |
| Legal basis | Executive resolution of the Union Cabinet | Executive resolution of the Union Cabinet |
| Head | Prime Minister | Prime Minister |
| Senior functional post | Deputy Chairman, the de facto executive head | Vice-Chairperson, with Cabinet Minister rank, plus a CEO |

The National Development Council was set up in August 1952 by executive resolution, on the recommendation of the First Five Year Plan's draft outline. It brought together the Prime Minister, Union Cabinet Ministers, state Chief Ministers, Union Territory Chief Ministers or administrators, and Planning Commission members. It approved national plans, including the 12th Plan, at its last recorded meeting, which was the 57th, in December 2012. A proposal to merge its powers into the NITI Aayog Governing Council was reported in 2016, but the chapter notes that no resolution had been passed to do so.133:T76f,The Commission is a multi-member body made up of a chairperson and five members. The chairperson is a retired Chief Justice of India or a retired judge of the Supreme Court. The members are a serving or retired Supreme Court judge, a serving or retired Chief Justice of a High Court, and three persons with knowledge or practical experience of human rights, at least one of them a woman. Seven ex-officio members also sit on the body: the chairpersons of the National Commissions for Minorities, SCs, STs, Women, BCs and Protection of Child Rights, and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities.

Appointment is made by the President on the recommendation of a six-member committee. The committee is headed by the Prime Minister and includes the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha, the leaders of the Opposition in both Houses and the Union Home Minister. A sitting Supreme Court judge or a sitting High Court Chief Justice may be appointed only after the Chief Justice of India has been consulted.

The chairperson and members serve for three years or until age 70, whichever comes first, and they can be re-appointed. After leaving office they may not take any further employment under the Union or a state government. Salaries and conditions of service are set by the Central government, but these cannot be changed to a member's disadvantage after appointment.

Removal is in the President's hands. The President can remove a member who has become insolvent, taken paid work outside the office, become unfit through infirmity of mind or body, been declared of unsound mind by a competent court, or been convicted and sentenced to imprisonment. Removal for proved misbehaviour or incapacity follows a different route: the President must refer the matter to the Supreme Court, and the member can be removed only if the Court upholds the charge and advises removal.134:T4f0,The Commission inquires into human rights violations and into negligence by public servants in preventing them. It can act on its own motion, on a petition, or on a court's order. Its other duties are to intervene in court proceedings where human rights allegations are pending, to visit jails and places of detention and recommend improvements, to review legal safeguards and terrorism-related factors that hinder rights, to study international instruments, to undertake research, to spread human rights literacy, and to encourage non-governmental organisations.

The Commission sits in Delhi and may set up offices elsewhere in India. It regulates its own procedure and has the powers of a civil court, and its proceedings have a judicial character. It has its own investigating staff and may use officers or agencies of the Central or state governments. It cannot inquire into a matter once one year has passed since the alleged violation, so it can take up only recent cases.

At the end of or during an inquiry, the Commission may recommend compensation or damages to the victim, prosecution or other action against a guilty public servant, or immediate interim relief. It may also approach the Supreme Court or the High Court for directions, orders or writs.135:T479,The Commission's functions are mainly recommendatory. It cannot punish violators, and it cannot itself award relief, including money. Its recommendations do not bind the government, but the government must report the action taken within one month. A former member argued that the Commission still carries great moral and practical weight, because no government can ignore its recommendations.

Its power over the armed forces is more limited. It may seek a report from the Central government and make recommendations, and the Central government must report the action taken within three months.

Annual and special reports go to the Central and state governments and are placed before the legislatures, together with a memorandum on the action taken and the reasons for rejecting any recommendation. The Commission has itself listed its problems: a need for devolved administrative and financial powers, a shortage of sanctioned staff, a shortage of experienced investigating officers, and a heavy complaint load of roughly one lakh cases a year. In 2017 the Supreme Court expressed concern about manpower and asked the government to address it.136:T5f6,A State Commission has a chairperson and two members. - The National Commission has a chairperson and five members; the State Commission has a chairperson and two members.
- The President appoints National Commission members on a six-member committee's recommendation, headed by the Prime Minister.
