The Central Government, and not the President, can remove the chairperson or a member before the term ends. The grounds are insolvency; a conviction for an offence that the government regards as involving moral turpitude; a competent court declaring the person of unsound mind; refusal or incapacity to act; three consecutive meetings missed without leave; and abuse of office that the government judges harmful to the public interest.13b:Ta00,The mandate has fourteen points. In brief, the Commission examines the constitutional and legal safeguards for women, reports on how they work every year, recommends better implementation or amendment of inadequate laws, takes up violations with the proper authorities and advises the government on policy. It also handles complaints and takes suo motu notice of rights violations, calls for special studies, carries out promotional research, advises on socio-economic planning, evaluates progress, inspects jails, remand homes and women's institutions, funds litigation that affects large numbers of women and deals with any matter the Centre refers to it.

For inquiries the Commission has the powers of a civil court trying a suit: it can summon people from anywhere in India, examine them on oath, call for documents, receive affidavits, requisition public records and issue summons. It may appoint committees for special issues and co-opt outsiders, who may take part in proceedings but cannot vote. The Commission sets its own procedure, and the Central Government must consult it on major policy affecting women.

Complaints may come orally or in writing, and the Commission also acts on suo motu cases. It registers them under 23 heads, from rape and acid attack to dowry death, bigamy, domestic violence, sex-selective abortion and traditional practices such as Sati and Devdasi, along with free legal aid. The way it acts depends on the kind of complaint:

| Kind of complaint | How the Commission acts |
|---|---|
| Police apathy | Referred to the police authorities for investigation, and the case is monitored |
| Family disputes | Settled or compromised through counselling |
| Information needs | Disaggregated data supplied to state authorities to prompt action |
| Sexual harassment | Concerned organisations urged to expedite cases, with disposal monitored |
| Serious violence | An Inquiry Committee set up to give immediate relief and justice to victims |

A footnote links workplace harassment to the Vishaka case of 1997, which required every employer to provide effective complaint procedures and remedies, including compensation for victims.

Annual reports go to the Central Government, and special reports may be sent at any time. The Centre lays them before both Houses of Parliament with a memorandum on the action taken, which must also give reasons for any recommendation not accepted. A report on a matter that concerns a state goes to that state government, which places it before the state legislature with the same memorandum.13c:T723,The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights was set up in 2007 under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005, which came into force on 5 February 2007. It is a statutory body, not a constitutional one, and it works under the administrative control of the Ministry of Women and Child Development. Its task is to protect, promote and defend child rights. Under the Act, child rights are those in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted on 20 November 1989 and ratified by India on 11 December 1992. The Convention defines a child as anyone below eighteen.

The Commission has a chairperson and six members, at least two of them women. The chairperson must be an eminent person with outstanding work for child welfare. The six members come from fields such as education, child health and development, juvenile justice or the care of neglected and disabled children, elimination of child labour, child psychology or sociology, and laws relating to children. The Central Government appoints them, but for the chairperson a three-member selection committee, chaired by the minister in charge of the women and child ministry, makes the recommendation.

Terms run for three years, and nobody may serve more than two terms. The upper age limit is 65 for the chairperson and 60 for members. Pay and service conditions are fixed by the Centre but cannot be varied to a holder's disadvantage after appointment. The chairperson can be removed only for proven misbehaviour or incapacity. Any member, and the chairperson on other grounds, can also be removed for insolvency, paid work outside the office during the term, refusal or incapacity to act, unsoundness of mind declared by a court, abuse of office, a conviction involving moral turpitude, or three consecutive meetings missed without leave.13d:T5f2,The mandate covers reviewing child-protection safeguards and recommending better implementation, annual and other reports to the Centre, and inquiries into violations of child rights, with a recommendation to start proceedings where needed. The Commission also examines what stops children affected by terrorism, communal riots, natural disasters, domestic violence, HIV/AIDS, trafficking or exploitation from enjoying their rights. It looks after children in need of special care, such as those in conflict with the law, juveniles, children without family and children of prisoners. It studies international instruments, promotes research, spreads child-rights literacy, inspects juvenile custodial homes and other places where children are kept, and acts on complaints or suo motu matters about rights deprivation, non-implementation of child laws and non-compliance with welfare decisions.

One limit must be remembered: the Commission cannot inquire into a matter already pending before a State Commission for Protection of Child Rights or another statutory commission.

During an inquiry the Commission has civil-court powers, much like the women's commission. When an inquiry ends, it may recommend prosecution or other action, approach the Supreme Court or a High Court for directions and writs, or recommend interim relief for the victim. Its annual and special reports go to the Central Government and to the concerned state government, and they are laid before the legislatures with a memorandum of action taken.13e:T446,The Government of India set up a Minorities Commission by an executive resolution issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs on 12 January 1978. The resolution recognised that, despite constitutional and legal safeguards, minorities still felt unequal and discriminated against, and that institutional machinery was needed to enforce those safeguards and protect secular traditions. Because a resolution carried little weight with state governments and Central ministries, the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992 gave the body statutory status. The Act came into force on 17 May 1993, the body was renamed the National Commission for Minorities, and the first statutory commission was constituted in 1993. It is autonomous and works under the Ministry of Minority Affairs, which was carved out of the social justice ministry in 2006.

The Act does not define "minority". Instead the Central Government notifies communities for its purposes. In 1993 it notified five: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Zoroastrians (Parsis). Jains were added by a notification dated 27 January 2014.13f:T56b,The Commission has a chairperson, a vice-chairperson and five members, all nominated by the Central Government from persons of eminence, ability and integrity. Terms are three years, and the Centre can remove a member for insolvency, a conviction involving moral turpitude, unsoundness of mind, refusal or incapacity to act, three consecutive absences without leave, or abuse of office that harms the interests of minorities or the public interest.

It is a high-powered independent body that receives complaints and decides appeals concerning offices, financial institutions and public sector undertakings under the Central Government and the Union Territories.

The Commission has a Chief Information Commissioner and not more than ten Information Commissioners. The President appoints them on the recommendation of a committee made up of the Prime Minister as chairperson, the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, and a Union Cabinet Minister whom the Prime Minister nominates. Appointees must be persons of eminence in public life with wide knowledge or experience in law, science and technology, social service, management, journalism, mass media or administration.

Some people are barred. A candidate may not be a Member of Parliament or a member of any state or Union Territory legislature. Pay, allowances and service conditions are prescribed by the Central Government and cannot be varied to a holder's disadvantage during service.

The President can remove the CIC or an Information Commissioner on five grounds: insolvency; a conviction for an offence that the President considers to involve moral turpitude; paid employment outside the office during the term; unfitness, in the President's opinion, through infirmity of mind or body; and acquiring a financial or other interest likely to affect official duties.

Removal for proved misbehaviour or incapacity follows a different route. The President must refer the matter to the Supreme Court for an enquiry, and removal can proceed only if the Court upholds the charge and advises it. Misbehaviour includes being interested in a central government contract, or sharing in its profit or benefit, other than as a member of an incorporated company that treats all members alike.143:T612,A person may complain to the Commission if no Public Information Officer (PIO) was appointed so that a request could not be filed, if information was refused, if no reply came within the time limit, if the fee seems unreasonable, if the information given is incomplete, misleading or false, or on any other matter about obtaining information. The Commission may also start an inquiry on its own motion where there are reasonable grounds.

For inquiries the Commission has civil-court powers: it can summon and examine persons on oath, call for documents, require discovery and inspection, receive affidavits, requisition public records and issue summons. Records under a public authority's control must be produced to it and cannot be withheld on any ground.

To enforce its decisions, the Commission may direct the authority to give information in a particular form, appoint a PIO where none exists, publish information, change how records are kept or destroyed, improve training for officials, seek an annual compliance report, order compensation for loss suffered by the applicant, impose penalties or reject the application. The penalty is levied on the PIO at the rate of ₹250 per day, up to ₹25,000 in all, and the Commission may also recommend disciplinary action against the official. Where an authority does not conform to the Act, the Commission may recommend the steps needed to bring it into line.

Third, it supervises the Delhi Special Police Establishment, which is the CBI, so far as the Establishment investigates offences under the 1988 Act. The CVC may give the CBI directions for that superintendence, review the progress of CBI investigations into these offences, and review pending applications for sanction to prosecute. Fourth, it exercises superintendence over the vigilance administration of the ministries and their organisations, advises the Central Government on referred matters, and handles complaints under the PIDPI Resolution.

The Central Government must consult the CVC when it frames rules and regulations on vigilance and disciplinary matters for the Central and All-India Services.147:T587,The CVC is the designated agency under the Public Interest Disclosure and Protection of Informers' Resolution, 2004, popularly called the Whistle Blowers Resolution. It receives and acts on complaints of corruption or misuse of office from whistle-blowers. It is also the only designated agency that may act against complainants who make motivated or vexatious complaints.

The Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 gives the same idea statutory form. It protects the identity of whistle-blowers, so that those who expose corruption or irregularities by public functionaries are not victimised, and it encourages disclosure of corruption or wilful misuse of power by public servants, including ministers. A disclosure is made before a competent authority, which for now is the CVC; the government may notify another body by notification. The Act punishes false or frivolous complaints with imprisonment of up to two years and a fine of up to ₹30,000.

Every disclosure must be made in good faith, with a personal declaration that the discloser reasonably believes the information and the allegation are substantially true. It may be made in writing or by email, with full particulars and supporting material. No action follows if the disclosure does not reveal the identity of the complainant or the public servant, or if that identity turns out to be wrong. The Act does not apply to the Special Protection Group.148:T403,- CVC set up in 1964 by executive resolution on the Santhanam Committee's advice; statutory from the CVC Act, 2003.
- Composition: a Central Vigilance Commissioner and not more than two Vigilance Commissioners, appointed by the President on a committee led by the Prime Minister.
- Committee members: Prime Minister, Union Home Minister and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha.
- Term: four years or age 65, whichever is earlier; no further government employment afterwards.
- Removal: President on the usual grounds; misbehaviour or incapacity needs a Supreme Court enquiry.
- Organisation: Secretariat, Chief Technical Examiners' wing, and Commissioners for Departmental Inquiries.
- Supervises the CBI only for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and reviews sanction applications.

- The CVC's annual report goes to the President, who lays it before Parliament.149:T6c1,The CBI is headed by a Director, who also serves as Inspector-General of the Delhi Special Police Establishment and runs the organisation. Special directors and additional directors assist the Director, and below them come joint directors, deputy inspectors-general, superintendents of police, forensic scientists and law officers.

The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 amended the 1946 Act and set out who recommends and who appoints the senior posts. The table shows the position:

| Post | Appointed by | Recommending body |
|---|---|---|
| Director of the CBI | Central Government | Panel of three: the Prime Minister presiding, the Leader of Opposition, and a Supreme Court judge who is the CJI or the CJI's choice |

The Delhi Special Police Establishment (Amendment) Act, 2014 altered the Director's committee. Where the Lok Sabha has no recognised Leader of Opposition, the leader of the single largest opposition party sits on the committee in that role.

The Director's tenure was fixed at two years under the CVC Act, 2003. The Amendment Act of 2021 let the Centre extend it to a maximum of five years in total. Each extension can last no longer than one year, and the Director can receive at most three annual extensions after the initial two years. An extension must be granted in the public interest, on the recommendation of the committee that made the original appointment, and the reasons must be recorded in writing.14a:T57e,The Bureau's remit is wide but has clear boundaries. The table lists its main duties:

| Area | What the CBI handles |
|---|---|
| Corruption and misconduct | Bribery, corruption and misconduct by employees of the central government |
| Economic and fiscal laws | Breaches of export-import control, customs, central excise, income tax and foreign exchange rules, usually in consultation with or at the request of the department concerned |
| Serious organised crime | Grave crimes of national or international reach committed by organised gangs of professional criminals |
| Coordination | Coordinating anti-corruption agencies and state police forces |
| State requests | Taking up a case of public importance at the request of a state government |
| Records | Keeping crime statistics and sharing criminal information |

The CBI's anti-corruption work normally covers offences by staff of the Union government, Union Territories and their public sector undertakings. It investigates conventional crimes such as murder, kidnapping or rape only on a reference from a state government, or when a Supreme Court or High Court directs it to. The Bureau also serves as India's National Central Bureau of Interpol. Its Interpol wing receives investigation-related requests from Indian agencies and from member countries and passes them on. The CBI further assists the Central Vigilance Commission and the Lokpal.14b:T480,The National Investigation Agency was constituted in 2009 under the National Investigation Agency Act, 2008. It is the central counter-terrorism law enforcement agency. The trigger was the 2008 Mumbai attacks, commonly called 26/11, which showed the need for a separate federal agency dedicated to terror-related crime. When the Bill was introduced, the government argued that cross-border terrorism had hit many parts of the country, and that many such attacks had inter-state and international links to arms and drug smuggling, fake currency and infiltration. Several expert committees and the Second Administrative Reforms Commission had also recommended a central agency.

The NIA's headquarters is in New Delhi, with branch offices in the states. It has a specialised cell, the TFFC Cell, which handles fake currency notes and terror funding. The agency is headed by a Director-General appointed by the Central Government, whose powers resemble those of a Director-General of Police in a state. The NIA works under the Ministry of Home Affairs, and state governments must give it all assistance and cooperation in investigating scheduled offences.14c:T4f0,The NIA has concurrent jurisdiction over offences that affect India's sovereignty, security and integrity, the security of the state, and friendly relations with foreign states. It also covers offences under laws that implement international treaties, agreements and conventions, and UN resolutions. Within this field it probes terror attacks such as bomb blasts, the seizure of aircraft or vessels, assaults on atomic facilities, and use of weapons of mass destruction. The 2019 extension brought in trafficking in persons, fake notes, dealing in banned weapons, cyber-terror and explosive materials.

The NIA (Amendment) Act, 2019 changed the Act in five main ways:

| Change | Effect |
|---|---|
| Scope abroad | Applies to scheduled offences committed outside India against Indian citizens or affecting India's interests |
| Powers abroad | NIA officers hold the powers that police officers have when investigating, both in India and outside it |
| Direction by the Centre | The Centre may direct the NIA to register and investigate a scheduled offence committed abroad as if it occurred in India |
| Courts | The Centre and the states may designate Sessions Courts as Special Courts for NIA trials |
| Schedule | New offences were inserted into the schedule |14d:T538,Three devices have been used around the world to redress grievances against administration: the ombudsman, the administrative courts and the procurator. The ombudsman is the oldest. Sweden created the office in 1809. The name comes from a Swedish word meaning a representative or spokesman, and the office holder is appointed by the legislature to examine complaints against administrative and judicial action. The Swedish ombudsman looks at abuse of discretion, maladministration, administrative corruption, nepotism and discourtesy.

The ombudsman supervises whether public officials, civil, judicial and military alike, act lawfully and impartially. It can act on a complaint or on its own initiative, and it may prosecute an erring official, judges included. It cannot reverse or quash a decision and has no direct control over the administration or the courts. Its only sanction is to report the matter to higher authorities. The model spread to Finland (1919), Denmark (1955) and Norway (1962). New Zealand adopted it in 1962 as a Parliamentary Commissioner for Investigation, the first Commonwealth country to do so, and the United Kingdom followed in 1967 with a Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration. France developed administrative courts for the same purpose, while the former USSR and China used a procurator system.14e:T542,India never relied on the ombudsman alone. Its existing framework spans several families of institution, summarised below:

| Category | Examples named in the chapter |
|---|---|
| Criminal and anti-corruption law | Indian Penal Code 1860, Prevention of Corruption Act 1988, Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act 1988, Delhi Special Police Establishment Act 1946, Commissions of Inquiry Act 1952 |
| Investigation and vigilance | Central Bureau of Investigation (1963), Central Vigilance Commission (1964), state vigilance commissions (1964), state anti-corruption bureaus, divisional vigilance boards |
| Conduct and service rules | All-India Services conduct and appeal rules, Central Civil Services conduct and appeal rules, Railway Services (Conduct) Rules, Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014 |
| Grievance redress | Directorate of Public Grievances in the Cabinet Secretariat (1988), Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (2007), the File to Field scheme in Kerala |
| Quasi-judicial and rights bodies | Consumer disputes commissions, national commissions for SCs, STs, BCs and minorities, administrative tribunals, the Supreme Court and High Courts |

The File to Field scheme in Kerala stands out because the administrator goes to the village or area, hears grievances on the spot and acts immediately where possible.14f:T756,The First Administrative Reforms Commission, headed by Morarji Desai, reported on the redressal of citizens' grievances in 1966 and recommended two authorities. A Lokpal would hear complaints against ministers and secretaries at the Centre and in the states. A lokayukta, one at the Centre and one in each state, would hear complaints against other specified senior officials. The Commission kept the judiciary outside both, following the New Zealand model. Its proposed Lokpal would be appointed by the President after consulting the Chief Justice of India, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

The Commission also wanted these institutions to be independent and impartial, non-political in appointment, and placed on a par with the highest judicial functionaries. It proposed private and informal proceedings, freedom from judicial interference, wide powers to obtain information, and no expectation of any benefit from the executive. The government accepted these recommendations, but a law took decades to arrive. Ten official bills were introduced, and their fates are shown below:

|---|---|---|

| December 2011 | Manmohan Singh (UPA) | Enacted as the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 |150:T88a,The Lokpal covers the Prime Minister, Union ministers, members of Parliament, and Group A, B, C and D officers and employees of the Central Government. The Prime Minister is within its purview, though some subject matters are excluded, and complaints against the Prime Minister follow a special process. The chapter notes that this process is considered non-transparent. Complaints that the Lokpal refers to the Central Vigilance Commission are handled according to group. For Group A and B officers, the CVC sends its preliminary enquiry report back to the Lokpal for decision. For Group C and D staff, the CVC proceeds under its own Act, subject to reporting to and review by the Lokpal.

The Lokpal may superintend and direct any investigating agency, including the CBI, in cases it refers. It can grant sanction to prosecute public servants in place of the Government or the competent authority. It can attach and confiscate property acquired by corrupt means, even while a prosecution is pending. Agencies financed wholly or partly by the Government fall within its reach, although aided institutions are excluded. Entities receiving foreign donations under the FCRA above ₹10 lakh a year are also covered.

The Act lifted the top sentence for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act from seven years to ten. It set minimum terms of three years for offences under sections 7, 8, 9 and 12, and two years for an attempt under section 15. It also fixed timelines for each stage:

| Stage | Initial period | Extension |
|---|---|---|
| Preliminary enquiry | Three months | Extendable by three months |
| Investigation | Six months | Extendable by six months at a time |
| Trial | One year | Extendable by one year, with special courts to be set up |

The Act also strengthens the CBI. It creates a Directorate of Prosecution under the Director of CBI, whose head is appointed on the CVC's recommendation. The CBI may maintain a panel of advocates other than government advocates, with the Lokpal's consent, for Lokpal cases. Officers who investigate Lokpal references can be transferred only with the Lokpal's approval, and the CBI must receive adequate funds for such cases.151:T489,Many states had Lokayuktas before 2013. Odisha passed its Act in 1970, and Maharashtra set up the first institution in 1971. The structure is not uniform. Some states have a Lokayukta and an Upalokayukta, while others have only a Lokayukta. The Governor appoints both. Judicial qualifications are prescribed in some states but not others. In most states the term is five years or until age 65, whichever comes earlier.

Jurisdiction differs even more. The Chief Minister falls within the Lokayukta's reach in some states and is excluded in others. Ministers and higher civil servants are covered in almost all states, members of the legislature in some, and local bodies, corporations, companies and societies in most. Most Lokayuktas can start an inquiry on a complaint or on their own initiative. Some handle both grievances (maladministration) and allegations (corruption), whereas others confine themselves to allegations. Each year the Lokayukta gives the Governor a consolidated report on its work. The Governor places it, with an explanatory memorandum, before the state legislature. Its recommendations are advisory and do not bind the state government.152:T40a,- Sweden created the first ombudsman in 1809; New Zealand adopted the model in 1962 and the UK in 1967.

- Lokayukta recommendations are advisory, and the report goes to the legislature through the Governor.153:T46e,The Act requires every state government to set up a State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA). The Chief Minister is the ex-officio chairperson. The chairperson of the State Executive Committee is an ex-officio member and also acts as the ex-officio chief executive officer. The chairperson of the SDMA nominates the other members, up to eight in number, and designates a vice-chairperson from among them. The total membership, including the chairperson, may not exceed nine.

The SDMA approves the State Plan in line with NDMA guidelines and approves the disaster plans of state departments. It lays down the state disaster management policy and guidelines for departments to integrate prevention and mitigation into their development plans. It coordinates the State Plan, recommends funds for mitigation and preparedness, and reviews the development plans of state departments to check that prevention is built in. The SDMA prepares an annual report on its work and submits it to the state government, which causes it to be laid before the state legislature. Where the legislature has two Houses, the report goes before each House.154:T639,The Act also requires a District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA) for every district in a state. The Collector, District Magistrate or Deputy Commissioner chairs it ex-officio. The local authority's elected representative serves as co-chair ex officio. In Tribal Areas under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution, the chief executive member of the autonomous district council takes that co-chair. Where a Zilla Parishad exists, its chairperson is also a co-chairperson. Three posts sit on the DDMA ex officio: its own chief executive, the district police chief (the superintendent of police) and the district's health head, the chief medical officer. The state government appoints not more than two further district-level officers as members, and it also appoints the chief executive officer. The DDMA's membership, excluding the chairperson, may not exceed seven.

The DDMA is the district planning, coordinating and implementing body. It prepares the district disaster management plan, including the district response plan, and coordinates and monitors the implementation of the national, state and district plans. It makes sure that vulnerable areas are identified and that departments and local authorities follow the prevention, mitigation, preparedness and response guidelines. It organises training for officers, employees and volunteer rescue workers, and it runs community awareness programmes. It maintains the early warning system and public information channels. It also identifies buildings and places that can serve as relief centres and arranges water and sanitation there.155:T418,- The Disaster Management Act, 2005 followed the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and created the NDMA.
- The NDMA was first constituted by executive order in 2005 and notified under the Act in 2006.
- The Prime Minister chairs the NDMA; the vice-chairperson has Cabinet Minister status and other members hold Minister of State status.
- The NDMA approves the National Plan and issues guidelines for State Plans and ministries' development plans.

- The NDMA and SDMA send annual reports to the Centre and the state government, which lay them before the legislatures.156:T4fb,The BCI sets the professional standards for the profession. It lays down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for advocates, and it prescribes the procedure that its own disciplinary committee and the disciplinary committees of the state councils must follow. It safeguards the rights, privileges and interests of advocates, promotes law reform, and decides matters that a State Bar Council refers to it. It also exercises general supervision and control over the SBCs.

On legal education, the BCI promotes legal learning and sets standards in consultation with universities and the SBCs. It recognises universities whose law degrees qualify a person for enrolment as an advocate, and it visits and inspects those universities. It can direct the SBCs to carry out inspections as well. Its wider work includes seminars, talks by eminent jurists, publications and legal aid for poor people. It recognises foreign law qualifications on a reciprocal basis. It manages and invests its funds, provides for the election of its members, and may set up funds for welfare schemes for indigent, disabled or other advocates, for legal aid and advice, and for law libraries. It may accept grants and benefactions for these purposes, and it may join international legal bodies.157:T5b9,The Advocates Act provides for a State Bar Council in each state. It also allows a common council for two or more states, or for a state and a union territory. At present there are 24 SBCs. Some serve several jurisdictions at once: one covers Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Mizoram and Nagaland; another covers Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu; and the Madras council covers Tamil Nadu and Puducherry.

Elected members are chosen by proportional representation through the single transferable vote, from advocates on the council's electoral roll. The number of elected members depends on the size of the electorate. An electorate of about five thousand gives 15 members, one of five to ten thousand gives 20, and one above ten thousand gives 25. Half of the elected members must have been advocates on a state roll for ten years.

Apart from the elected members, the Advocate-General of the state is an ex-officio member of the SBC. For a common council, the Advocate-General of each state sits on it. The Delhi council also has the Additional Solicitor-General of India as an ex-officio member. Each SBC elects its own Chairman and Vice-Chairman. Its elected members serve for five years. If a council fails to hold elections before that term ends, the BCI may extend the term by up to six months. The SBC's committees are a disciplinary committee, a legal aid committee, an executive committee, an enrolment committee and any others it needs.158:T494,Three categories of advocate may practise before the Supreme Court: Senior Advocates, Advocates-on-Record (AORs) and other advocates. An AOR is entitled under the Supreme Court Rules to act for a party and to plead on its behalf. No advocate other than an AOR may file an appearance or act for a party in the court.

The system has a history. The Supreme Court began in 1950 by inheriting the jurisdiction of the Federal Court and the Privy Council, and it initially kept the Federal Court's rules, including the system of agents. A revision in 1954 replaced agents with AORs. Advocates of seven years' standing could register as AORs, alongside the agents already registered. In 1959 the rules added an AOR examination, conducted by the court's Registry under a Board of Examiners appointed by the Chief Justice of India. A candidate must first train for one continuous year with an AOR of at least ten years' standing, starting from the end of the fourth year after enrolment.

Other advocates are those on the roll of a State Bar Council. They cannot appear, plead or address the Supreme Court for a party unless they are instructed by an AOR or permitted by the court.159:T415,- The 1951 All India Bar Committee under Justice S.R. Das recommended national and state bar councils in 1953.
- The Law Commission endorsed the recommendation in 1958, and the Advocates Act, 1961 created the BCI and the SBCs.
- The BCI is a statutory and autonomous body under the Department of Legal Affairs, not a constitutional one.
- Each SBC elects one member to the BCI; the Attorney-General and Solicitor-General of India sit ex officio.
- The BCI Chairman and Vice-Chairman are elected from among the members and serve for two years.
- There are 24 State Bar Councils, some covering several states or a union territory.
- SBC elected membership is 15, 20 or 25, depending on the electorate size.

- Only an Advocate-on-Record may act for a party in the Supreme Court; the AOR examination began in 1959.15a:T613,The Constitution gave law reform a new direction, with Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles set out in separate chapters. Article 372 keeps pre-Constitution laws in force until they are amended or repealed, so the old statute book stayed in use unless someone reviewed it. Demands in Parliament and outside for a body to update outdated laws led the government to set up the First Law Commission of independent India in 1955. It ran for three years under M. C. Setalvad, who was then Attorney-General of India.

Since 1955, twenty-one more commissions have been constituted, making twenty-two in all. Their nominal terms were usually three years, but some ran longer or shorter, and one chairman sometimes headed two consecutive commissions. The table lists selected commissions.

| Commission | Term | Chairman |
|---|---|---|
| First | 1955–1958 | M. C. Setalvad, former Attorney-General |

| Twenty-First | 2015–2018 | Justice B. S. Chauhan |

The Twenty-Second Commission shows how a term can drift. It was constituted in February 2020 for three years, but its chairman and members were not appointed until November 2022, and the Union Cabinet later extended its term to 31 August 2024.15b:T4fe,A project begins in a meeting of the Commission, where priorities are set, topics chosen and preparatory tasks given to members. The research methods depend on the reform in view. The outcome of this stage is a working paper, which sets out the problem and the reforms that look necessary. The paper goes out to the public and interested groups, their responses are evaluated, and the material is organised into a report. The full Commission then scrutinises the draft in long sittings before finalising it.

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1. Initiation | Project raised in a meeting; priorities set; members assigned preparatory work |
| 2. Research | Methods chosen to suit the proposed reform |
| 3. Working paper | Problem and possible reforms written up |
| 4. Consultation | Paper circulated to the public and interest groups; replies assessed |
| 5. Finalisation | Full Commission scrutinises the draft in extended meetings |
| 6. Submission | Final report forwarded to the Ministry of Law and Justice |
| 7. Parliament | Ministry consults the administrative ministries, then the report goes to Parliament from time to time |

So far the Commission has submitted 277 reports. | Item | Position after the 2001 and 2003 amendments |
|---|---|
| Lok Sabha seats for each state | Kept at the 1971 census allocation until the first census after 2026 |

The freeze runs on two clocks. Seat totals stay tied to the 1971 census, while boundaries and reserved seats follow the 2001 census. Both stay put until the first census after 2026.15e:T4ff,The Delimitation Act of 2002 provided for a commission to readjust constituencies in every state except the erstwhile Jammu and Kashmir, using the 2001 census. The body had three members. The chairperson had to be a serving or retired judge of the Supreme Court. The Chief Election Commissioner, or an Election Commissioner whom the CEC nominates, sat ex officio, and so did the State Election Commissioner of the concerned state or Union Territory.

The commission also had ten associate members for each state. Five were Lok Sabha members from that state and five were members of its assembly, and the Speakers nominated them. Where fewer than five Lok Sabha members came from a state, all of them served as associates. Associates had no right to vote and could not sign the commission's orders. Justice Kuldip Singh, a retired Supreme Court judge, chaired the body.

The commission submitted its recommendations in 2007, and the President signed the notification implementing them in 2008. Five states were left out of that exercise: Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Nagaland and Jharkhand. The government deferred the work in the four north-eastern states and nullified the order for Jharkhand. The 2009 Lok Sabha elections used the new boundaries for 499 of the 543 seats.15f:T408,In February 2020 the government withdrew the 2008 notifications that had deferred delimitation in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur and Nagaland. It said security and law and order had improved enough for the work to go ahead. In March 2020 a fresh commission was set up for those four states and for the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir. It was headed by Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai, a retired Supreme Court judge, with Election Commissioner Sushil Chandra and the State Election Commissioner as ex officio members. Her appointment ran for one year or until further orders, whichever came first.

In March 2021 the government removed the four north-eastern states from the commission's remit and extended its term to March 2022 for the J&K work. A two-month extension followed in February 2022, to May 2022. Five Lok Sabha members from J&K took part as associates, nominated by the Speaker and without any vote. The work ended in May 2022, and its report is titled "Delimited Landscape of Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir".160:T4d5,Before 2019 the Constitution governed delimitation of Lok Sabha seats in J&K, while the state's own constitution and the J&K Representation of the People Act, 1957, governed its assembly seats. Assembly seats had been delimited in 1957, 1966, 1975 and 1995, and the last exercise, based on the 1981 census, shaped the 1996 elections. No census was held in 1991, and after 2001 the state law froze fresh delimitation until the first census after 2026. The old assembly had 111 seats, including 4 for Ladakh, and 24 seats were kept for the area under Pakistani occupation.

The J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019 created the Union Territory and fixed the directly elected seats in its assembly at 114. The Lieutenant Governor may nominate two women if the community is inadequately represented. The 24 seats for the area under Pakistani occupation remain vacant and that area is excluded from delimitation. The 2011 census population had risen by more than 100 per cent over 1981, so the old constituencies had become badly malapportioned. Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes was worked out on the 2011 census, under Articles 330 and 332. The earlier state constitution had made no provision for ST reservation at all.161:T4ca,| Feature | Order of the commission |

| Reserved seats | Nine for Scheduled Tribes (six Jammu, three Kashmir) and seven for Scheduled Castes |
| Names | One constituency renamed after Shri Mata Vaishno Devi |

The commission also took representations from Kashmiri migrants and from displaced persons of the area under Pakistani occupation. It recommended that the Centre give at least two Kashmiri migrants, one of them a woman, a place in the J&K assembly with powers equal to those of nominated members in Puducherry. It also suggested that the Centre consider nominating displaced persons from that area to the assembly.

Among the national bodies listed by nodal ministry, the Delimitation Commission of India falls under the Ministry of Law and Justice, the same ministry that handles the Election Commission of India.162:T49e,The state legislature may provide for incorporation, regulation and winding up of co-operatives. Its rules must rest on voluntary membership, democratic control by members, members' economic participation and autonomous working.

Part IX-B also controls the board, meaning the body of directors or governing council that runs a society. The state law fixes the number of directors, but the total cannot exceed twenty-one. Functional directors who sit on the board are members of it but are not counted against that limit. Up to two co-opted experts, drawn from banking, management, finance or a related field, may be added on top of the twenty-one. Co-opted members cannot vote in the society's elections and cannot hold office-bearer posts.

| Rule | Limit or requirement |
|---|---|
| Maximum number of directors | Twenty-one, excluding functional directors |
| Co-opted experts | Up to two, in addition to the twenty-one; no vote; no office-bearer post |
| Reserved board seats | One for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes and two for women, where the society has members from those groups |
| Term of elected members and office-bearers | Five years from the date of election |163:T62c,The state law must provide for accounts to be kept and audited at least once in every financial year, and it sets the minimum qualifications and experience for auditors and audit firms. The general body of each society appoints its auditor, but only from a panel approved by the state government or by a body it authorises. The audit of a society's accounts must be finished within six months of the year's end. The audit report of an apex co-operative must be laid before the state legislature.

The state law may also require the annual general body meeting to be held within six months of the year's end, and it may give every member access to the society's books and accounts. It may further provide for members to take part in management and for co-operative education and training. Every society must file returns within six months of the financial year's end with the authority the state names. The returns cover the annual activity report, the audited accounts, a plan for disposing of surplus approved by the general body, a list of by-law amendments, and a declaration about the general body meeting and any elections due.

|---|---|
| Six months after year-end | Audit of accounts completed |
| Six months after year-end | Returns filed with the designated authority |
| Six months after year-end | Annual general body meeting (where the state law so provides) |
| Five years | Term of elected directors and office-bearers |
| Fourteen days | Time within which an employer must pass on amounts deducted from an employee for the society |164:T618,Article 343 makes Hindi, written in Devanagari, the official language of the Union. The numerals used for official purposes, however, take the international form of Indian numerals and not Devanagari digits.

The framers did not switch languages overnight. English kept its official role for fifteen years from the commencement of the Constitution, that is, from 1950 to 1965. Even after that, Parliament may provide for English to continue for specified purposes.

Article 344 asks the President to appoint a commission at the end of five years and again at the end of ten years. Each commission recommends how Hindi should be used more widely, how English should be restricted and related matters. A committee of Parliament then examines those recommendations and reports its views to the President.

In practice the first commission was appointed on time. The President set up the Official Language Commission under B.G. Kher in 1955; it reported in 1956, and a parliamentary committee under Govind Ballabh Pant examined it in 1957. The second commission, which was due in 1960, was never appointed.

The **Official Languages Act, 1963** filled the gap that the Constitution left open. It lets English continue alongside Hindi for all official purposes of the Union and for business in Parliament, with no time limit. A 1967 amendment made bilingual use compulsory for several categories of central documents, such as resolutions, notifications, administrative reports laid before Parliament, and contracts or licences issued by the Centre or its companies.165:T46d,The Constitution does not name the official language of any state. A state legislature may adopt one or more languages in use within the state, or Hindi, as its official language. Until it does, English remains the state's official language. Most states chose their major regional language, and the choice is not confined to the languages of the Eighth Schedule.

For communication between the Union and the states, or between one state and another, English stays the link language for now. Two or more states are free to agree between themselves to use Hindi instead. Under the 1963 Act, Union communications with a non-Hindi state are made in English. Where a Hindi state and a non-Hindi state exchange letters in Hindi, the Hindi letter must carry an English translation.

Article 347 protects a language spoken by a section of a state's people. If the President is satisfied, on a demand, that a substantial proportion of the population wants a language it speaks to be recognised, the President may direct that the language be officially recognised in that state. The power rests on a presidential direction, not on a state law.166:T578,Until Parliament provides otherwise, proceedings in the Supreme Court and the High Courts, and the authoritative texts of Bills, Acts, ordinances, rules and similar instruments, must be in English. The rules below carve out the exceptions.

| Forum or instrument | Language rule |
|---|---|
| Supreme Court | English only. Parliament has made no provision for Hindi, so the Court hears petitions and appeals in English alone |
| High Court proceedings | The Governor may, with the President's previous consent, allow Hindi or another official language of the state |
| High Court judgments, decrees and orders | Stay in English under the Constitution. The 1963 Act allows a Hindi version if an English translation accompanies it |
| State legislation | A state legislature may prescribe a language other than English for its laws, but an English translation must be published |
| Central Bills and Acts | Every Bill introduced in Parliament must come with a Hindi translation; Hindi translations of central texts issued under the President's authority are authoritative |
| Eighth Schedule translations | The Authorised Translations (Central Laws) Act, 1973 makes translations of central texts into Eighth Schedule languages, other than Hindi, authoritative |

Article 349 lays down a special procedure for enacting certain laws relating to language, which Parliament must follow when it passes them.167:T48e,The Eighth Schedule lists the languages recognised by the Constitution. It began with fourteen and has grown through amendments:

| Amendment | Languages added or changed |
|---|---|
| Original Constitution | Fourteen languages |
| 21st Amendment, 1967 | Sindhi |
| 71st Amendment, 1992 | Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali |
| 92nd Amendment, 2003 | Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali |
| 96th Amendment, 2011 | Oriya renamed Odia |

The schedule now lists 22 languages: Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Malayalam, Manipuri, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Santhali, Sindhi, Tamil, Telugu and Urdu.

The schedule serves two purposes. Members of these languages are to be represented on the Official Language Commission, and their forms, styles and expressions are to be drawn on to enrich Hindi. Article 351 places a duty on the Union to promote the spread of Hindi so that it becomes the lingua franca of the composite culture of India. Hindi is to be enriched by drawing on Hindustani and the Eighth Schedule languages, with its vocabulary taken chiefly from Sanskrit and secondarily from other languages.168:T4a5,The Official Languages Act, 1963 provided for a Committee of Parliament on Official Language, to be set up ten years after the Act came into force, that is, from 26 January 1965. In fact it was constituted only in 1976. The committee has 30 members, of whom 20 come from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.

Its job is to review the progress made in using Hindi for the official purposes of the Union, and to report to the President with recommendations. The President lays that report before each House of Parliament and sends it to every state government. After considering the report and the states' views, the President may issue directions covering all or part of it.

The committee elects its own chairman, and by convention the Union Home Minister has held that post. Its remit is wide: it looks at the progressive use of Hindi in central government offices and also at the medium of instruction in schools, colleges and universities, the mode of recruitment to central services, and the medium of departmental examinations. Its secretariat is headed by a Secretary and functions as a subordinate office of the Department of Official Language in the Ministry of Home Affairs.169:T425,Classical language status is not a constitutional category. The Government of India created it in 2004 by its own decision. Six languages have received it so far:

| Language | Year of declaration |
|---|---|
| Tamil | 2004 |
| Sanskrit | 2005 |
| Telugu | 2008 |
| Kannada | 2008 |
| Malayalam | 2013 |
| Odia | 2014 |

The government set four criteria. The language must have high antiquity, with early texts or recorded history spanning roughly 1500 to 2000 years. It must have a body of ancient literature that generations of speakers value as heritage. Its literary tradition must be original and not borrowed from another speech community. Finally, a gap between the classical language and its later forms is acceptable.

Declared languages receive three benefits: two major international awards for eminent scholars in classical Indian languages each year, a Centre of Excellence for studies in classical languages, and a request to the University Grants Commission to create professional chairs for classical languages, starting in central universities.16a:T6a6,Article 350B, inserted by the Seventh Amendment Act of 1956, provides for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities appointed by the President. The officer investigates all matters relating to the constitutional safeguards for linguistic minorities and reports to the President at intervals the President directs. The President places each report before both Houses of Parliament and sends it to the governments of the states concerned. The Constitution says nothing about this officer's qualifications, tenure, salary, service conditions or the procedure for removal.

The office was created in 1957 and is designated the Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (CLM). A linguistic minority is defined state by state: it is a group whose mother tongue differs from that of the majority in the state or part of it. The CLM's headquarters is in New Delhi. It was set up there in 1957, moved to Allahabad for a time, and returned to New Delhi in 2015. Three regional offices sit at Belgaum (Karnataka), Chennai (Tamil Nadu) and Kolkata (West Bengal), each headed by an Assistant Commissioner.

Administratively the CLM falls under the Ministry of Minority Affairs, and its reports reach the President through the Union Minority Affairs Minister. Its functions are to investigate safeguard matters, to report to the President on how the Constitutional and nationally agreed safeguards are being implemented, and to monitor implementation through questionnaires, visits, conferences and review meetings. It also takes up representations about grievances and tries to spread awareness of the safeguards among minority groups. In practice it liaises with states and Union Territories through nodal officers.16b:T494,- Article 343: Hindi in Devanagari is the Union's official language; numerals take the international form.

- The CLM is under the Ministry of Minority Affairs and has regional offices at Belgaum, Chennai and Kolkata.16c:T99b,There are three all-India services: the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), the Indian Police Service (IPS) and the Indian Forest Service (IFoS). The IAS and IPS trace back to the Indian Civil Service and the Indian Police, which were replaced in 1947 and recognised by the Constitution. The IFoS was established in 1966, making it the third. All three are Class I, or Group A, services.

Article 312 lets Parliament create new all-India services. It cannot do so on its own: the Rajya Sabha must first pass a resolution, supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting, declaring that a new service is necessary or expedient in the national interest. The actual creation then requires an Act of Parliament. The safeguard protects the states, because the Rajya Sabha represents them. The Constitution's Article 312 also covers an all-India judicial service, but it may not include any post below district judge. Although the 42nd Amendment made provision for that service, no law has been passed so far.

The Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly had not given the services any constitutional status, so the draft did not mention them. The Assembly added the provisions that were approved. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel was their chief champion, and he is therefore called the Father of All-India Services.

The All-India Services Act, 1951 empowers the Central Government to make recruitment and service rules, in consultation with the states. The Centre recruits and trains the officers, but it has no cadre of its own. Officers are borne on state cadres and are posted to the Centre on deputation for a fixed tenure, after which they return to their states. Each service still forms one service with common rights and uniform pay across India. Officers join in the junior scale and move to the senior and super time scales over their careers.

Control is shared. The Centre has ultimate control, while the states exercise immediate control. The states pay salaries and pensions, but disciplinary penalties can be imposed only by the Central Government. The three services are administered by three ministries: the IAS by the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, the IPS by the Ministry of Home Affairs, and the IFoS by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. There are 26 state cadres in all, including two joint cadres, Assam-Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Mizoram and the Union Territories (AGMUT).16d:T42a,Central services work exclusively under the Union. Most are managed by their own ministries or departments, while the Ministry of Personnel, the central personnel agency, sets the general policy for all of them.

The classification has changed twice. Before independence the services were Class I, Class II, Subordinate and Inferior. The First Pay Commission (1946–47) replaced the last two with Class III and Class IV. In 1974, on the recommendation of the Third Pay Commission (1970–73), the classes were renamed Group A, B, C and D. There are now 66 Group A central services. Most have a Group B counterpart. Groups C and D are non-gazetted: Group C is clerical and Group D is manual, while Groups A and B are gazetted.

The Indian Foreign Service is the highest-ranked central service in prestige, status and pay. It competes with the all-India services on those counts, comes next to the IAS in ranking and has a higher pay scale than the IPS. It is managed by the Ministry of External Affairs, and its members serve in Indian missions and embassies abroad.16e:T4b9,State services work under the exclusive jurisdiction of the state government. The number of services differs from state to state, but about fifteen are common to all states, among them Civil, Police, Forest, Agricultural, Medical, Judicial, Educational, Co-operative and Jail Service. Each takes the state's name as a prefix. The State Civil Service, also called the administrative service, is the most prestigious.

State services follow the same four-class scheme, Class I to IV, which is the same as Group I to IV. Classes I and II are gazetted, and Classes III and IV are non-gazetted. Gazetted members are called officers, and their names are published in the Government Gazette for appointment, transfer, promotion and retirement. Non-gazetted members are called employees, and their names are not published, while gazetted members enjoy privileges that the others do not.

The All-India Services Act, 1951 also reserves a share of senior posts for state officers. Not more than 33⅓ per cent of senior posts in the IAS, IPS and IFoS may be filled by promotion from state services. A selection committee set up in each state, presided over by the UPSC chairman or a UPSC member, makes these promotions.16f:T691,Article 311 limits the doctrine of pleasure with two safeguards. First, a civil servant cannot be dismissed, or removed, by an authority subordinate to the one that appointed him or her. Second, a civil servant cannot be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank except after an inquiry in which the charges are stated and the person is given a reasonable opportunity to be heard. These safeguards apply to civil servants and to persons in civil posts, but not to members of the defence services or those holding military posts.

The inquiry requirement does not apply in three cases: where the dismissal follows a conviction on a criminal charge; where the authority records in writing that holding an inquiry is not reasonably practicable; and where the President or the Governor is satisfied that, in the interest of the security of the state, an inquiry is not expedient.

The 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 changed the second stage of the process. A civil servant used to have two chances to respond, at the inquiry stage and again at the punishment stage. That amendment removed the second chance, so a penalty proposed after an inquiry may be imposed on the evidence taken at the inquiry, without a further representation on the penalty.

The Supreme Court has held that a reasonable opportunity includes three elements: knowing the charges and the allegations behind them, defending oneself by cross-examining witnesses and calling one's own, and receiving a copy of the inquiry officer's report before the disciplinary authority considers it. Dismissal and removal differ in one respect: dismissal disqualifies a person from future government employment, whereas removal does not.170:T412,- Three tiers: All-India (IAS, IPS, IFoS), Central (Groups A to D) and State (Classes I to IV).

- Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel is called the Father of All-India Services.
- All-India officers serve on state cadres, with the Centre having no cadre of its own; there are 26 cadres in all.
- Centre has ultimate control; states have immediate control and pay; penalties come from the Centre.
- The Indian Foreign Service ranks next to the IAS and is managed by the Ministry of External Affairs.
- Article 310: Union officers serve at the President's pleasure; state officers at the Governor's pleasure.

- Article 312A lets Parliament vary the conditions of certain pre-1950 Crown services.171:T5ee,The East India Company was first a trader and later a sovereign power. It could be sued for its trading functions but not for its sovereign ones. The immunity rested on an old English common-law idea that the monarch cannot commit a wrong. Britain abolished the rule through the Crown Proceedings Act of 1947, but in India the government can still be sued for torts only in its non-sovereign functions. Administering justice, constructing a military road and commandeering goods during war are sovereign functions and carry immunity. The distinction was set by the P and O Steam Navigation Company case in 1861.

The later cases moved steadily away from that immunity:

| Case | Year | What the Supreme Court held |
|---|---|---|
| Kasturilal | 1964 | Reaffirmed the sovereign and non-sovereign distinction, but the Court began to read "sovereign functions" narrowly |
| Nagendra Rao | 1994 | Rejected the distinction as unsound; the State is liable for negligence, except for a few functions such as justice and law and order. Kasturilal was not overruled but confined to rare cases |
| Common Cause | 1999 | Rejected the sovereign immunity rule; the State must answer for all tortious acts of its employees |
| Prisoner's Murder case (State of A.P. v Challa Ramkrishna Reddy) | 2000 | Said Kasturilal had lost its binding value in the process of judicial advancement |

The result is that the State's liability in tort has become close to that of any other legal person, leaving aside a narrow set of core functions.172:T518,The Constitution gives ministers no immunity for official acts. But because ministers do not countersign the official acts of the President or Governors, as British ministers do, they are not liable in court for those acts. Courts are also barred from inquiring into the advice the ministers tendered. Ministers have no immunity for personal acts and can be sued for crimes and torts like any citizen.

Judicial officers are immune from suit for official acts. The Judicial Officers Protection Act, 1850 bars civil suits against judges, magistrates, justices, collectors and others acting judicially for anything done in the discharge of official duty.

Civil servants have personal immunity from liability on official contracts, because the government is the party bound by them. They are also immune for torts committed in sovereign functions. In other cases a civil servant is liable like any citizen. Civil proceedings for official acts require two months' advance notice, but no notice is needed for acts outside the scope of official duty. Criminal proceedings for official acts need the prior sanction of the President or Governor where required, and the Criminal Procedure Code requires the central or state government's sanction for offences by public servants removable only with such sanction.173:T47c,- Articles 294–295: pre-1950 property and liabilities pass to the Union or the corresponding state.
- Article 296: escheat, lapse and bona vacantia go to the state where the property lies, otherwise to the Union.
- Article 297: things of value in territorial waters, continental shelf and EEZ vest in the Union (12 and 200 nautical miles).

- Article 299: three mandatory conditions; a non-compliant contract is void and the executing officer is personally liable.

- Ministers: no official-act liability, because they do not countersign and courts cannot inquire into their advice.174:T531,The Constitution does not itself name the castes or tribes that count as SCs or STs. The President does that, through an order for each state and union territory, and for a state the President first consults the Governor. The lists therefore differ from one state or union territory to the next. Once a community appears in a Presidential order, only Parliament can add it or remove it. A later Presidential notification cannot do that job, and Parliament has amended these orders several times.

Backward classes went through two stages of change. The 102nd Amendment (2018) allowed the President to specify socially and educationally backward classes for a state or union territory. The 105th Amendment (2021) narrowed that power to a Central List, meant for central purposes, and allowed each state or union territory to keep a list of its own. A state list may differ from the Central List, but a state can create or change it only by law.

Anglo-Indians are the one group the Constitution defines in express terms, in clause (2) of Article 366. The test has three limbs. The person's father, or a male ancestor in the paternal line, must have been of European descent. The person must be domiciled in India. And the person must have been born in India to parents who lived there ordinarily, not only for a temporary purpose.175:T499,Articles 330 and 332 reserve seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha and the state assemblies, in proportion to their population. The President may also set up an Administrative Tribunal for disputes over appointment, allotment or promotion to state civil posts. The tribunal works outside the High Court's jurisdiction, and no court other than the Supreme Court may hear matters that fall within its remit.
