Four types are usually distinguished, and each maps onto a position on the left–centre–right scale.

| Type | Attitude to existing institutions | Position on the scale |
|---|---|---|
| Reactionary | Wants to restore older social, economic and political arrangements | Right |
| Conservative | Prefers to keep the present arrangement as it is | Right |
| Liberal | Wants to reform existing institutions | Centre |
| Radical | Wants a new order, even if it means overthrowing existing institutions | Left |

In India the CPI and CPM are leftist parties, the Congress is a centrist party and the BJP is a rightist party.

Parties also combine into systems. Three arrangements are described. In a **one-party system** a single ruling party exists and no opposition is allowed, as in the former communist states of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. In a **two-party system** two major parties alternate in power, as in the United States, where the parties are the Democrats and Republicans, and in Britain, where they are the Conservatives and Labour. In a **multi-party system** several parties compete, as in France, Switzerland and Italy.17d:Tb3e,India has more political parties than any other country in the world. The size of the country, the diversity of its society and the adoption of universal adult franchise all contributed. Every category exists, from left and centrist to rightist, and from communal to non-communal parties. Hung Parliaments, hung assemblies and coalition governments are therefore common.

Despite this crowd of parties, the political scene for a long time revolved around the Congress. Rajni Kothari, the political analyst, called the system a "one-party dominance" or "Congress system". That dominance weakened from 1967 as regional parties and national rivals, including the Janata Party (1977) and the Janata Dal (1989), rose, and the system became a competitive multi-party one. The table gives the founding years of some major parties, which examiners sometimes use as a chronology question.

| Party | Founder | Year formed |
|---|---|---|
| Indian National Congress | A.O. Hume | 1885 |
| Communist Party of India | M.N. Roy | 1925 |
| Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam | C.N. Annadurai | 1949 |
| Shiv Sena | Bal Thackeray | 1966 |
| All India Anna DMK | M.G. Ramachandran | 1972 |
| Bharatiya Janata Party | A.B. Vajpayee and L.K. Advani | 1980 |
| Bahujan Samaj Party | Kanshi Ram | 1984 |
| Samajwadi Party | Mulayam Singh Yadav | 1992 |
| All India Trinamool Congress | Mamata Banerjee | 1998 |
| Aam Aadmi Party | Arvind Kejriwal | 2012 |

Several other features mark the system. Apart from the BJP and the two communist parties, few parties have a clear-cut ideology. Most of them endorse democracy, secularism, socialism and Gandhism, and their programmes look alike. Power capture guides them all, which has made politics issue-based and pragmatic rather than principled.

Many parties also revolve around one leader, so they are known by that leader more than by their manifesto. This is why it is said that India has political personalities more than political parties. Western parties usually grow out of socio-economic programmes, but many Indian parties are formed on religion, caste, language, culture or race. Such parties tend to promote sectional interests at the expense of the general public interest.

Factionalism, splits, mergers and defections are also common. Greed for power and material gain have prompted politicians to switch parties or create new ones. Defections became more frequent after the Fourth general elections of 1967, and they have caused instability at both levels and fragmented parties.

Finally, parliamentary democracy needs a strong opposition to check the ruling party and offer an alternative government. Since the first general elections, a strong, organised and viable national opposition has appeared only in flashes. Opposition parties often take mutually conflicting positions, and they have contributed little to the nation-building process.17e:T82d,The Election Commission enrols parties for electoral purposes and, based on how they perform at the polls, confers national or state status on them. Parties that do not qualify remain enrolled but unrecognised. Recognition matters because it carries three privileges: a reserved party symbol, time for political broadcasts on state-owned television and radio, and access to electoral rolls. A national party has a symbol reserved for its use across the country, and a state party has one reserved for the state or states where it is recognised. An unrecognised party can only pick a symbol from the free list. National parties are also called all-India parties, and state parties are called regional parties.

A party can become a national party by meeting any one of three tests:

| Route | Condition |
|---|---|
| Vote share and seats | Six per cent of valid votes in four or more states at a Lok Sabha or assembly general election, plus four Lok Sabha seats from one or more states |
| Seat share | Two per cent of Lok Sabha seats, with the winning candidates drawn from at least three states |
| Recognition elsewhere | Recognised as a state party in four states |

A party can become a state party in a state by meeting any one of five tests:

| Route | Condition |
|---|---|
| Assembly votes and seats | Six per cent of valid votes in the state at an assembly election, plus two assembly seats |
| Lok Sabha votes and seat | Six per cent of valid votes from the state at a Lok Sabha election, plus one Lok Sabha seat from that state |
| Assembly seats | Three per cent of the assembly's seats or three seats, whichever is more |
| Lok Sabha seats | One Lok Sabha seat for every 25 seats, or fraction of 25, allotted to the state |
| Combined votes | Eight per cent of total valid votes in the state at a Lok Sabha or assembly election |

The number of recognised parties changes with each election. At the first Lok Sabha elections in 1952 there were 14 national parties and 39 state parties. On the eve of the 2019 Lok Sabha elections there were 7 national parties and 52 state parties.17f:T48f,Regional parties are a defining feature of Indian politics. They operate at local, state and national levels, and their importance has grown in the era of coalition politics. A regional party usually works within one state or region, so its electoral base is limited to that area. It articulates the interests of a particular culture, religion, language, ethnic group or region. It focuses on local issues, aims to win power at the state level, and wants greater autonomy for the states within the Union.

Regional parties fall into four categories, and the table gives an example of each:

| Category | Basis | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Culture or ethnicity based | Regional identity and culture | Shiromani Akali Dal, National Conference, DMK, Telugu Desam, Shiv Sena, Asom Gana Parishad |
| All-India outlook, no national base | Ambitions beyond the state but a narrow electoral base | Samajwadi Party, Nationalist Congress Party |
| Split from a national party | Breakaway from a larger party | Biju Janata Dal, Rashtriya Janata Dal, Trinamool Congress, YSR Congress |
| Personalised | Built around one leader's charisma; short-lived | Not named in the chapter |180:T4ec,On the positive side, regional parties have provided stable government at the state level and challenged the dominance of one party, leading to a decline in the Congress's position. Their most lasting effect has been on centre–state relations. Because tensions over autonomy were so visible, the central leadership had to become more responsive to regional actors. The same competition has made politics more contested, broadened popular participation at the grass roots and widened voter choice in both Lok Sabha and assembly elections, because a voter can back a party that defends the interests of the state.

They have also checked the Centre. By opposing the ruling party on particular issues, they forced it to adopt a more reasonable approach to conflict resolution. They have helped parliamentary democracy work as intended, where the minority has its say and the majority its way: regional parties rule some states while opposing the Centre elsewhere. They have exposed the partisan role some Governors played in appointing and dismissing Chief Ministers, issuing ordinances and holding bills back for the President. Since coalition governments became the norm, regional parties have joined central coalitions and shared power with national parties.181:T4df,- Radical parties sit on the left, liberal parties at the centre, and conservative and reactionary parties on the right.
- The three party systems are one-party, two-party and multi-party; India is multi-party with a long Congress dominance.
- Kothari called the Indian system the "Congress system", and that dominance declined from 1967.
- Most Indian parties share similar policies; several are built on a single leader or on identity.
- A national party needs one of three routes: 6 per cent in four states plus 4 Lok Sabha seats, 2 per cent of Lok Sabha seats from three states, or state recognition in four states.
- A state party in a state can qualify through five routes, such as 6 per cent of votes plus 2 assembly seats, or 8 per cent of combined votes.
- Recognition brings reserved symbols, broadcast time on state-owned media and access to electoral rolls.
- Regional parties come in four categories: culture-based, all-India outlook without a national base, split-off, and personalised.
- Regional parties check Centre overreach and widen participation, but they can also encourage regionalism and delay inter-state disputes.
- Since the era of coalition politics, regional parties share power at the Centre as well as ruling states.182:T9b1,Part XV of the Constitution, Articles 324 to 329, governs the electoral system. The core rules are these. Article 324 creates an independent Election Commission and vests in it the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, the state legislatures, and the offices of the President and Vice-President. Article 325 says there is only one general electoral roll for each territorial constituency and that nobody may be kept off the roll, or claim a special roll, on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex alone. Article 326 requires adult suffrage for the Lok Sabha and state assemblies. Article 327 lets Parliament legislate on all election matters, and Article 328 lets a state legislature do the same for its own elections. Article 329 bars courts from interfering in electoral matters, except through the election petition route.

| Article | Subject-matter |
|---|---|
| 324 | Superintendence, direction and control of elections vested in an Election Commission |
| 325 | One general roll per constituency; no ineligibility or special roll on religion, race, caste or sex |
| 326 | Adult suffrage for the House of the People and state assemblies |
| 327 | Parliament's power to legislate on elections to the Legislatures |
| 328 | A state legislature's power to legislate on elections to its own House |
| 329 | Bar on interference by courts in electoral matters |

The abolition of separate electorates follows from Article 325, which ended the communal representation that had helped lead to partition. Voting age is 18, after the 61st Amendment (1988) reduced it from 21; the change took effect on 28 March 1989. A voter must not be disqualified on grounds of non-residence, unsound mind, crime or corrupt or illegal practice.

A state legislature may supplement the parliamentary law, but only on matters Parliament has not covered. It cannot override the central law. A law on delimitation or seat allocation cannot be questioned in any court, so the orders of the Delimitation Commission are final. Elections to Parliament and state legislatures may be questioned only through an election petition. Election petitions are heard by the High Court, with appeal to the Supreme Court alone. Article 323B allows an election tribunal to be set up, but none has been established. In *L. Chandra Kumar* (1997), the Supreme Court struck down clause 3(d) of Article 323B as unconstitutional, so any tribunal decision would now go to the High Court on appeal.183:T519,The Election Commission of India has three members: a Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners. The President appoints all of them. Below the Commission, the work is spread through a chain of officers, each appointed or designated in consultation with the state or Union Territory government.

| Officer | Role |
|---|---|
| Chief Electoral Officer | Supervises election work in a state or Union Territory, under the Commission's overall control |
| District Election Officer | Supervises election work in a district; appoints presiding and polling officers in states |
| Returning Officer | Runs the election in a parliamentary or assembly constituency; scrutinises nominations and declares the winner |
| Electoral Registration Officer | Prepares the electoral rolls for a constituency |
| Presiding Officer | Conducts the poll at a polling station with the help of polling officers |

Observers form a separate layer. General Observers watch every stage of the process. Expenditure Observers monitor the spending of candidates. Police Observers are IPS officers deployed at state and district level where the constituency is sensitive, to watch force deployment and coordinate with the civil administration. In Union Territories, the Returning Officers appoint the presiding officers.184:T4e5,Elections to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies must be held every five years, unless the House is dissolved earlier. The President may dissolve the Lok Sabha before its term ends if the government can no longer command its confidence and no alternative government is available. The Constitution also requires that no more than six months pass between the last sitting of the dissolved Lok Sabha and the first sitting of the new House, so the poll must conclude within that window.

The Commission usually announces the schedule at a press conference a few weeks before the formal process begins. The Model Code of Conduct takes effect at once. The process then starts with notifications calling for elections. Candidates have a week to file nominations. The Returning Officer scrutinises the papers and may reject a nomination after a summary hearing. A validly nominated candidate may withdraw within two days after scrutiny.

Before nominations are accepted, a candidate must make and sign an oath or affirmation before an authorised officer, usually the Returning Officer or an Assistant Returning Officer. The candidate does this personally, immediately after presenting the nomination papers, and in any case no later than the day before scrutiny.185:T50b,The campaign is the period in which parties and candidates present themselves and their arguments. The official campaign runs for at least two weeks from the drawing up of the list of candidates, and it ends 48 hours before polling closes. Parties issue manifestos setting out their programmes, the strengths of their leaders and the failures of rivals, and they hold rallies to persuade or denounce.

The Model Code of Conduct is a set of guidelines agreed by political parties on a consensus basis. Parties accepted it in 1968, but the Election Commission first used it effectively in 1991. It aims to keep the campaign healthy, avoid clashes between parties or their supporters, and keep the peace until results are declared. It also tells the ruling party, whether at the Centre or in a state, how to keep the playing field level so that it cannot be accused of using official position to campaign.

Media coverage is encouraged, subject to protecting the secrecy of the vote. Reporters receive special passes to enter polling stations and counting halls. Opinion polls may not be published from two days before polling begins until polling closes in the constituencies concerned. Exit poll results may be published only after half an hour has passed since polling ended on the last day.186:T558,Polling is spread across several days in different constituencies, so that security forces and monitors can keep order. Voting is by secret ballot. Polling stations are usually set up in schools or community halls. The Commission aims to place a polling station within two kilometres of every voter and to keep each station to no more than 1,200 voters. Each station is open for at least eight hours on polling day.

Electronic Voting Machines have replaced ballot boxes. The Commission began using them in 1998 and used them in all state and by-elections in 2003. In 2004 it took the historic decision to use only EVMs for the Lok Sabha election, which involved more than a million machines. EVMs help in four ways: they remove invalid and doubtful votes, which are often at the root of disputes and petitions; they speed up counting; they use far less paper; and they cost almost nothing to print, since a single ballot sheet is needed for each polling station.

On arrival, a voter is checked against the electoral roll and their identity is verified. Indelible ink is applied to the left forefinger, a voter slip is issued, and the presiding officer activates the ballot button on the control unit so that the voter can cast a vote. The electoral roll is revised each year to add those who turn 18 by 1 January and to remove the dead and those who have moved away.187:T4f7,Articles 81 and 170 set the maximum number of seats in Parliament and the state assemblies, and lay down principles for allocating seats, but leave the actual allocation to law. Article 171 does the same for state legislative councils. The Representation of the People Act, 1950 filled that gap. It allocated seats in the House of the People, the assemblies and the councils, empowered the President, after consulting the Election Commission, to delimit constituencies, and provided for the registration of electors and the qualifications for it. It also covered election officers, the filling of Council of States seats from Union Territories, and the bar on civil courts.

The 1951 Act supplied the rest of the framework. It covers qualifications and disqualifications for membership, notification of elections, the administrative machinery, the registration of political parties and the conduct of elections, including nominations, the poll, counting and declaration of assets and liabilities. It also deals with election expenses, corrupt practices and electoral offences, and the disposal of election disputes, including the trial and withdrawal of petitions and appeals to the Supreme Court. Recognised party candidates receive certain free supplies under this Act.188:T67d,Articles 82 and 170 provide for readjusting and dividing states into parliamentary and assembly constituencies on the basis of the census, and Articles 330 and 332 re-fix seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes on the same basis. The previous delimitation rested on the 1971 census. Population growth had been uneven, and migration from rural to urban areas had produced very different constituency sizes even within the same state. The Delimitation Act, 2002 set up a Delimitation Commission to redraw constituencies on the basis of the 2001 census.

Other statutes relate to elections. The Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959 says certain offices of profit under the government do not disqualify their holders from membership of Parliament. The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 regulates those two elections, and the Government of Union Territories Act, 1963 and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991 cover the territories concerned.

The subordinate rules include the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, the Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950, the defection-disqualification rules for each House (1985), the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Rules, 1974, and the assets-and-liabilities declaration rules for each House (2004). The Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 governs symbols and their link to recognition, and the Registration of Political Parties (Furnishing of Additional Particulars) Order, 1992 covers the particulars that a body of citizens must file to register as a party.189:T4e4,- Articles 324 to 329 set the base: Article 324 creates the Election Commission, and Article 326 requires adult suffrage.
- One general roll per constituency; no exclusion on religion, race, caste or sex; voting age is 18 after 1988.
- The Election Commission has three members, all appointed by the President; the Returning Officer declares the winner.
- Lok Sabha elections fall due every five years, and the House must meet within six months of the last sitting of its predecessor.
- The campaign lasts at least two weeks and ends 48 hours before polling closes; the Model Code dates from 1968 and was first used effectively in 1991.
- Opinion polls are barred for a window around polling; exit polls wait half an hour after polling closes on the last day.
- EVMs were used in all state and by-elections in 2003 and in the Lok Sabha election of 2004.
- Election petitions are tried by the High Court, with appeal to the Supreme Court; no election tribunal has been set up.
- The Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951 handle seats, roll and conduct; the Delimitation Act of 2002 uses the 2001 census.
- The Model Code, the Symbols Order and the Defection Rules are subordinate or non-statutory instruments, not parts of the Constitution.18a:T499,| Body | Year | Remembered for |

| Reform | Year | Substance |
|---|---|---|
| Voting age lowered | 1988 (61st Amendment) | Age cut from 21 to 18 for Lok Sabha and Assembly polls, to bring young people into politics |
| Deputation to the Commission | 1989 | Staff working on preparing and correcting electoral rolls are treated as on deputation to the Election Commission, under its control and discipline |

- **Ballot listing.** Candidates appear in three blocs, in this order: recognised parties, registered-but-unrecognised parties, and independents, with alphabetical order inside each bloc.
- **Insults to national honour.** Conviction under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 (for insulting the flag or the Constitution, or obstructing the national anthem) bars a person from contesting for six years.
- **Dry period.** No liquor or intoxicant may be sold or distributed in the polling area for 48 hours before the close of polling.
- **Proposers.** A candidate not sponsored by a recognised party needs ten registered electors as proposers; a recognised party's nominee needs only one.
- **Death of a candidate.** The poll is no longer countermanded automatically; if the deceased belonged to a recognised party, that party may field a replacement within seven days.
- **By-elections.** They must be held within six months of a vacancy, except where less than a year of the term remains or the Commission, after consulting the Centre, certifies that it is not feasible.
- **Paid holiday** on polling day for employed voters, including daily wagers, unless their absence would cause danger or heavy loss.
- **Two-seat limit.** No one may contest from more than two Parliamentary or Assembly constituencies in one general election or simultaneous by-elections; similar limits apply to Rajya Sabha and Council polls.
- **Arms.** Entering the area near a polling station with arms is a cognizable offence, except for officials and police on duty.
- **Campaign period.** The gap between last date of withdrawal and polling day was shortened from 20 to 14 days.18d:T6f8,Many items in this phase are clustered around 2003, when the Election Laws (Amendment) Act and the Representation of the People (Amendment) Act changed several things together.

| Reform | Year | Substance |
|---|---|---|
| President and Vice-President polls | 1997 | Proposers and seconders raised from 10 to 50 (President) and from 5 to 20 (Vice-President); security deposit raised from ₹2,500 to ₹15,000 for both |

- **Exit polls** may not be conducted or published during the period notified by the Election Commission for Lok Sabha and Assembly elections.
- **Corrupt practice cases.** The specified authority has three months to send the matter to the President for a disqualification decision; every official appointed or deputed by the Commission for the election now falls within the corrupt-practice rule on obtaining official help.
- **Security deposit.** For Lok Sabha, general candidates pay ₹25,000 (earlier ₹10,000) and SC/ST candidates ₹12,500 (earlier ₹5,000); for Assemblies, ₹10,000 (earlier ₹5,000) and ₹5,000 (earlier ₹2,500).
- **Appeals on rolls** against an Electoral Registration Officer go to a district-level authority (District Magistrate, Collector or equivalent); a further appeal lies to the state's Chief Electoral Officer.
- **Overseas citizens (2010).** A citizen who holds no other nationality and is away for work or study can be enrolled in the constituency of the home address in the passport.
- **Online enrolment (2013)** through the Registration of Electors (Amendment) Rules, 2013.18f:T67f,**NOTA.** On the Supreme Court's direction, ballot papers and EVMs carry a "None of the Above" button, so that a voter can reject all candidates without breaching secrecy. It was used from the 2013 Assembly elections and in the 2014 Lok Sabha polls. NOTA does not change the result: the candidate with the most votes still wins even if NOTA gets more.

**VVPAT.** The Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail is a separate unit attached to the EVM. A slip showing serial number, name and symbol of the chosen candidate stays visible through a window for seven seconds and then drops into a sealed box. The Supreme Court in 2013 allowed a phased rollout, calling it an indispensable part of free and fair elections. Its first use was in the Noksen by-election in Nagaland, 2013.

**Persons in custody.** After the Court upheld a Patna High Court view that a prisoner is not an elector and so cannot contest, Parliament amended the 1951 Act in 2013: such a person remains an elector, and a legislator is disqualified only on grounds in the Act itself. The result is that people in jail or police custody may contest.

**Convicted legislators.** In Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) the Court struck down Section 8(4) of the 1951 Act, which had given convicted MPs and MLAs three months to appeal and obtain a stay. Disqualification now follows conviction at once. A Bill to undo this was introduced in 2013 but the government withdrew it.

**Candidate photographs.** From elections after 1 May 2015, ballots and EVMs show the candidate's picture next to name and symbol, to avoid confusion between namesakes; failure to supply a photo does not invalidate a nomination.190:T672,| Measure | Year | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Cash donations ceiling | 2017 Budget | Anonymous cash donations to a party cut from ₹20,000 to ₹2,000; parties keep records of donors above ₹2,000 |
| Corporate cap removed | 2017 Budget | The old limit of 7.5 per cent of three-year average net profit was dropped, and companies need not disclose such gifts in their accounts |
| Electoral bonds | Scheme notified 2018 | Bearer instruments without buyer or payee name; bought by Indian citizens or Indian entities; usable only for registered parties with at least one per cent of votes in the last Lok Sabha or Assembly election; encashed through a party's bank account; denominations of ₹1,000 to ₹1 crore; buyer details kept confidential unless a court or criminal case requires disclosure |
| Foreign funding | 2018 Budget | Parties may receive funds from foreign companies after the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 changed the meaning of a foreign company |

The electoral bond scheme was later struck down by the Supreme Court in 2024, so questions on it should be read as questions on how the scheme was designed.

The **Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021** did four things: allowed roll data to be linked with Aadhaar to stop duplicate enrolment; set four qualifying dates a year (1 January, 1 April, 1 July, 1 October) instead of 1 January alone; replaced "wife" with "spouse" in the service-voter provisions so that husbands of women service voters are covered; and widened the power to requisition buildings, now covering counting, storage of EVMs and VVPATs and material, and housing for security forces and polling staff.191:T4d9,- 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.
- The 1988 Act (from 1989) brought EVMs, booth-capturing rules and deputation of roll staff to the Commission; EPIC was decided in 1993.
- The Goswami Committee (1990) ideas became law in 1996: three-bloc ballot listing, dry period of 48 hours, two-seat limit, by-election within six months.
- 1997: President and Vice-President nomination support raised to 50 and 20; deposit ₹15,000.
- 2003 cluster: affidavit disclosure of criminal record and assets, open ballot and no domicile rule for Rajya Sabha, proxy voting for service voters, new rules on party donations.
- 2009 Act (effective 2010): exit-poll ban during notified period, Lok Sabha deposit ₹25,000 and ₹12,500.

- Election Laws (Amendment) Act 2021: Aadhaar linking, four qualifying dates, "spouse" for service voters, wider requisition of premises.192:T452,Psephology is a branch of political science concerned with the scientific study of voting. The word comes from the Greek *psephos*, a pebble or piece of pottery used to record votes, most famously on whether to banish people regarded as dangerous to the city. Records of voting go back at least as far as the Greek polis, which is why the subject has such a long history.

Studying voting behaviour helps in several ways. It sheds light on political socialisation, on how far democracy has been internalised as a value by both the elite and the masses, and on the real effect of the ballot box as a tool of change. It shows whether electoral politics continues or breaks with the past, and whether a political system is modern or still shaped by primordial loyalties. N.G.S. Kini identified several roles that voting plays: it legitimises democratic rule, it shows participation and integration into the political community, it is an act of decision-making, it expresses a political orientation rooted in a particular political culture, and it links an individual citizen directly to the formal government.193:T79a,Indian society is highly diverse, so voting is shaped by many factors. Socio-economic and political factors are the two broad groups. The social identities form the first group, and four of them recur in examinations.

**Caste** is perhaps the most important. Rajni Kothari argued that Indian politics is casteist and that caste is politicised, and parties plan their election strategies with caste in mind. Paul Brass found that in rural constituencies, the leading castes usually throw their weight behind either a figure from among them who commands respect, or a party they feel close to, which makes caste solidarity the chief influence locally.

**Religion** also shapes voting. Parties use communal propaganda and appeal to religious sentiment, and communal parties have added to the politicisation of religion. India is a secular state, yet no party ignores the influence of religion on voters.

**Language** matters as well. Parties stir linguistic feeling during campaigns. The reorganisation of states on linguistic lines, begun in 1956 and continued later, shows how important language has been in Indian politics. The rise of the DMK in Tamil Nadu and the TDP in Andhra Pradesh is attributed to linguistic sentiment.

**Region** is the fourth identity. Regionalism and sub-regionalism drive voting, and the parochial feelings they produce gave rise to regional parties, which appeal to regional identity and sentiment. Some secessionist parties have called for boycotts of elections.

| Factor | How it works | Example in the chapter |
|---|---|---|
| Caste | Solidarity and identification with a caste leader or party | Brass on rural constituencies |
| Religion | Communal propaganda and appeal to sentiment | Communal parties |
| Language | Linguistic feeling during campaigns | DMK in Tamil Nadu, TDP in Andhra Pradesh |
| Region | Regional identity and sub-nationalism | Regional parties; boycott calls by secessionist parties |194:T45e,**Personality** is the next factor. A charismatic leader can draw a national vote. The chapter names Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Rajiv Gandhi, Jayaprakash Narayan, Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Narendra Modi as leaders whose towering images influenced the electorate. At the state level, the charisma of a regional party leader has also been a significant source of popular support. Charisma here means exceptional and attractive qualities in a leader.

**Money** is the third factor. Despite limits on election spending, large sums are spent, and voters may seek cash, liquor or goods in return for their votes, so that votes are exchanged for notes. Money can sway voters in normal circumstances, but not in a wave election.

Paul Brass defined a wave election as one in which the electorate moves clearly in one direction, towards a national party or its leader, on an issue that goes beyond local calculations and coalitions. Such an election draws in the uncommitted and wavering voters, and the trend spreads from village to village. In a wave, the appeal of the issue or leader outweighs the influence of money.195:T40d,- Voting behaviour is the study of how and why voters choose; psephology is its scientific branch and the term came from American political scientists.
- Psephology takes its name from the Greek psephos, a pebble or pottery piece used for votes.
- Voting studies reveal political socialisation, the internalisation of democracy and whether electoral politics breaks with the past.
- Caste solidarity matters most in rural constituencies, according to Paul Brass.
- Religion and language are exploited in campaigns; states were reorganised on language from 1956.
- Regionalism gave rise to regional parties, and some secessionist groups call for election boycotts.
- Charismatic leaders such as Nehru, Indira Gandhi and Modi shape national votes.
- Money influences voters in normal elections, but not in a wave election.
- Anti-incumbency, shown by the Congress defeat of 1977 and the Janata defeat of 1980, is a political determinant.
- Party identification and ideology shape votes, and events, economy and media add further influence.196:T86c,The pattern before 1977 was different. Congress won a majority in the first four Lok Sabha elections, in 1952, 1957, 1962 and 1967. After the party split in 1969, Indira Gandhi led a minority government that survived on support from the CPI, the DMK and others, and in 1971 Congress won again with a single-party majority. Its heavy defeat in 1977 opened the coalition era, which has since produced a long run of governments:

| Period | Government (Prime Minister) | Partners and outside support |
|---|---|---|
| 1977–79 | Janata Party (Morarji Desai) | Congress (O), Jana Sangh, Lok Dal, Socialists and former Congress members |
| 1979–80 | Janata (Secular) (Charan Singh) | Congress (U) joined; Congress (I) gave outside support |
| 1989–90 | National Front (V.P. Singh) | Janata Dal, TDP, DMK and AGP; BJP and Left parties from outside |
| 1990–91 | Janata Dal (Socialist) (Chandra Shekhar) | Janata Party as partner; Congress (I) from outside |
| 1996–97 | United Front (H.D. Deve Gowda) | Janata Dal, CPI, TMC, DMK, TDP and others; Congress and CPM from outside |
| 1997–98 | United Front (I.K. Gujral) | Janata Dal, CPI, TMC, SP, DMK, AGP, TDP and others; Congress from outside |
| 1998–99 | BJP-led coalition (A.B. Vajpayee) | BJP, AIADMK, BJD, Shiv Sena and others; TDP and Trinamool from outside |
| 1999–2004 | NDA (A.B. Vajpayee) | BJP, JD(U), Trinamool, Shiv Sena, BJD and many more |
| 2004–09 | UPA (Manmohan Singh) | Congress, NCP, DMK, RJD and others; CPI and CPM from outside |
| 2009–14 | UPA-II (Manmohan Singh) | Congress, NCP, DMK, Trinamool, National Conference and others |
| 2014–19 | NDA (Narendra Modi) | BJP, LJP, TDP, Shiv Sena and others; TDP left in 2018 |
| 2019 onward | NDA (Narendra Modi) | BJP, Akali Dal, LJP, Shiv Sena and others; Shiv Sena left in 2019, Akali Dal in 2020 |

Two entries in this run deserve a note. The United Front governments of 1996–98 were built mainly from regional parties, and the Congress and the CPM supported them from outside rather than sharing ministries. The NDA of 1999 counted many more partners than the BJP alone, which shows how wide an alliance can become.197:T661,Any question about disqualification arising from defection is decided by the presiding officer of the House, that is, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of Rajya Sabha, or the corresponding officer of a state legislature. The Tenth Schedule set no time limit for that decision. As enacted, the decision was final and could not be questioned in any court.

In the Kihoto Hollohan case (1992), the Supreme Court struck down that finality clause as unconstitutional, because it sought to take away the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and the high courts. The Court held that the presiding officer, when deciding such a question, acts as a tribunal. The decision is therefore open to judicial review on grounds such as mala fides and perversity. The Court did reject the argument that giving adjudicatory power to a presiding officer was invalid in itself because of political bias.

The presiding officer may also make rules to give effect to the Tenth Schedule. The rules must be placed before the House for 30 days, and the House may approve, modify or disapprove them. A wilful breach of these rules may be treated as a breach of privilege of the House. The rules shape the procedure in practice:

| Stage | Position under the rules |
|---|---|
| Starting a case | Only on a complaint from a member of the House |
| Hearing | The member complained against must be given a chance to submit an explanation |
| Inquiry | The presiding officer may refer the matter to the committee of privileges |
| Judicial check | The final decision is reviewable by the courts |
| Effect | Defection has no immediate or automatic effect |198:T64e,The schedule is meant to prevent defections driven by the lure of office or material benefit, and to curb unprincipled switching in parliamentary democracy. Rajiv Gandhi, then Prime Minister, called it the first step towards cleaning up public life. Its supporters point to the following gains:

| Advantage | What it achieves |
|---|---|
| Stability | Deters legislators from changing parties, so governments are less easily upset |
| Democratic realignment | Lets parties regroup in the legislature through lawful mergers |
| Cleaner politics | Reduces corruption and the non-developmental cost of repeated elections |
| Constitutional recognition | Gives political parties, for the first time, clear recognition in the Constitution |

Critics say the law has not stopped defections in full, and they raise the following objections:

| Criticism | Substance |
|---|---|
| No line between dissent and defection | The law curbs a legislator's right to dissent and freedom of conscience, and so strengthens party bosses |
| Individual versus group defection | Individual switching is penalised, but a group switch passes as a merger, so bulk defections survive |
| No expulsion for outside conduct | A party cannot have a legislator removed for activities outside the House |
| Unequal treatment of members | An independent who joins a party is disqualified, whereas a nominated member may do the same after six months |
| The presiding officer as judge | Politics may sway the officer, who may lack legal training; two Lok Sabha Speakers, Rabi Ray in 1991 and Shivraj Patil in 1993, doubted their own suitability |199:T61b,The government justified the 91st Amendment by pointing to repeated demands to strengthen the law. It argued that the Tenth Schedule allowed bulk defections while penalising individual ones, and that the exemption for splits had a destabilising effect on governments. Several bodies had recommended removing the split exemption: the Dinesh Goswami Committee on electoral reforms (1990), the Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) and the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002). The National Commission also wanted defectors barred from ministerial and other remunerative political posts for the rest of the legislature's term, and it proposed a ceiling of 10 per cent of the House's strength on the size of ministries.

The amendment did not adopt the 10 per cent ceiling. It set a higher cap and added the following provisions:

| Change | Detail |
|---|---|
| Union ministry | Total ministers, including the Prime Minister, must not exceed 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha's strength |
| State ministry | Ministers, including the Chief Minister, must not exceed 15 per cent of the Assembly's strength, but must be at least 12 |
| Defectors as ministers | A member disqualified for defection cannot be appointed a minister, at the Centre or in a state |
| Defectors in remunerative posts | Such a member cannot hold a remunerative political post, meaning an office paid from public revenue or in a body largely owned by government, except where the pay is compensatory |
| Split exemption | Deleted; a split no longer protects defectors |19a:T4d5,India has a large number of pressure groups, but they are less developed than in the United States or in Britain, France and Germany. The chapter sorts them into categories by the interest they serve. The categories are a convenient way to revise, though in practice a single body can straddle more than one, and a group's strength often depends on its access to party politics.

These are the groups with the most resources. The chapter describes business groups as the most sophisticated, the most powerful and the largest of all pressure groups in India. Examples include the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India (ASSOCHAM), the Federation of All India Foodgrain Dealers Association (FAIFDA) and the All-India Manufacturers Organisation (AIMO).

Professional associations speak for doctors, lawyers, journalists and teachers. Despite legal restrictions on some of them, they press government through agitation for better service conditions. Examples are the Indian Medical Association (IMA), the Bar Council of India (BCI), the Indian Federation of Working Journalists (IFWJ) and the All India Federation of University and College Teachers (AIFUCT).19b:T4ed,Trade unions voice the demands of industrial workers. A peculiar feature in India is that most are tied to political parties, directly or indirectly. The All-India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was founded in 1920, with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president. Until 1945 Congressmen, Socialists and Communists worked together in it. The movement then split on political lines. The main unions of today are linked to parties as follows:

| Trade union | Political link |
|---|---|
| All-India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) | CPI |
| Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC) | Congress |
| Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS) | Socialists |
| Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU) | CPM |
| Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) | BJP |

Agrarian groups represent farmers and agricultural labour. The All India Kisan Sabha is described as the oldest and largest of them. Others include the Bharatiya Kisan Union, strong in the wheat belt of north India, the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh in Gujarat and the Shetkari Sanghatana in Maharashtra.

Student unions follow the same pattern. The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad is linked to the BJP, the All India Students Federation to the CPI, the National Students Union of India to Congress, and the Students Federation of India to the CPM.19c:T520,Religious organisations have become important in Indian politics. Those listed include the Vishwa Hindu Parishad, the Jamaat-e-Islami, the All-India Conference of Indian Christians and the Shiromani Akali Dal. The chapter quotes a view that the Akali Dal is better treated as a religious pressure group than a party, because its concern is protecting the Sikh community from absorption into the wider Hindu society rather than pursuing a separate Sikh homeland.

Caste is equally important, and in several states competitive politics has run along caste lines:

| State | Caste rivalry named in the chapter |
|---|---|
| Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra | Brahmin versus non-Brahmin |
| Rajasthan | Rajput versus Jat |
| Andhra Pradesh | Kamma versus Reddy |
| Haryana | Ahir versus Jat |
| Gujarat | Baniya-Brahmin versus Patidar |
| Bihar | Kayastha versus Rajput |
| Kerala | Nair versus Ezhava |
| Karnataka | Lingayat versus Okkaliga |

Tribal organisations are active in central and eastern India and in the North-East. Their demands range from reform to secession, and some are involved in insurgency. Language, too, has been decisive: it was the main basis for reorganising states, and linguistic bodies such as the Tamil Sangam, the Hindi Sahitya Sammelan and the Andhra Maha Sabha operate as pressure groups.19d:T4b0,Casteism is loyalty to one's own caste group above the general national interest. It stems mainly from the politicisation of caste. Its manifestations include caste-based parties such as the Justice Party in Madras, the Republican Party and the Bahujan Samaj Party; caste-based pressure groups such as the Nadar Association, the Harijan Sevak Sangh and the Kshatriya Mahasabha; the allotment of party tickets and the formation of state ministries on caste lines; caste conflicts between higher and lower castes or between dominant castes; and violent agitations over reservation.

B. K. Nehru argued that the communal electorates of the British period survive in a weaker form as reservations for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. In his view these keep caste origin in focus, which the chapter says does not help integration. At state level, politics often reduces to a contest between two dominant castes.

| State | Caste rivalry cited |
|---|---|
| Andhra Pradesh | Kamma versus Reddy |
| Karnataka | Lingayat versus Vokkaliga |
| Kerala | Nair versus Ezhava |
| Gujarat | Bania versus Patidar |
| Bihar | Bhumihar versus Rajput |
| Haryana | Jat versus Ahir |
| Assam | Kalita versus Ahom |19e:T4b3,Linguism is loyalty to one's language and its speakers. It has two dimensions: the reorganisation of states on linguistic lines, and the choice of the Union's official language. Both dimensions have a clear sequence.

| Year | Development |
|---|---|
| 1953 | Andhra is carved out of Madras state as the first linguistic state, and a nationwide demand for reorganisation follows |
| 1956 | States are reorganised on a large scale on the basis of the States Reorganisation Commission (1953–55) |
| 1963 | The Official Languages Act makes Hindi the Union's official language, with English kept as an associate official language |

The Hindi decision triggered anti-Hindi agitation in South India and West Bengal. The Centre assured non-Hindi states that English would continue as an associate official language as long as they wished. The three-language formula (English, Hindi and a regional language) has not been implemented in Tamil Nadu, which teaches only English and Tamil. For this reason, the chapter concludes that Hindi has not become the lingua franca of composite Indian culture that the framers hoped for. Regional parties such as the TDP, the AGP and the Shiv Sena made the problem worse.19f:T4db,The National Integration Conference of 1961 was convened to counter communalism, casteism, regionalism, linguism and narrow-mindedness. It recommended a standing body to review national integration. The National Integration Council was constituted in 1961 and held its first meeting in 1962.

The Prime Minister chairs the Council. Its members include Union ministers, the Leaders of the Opposition in both Houses, the Chief Ministers of states and of Union Territories with legislatures, leaders of national and regional parties, chairpersons of national commissions, eminent journalists and public figures, and representatives of business and women's organisations.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Origin | 1961 National Integration Conference |
| Constituted | 1961; first meeting in 1962 |
| Chairman | Prime Minister |
| Meeting schedule | Convened as required, with no regular or fixed interval |
| Meetings recorded | 16 in total, as of the chapter's latest record |

The 16th meeting, on 23 September 2013, passed a resolution condemning violence, atrocities against Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and sexual abuse. It also called for equal opportunities for women and their right to move freely in public spaces at any hour.1a0:T46e,- Four divisive forces: regionalism, communalism, casteism and linguism.
- Regionalism runs from secession demands to statehood demands, boundary and river disputes, and sons-of-the-soil preferences.
- Communalism is rooted in the communal representation of the 1909, 1919 and 1935 Acts.
- Communal manifestations: religion-based parties, religion-based pressure groups, riots and disputes over places of worship.
- Casteism: caste-based parties and pressure groups, ticket allocation on caste lines, caste conflicts and reservation agitations.
- Linguism has two dimensions: linguistic reorganisation of states and the choice of the Union's official language.
- Andhra (1953), carved out of Madras, was the first linguistic state; the Official Languages Act of 1963 made Hindi the official language, with English as an associate.
- The three-language formula is not implemented in Tamil Nadu.
- National Integration Council: constituted 1961, first met 1962, chaired by the Prime Minister, meets as required.
- National Foundation for Communal Harmony: set up 1992, autonomous, under the Union Home Ministry's administrative control.1a1:T4bd,The first three principles share a common logic: peace is a precondition for development, and colonial or racial domination destroys peace. The chapter links them to the Constitution's Directive Principles, where Article 51 directs the state to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, respect international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration.

| Principle | India's stance | Example in the chapter |
|---|---|---|
| World peace | Peace and security are the aim, and economic development depends on them | Article 51 of the Directive Principles |
| Anti-colonialism | Opposes colonial and imperial exploitation, and now neo-colonialism and neo-imperialism | Support for liberation in Indonesia, Malaya, Tunisia, Algeria, Ghana and Namibia |
| Anti-racialism | Opposes discrimination on the basis of race | Broke diplomatic ties with South Africa in 1954 over apartheid |

India also helped liberate Zimbabwe (then Rhodesia) and Namibia from white domination. When apartheid ended and a democratic government came to power under Nelson Mandela, India restored full diplomatic relations with South Africa in 1994.1a2:T477,When India became independent in 1947, the world was split into a capitalist bloc led by the USA and a communist bloc led by the USSR. India refused to join either bloc and adopted non-alignment. Nehru's justification was that India should not be tied to power groups whose rivalries had led to world wars.

The chapter explains non-alignment as three commitments: no military alliance with any bloc or nation, an independent approach to every issue, and friendly relations with all countries. It is therefore not isolation from the world.

Panchsheel refers to five principles of conduct in relations between states. They were set out in the preamble to the 1954 treaty on Tibet between India and China, which Nehru and Chou En-lai signed. The five are mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference in each other's internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful co-existence. Countries such as Burma, Yugoslavia and Indonesia adopted the code. The chapter counts Panchsheel and non-alignment as India's two greatest contributions to the theory and practice of international relations.1a3:T4cc,India, while friendly with all, shows a special bias towards Afro-Asian nations. It seeks their unity, a voice in international bodies, and outside help for their development. The table lists the milestones the chapter gives.

| Year | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1947 | First Asian Relations Conference, held in New Delhi |
| 1949 | Asian countries brought together on the issue of Indonesian freedom |
| 1955 | Active role at the Afro-Asian Conference at Bandung, Indonesia |
| 1964 | Group of 77 |
| 1985 | SAARC |
| 1990 | Group of 15 |
| 1997 | Indian Ocean Rim Association and BIMSTEC |

Neighbours have called India the "Big Brother" in this regional setting.

On the Commonwealth, India declared in 1949 that it would continue as a full member and accept the British Crown as head of the Commonwealth. The chapter calls this extra-constitutional, but says it does not affect India's sovereignty or republican character, because the Commonwealth is a voluntary association and India owes no final allegiance to the Crown. India stayed for pragmatic reasons, seeing economic, political and cultural gains. It has played an active role at CHOGM, the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, and hosted it in New Delhi in 1983.1a4:T44a,I. K. Gujral, then Foreign Minister in the Deve Gowda government, propounded the Gujral Doctrine in 1996. Its core idea is that India, as the largest country in South Asia, should extend unilateral concessions to its smaller neighbours. This rests on the principle of non-reciprocity: India gives without demanding a return in kind. The doctrine's five principles are set out below.

| Principle | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | With Bangladesh, Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka, India does not seek reciprocity and gives what it can in good faith |
| 2 | No South Asian country allows its territory to be used against another's interest |
| 3 | No country interferes in another's internal affairs |
| 4 | Every South Asian country respects the others' territorial integrity and sovereignty |
| 5 | Every South Asian country settles disputes through peaceful bilateral negotiation |

Gujral's own explanation was strategic. India faced two hostile neighbours, to the north and the west, so it needed total peace with the rest of its neighbourhood to contain the influence of Pakistan and China.1a5:T4c2,The chapter summarises India's nuclear doctrine around a credible minimum deterrent. Its features are a no-first-use posture, under which nuclear weapons are used only in retaliation against a nuclear attack on Indian territory or on Indian forces anywhere. Any retaliation is meant to be massive enough to inflict unacceptable damage. Nuclear weapons are not used against non-nuclear-weapon states. The doctrine keeps one exception: a major biological or chemical attack on India or its forces may prompt a nuclear response. India also commits to strict export controls, to the Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty negotiations, to its test moratorium, and to a nuclear-weapon-free world through verifiable, non-discriminatory disarmament.

Authority is divided between two councils of the Nuclear Command Authority, which is the decision structure for these weapons. Retaliatory attacks can be authorised only by the civilian political leadership.

| Council | Chaired by | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Political Council | Prime Minister | The sole body that can authorise the use of nuclear weapons |
| Executive Council | National Security Adviser | Gives inputs for decisions and executes the Political Council's directives |1a6:T6bc,India launched the Connect Central Asia policy in 2012 to deepen ties with Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. It is a broad approach that covers political, security, economic and cultural links.

| Area | Elements the chapter lists |
|---|---|
| Political | Continued exchange of high-level visits |
| Security | Military training, joint research and counter-terrorism coordination |
| Multilateral | Engagement through the SCO, the Eurasian Economic Community and the Customs Union |
| Energy and resources | Central Asia as a long-term partner in energy and natural resources |
| Education and health | A Central Asian University in Bishkek, an e-network with its hub in India for tele-education and tele-medicine, and medical cooperation |
| Connectivity and trade | Reactivation of the International North-South Transport Corridor, air links, banking presence and construction projects |

The Act East Policy is the later successor to the Look East Policy. The Look East Policy was launched in 1992 by P. V. Narasimha Rao. In 2014 the Modi government upgraded it and renamed it Act East. The policy's focus is the extended neighbourhood in the Asia-Pacific. It began as economic, and it now also has political, strategic and cultural dimensions. The chapter highlights India–ASEAN cooperation, with the North East, including Arunachal Pradesh, as the interface with ASEAN. Other elements are links between Buddhist and Hindu traditions, a connectivity strategy linking ASEAN with the North East, a trade-in-services and investment agreement with ASEAN that entered into force for India and seven ASEAN countries in 2015, and closer security cooperation on terrorism and maritime security.1a7:T427,The terms of reference asked the Commission to examine, in the light of fifty years of experience, how far the existing provisions can respond to efficient, smooth and effective governance and to socio-economic development, and to recommend changes where needed. Two limits applied. Changes had to stay within the framework of parliamentary democracy, and they must not interfere with the basic structure or basic features of the Constitution.

The Commission described its own role modestly. Its task was to review the working of the Constitution, not to rewrite it, and its functions were recommendatory and advisory. Parliament alone would decide whether to accept or reject any recommendation. The Commission began with no agenda of its own. It chose eleven areas of study, among them strengthening parliamentary institutions, electoral reform and standards in public life, Union-State relations, decentralisation, enlarging Fundamental Rights, giving effect to Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles, and the legal control of fiscal and monetary policy.1a8:T4cb,The Commission's diagnosis was blunt. It saw a breach of constitutional faith by governments, which neglect the people from whom all political authority flows. It found the state poorly equipped to anticipate global change, and it found fiscal deficits and the cost of government alarming. Other concerns were the criminalisation of politics, weak early-warning mechanisms for social unrest, poor disaster management and an administration that reacts rather than plans. The Commission also warned of a debt-trap in the economy, the growth of black money and parallel economies, a justice system whose delays and costs have become proverbial, and a social sector that remains inadequate. Among the figures it cited were 380 million children below the age of fourteen, and a finding that 96.4 per cent of the primary education budget went to salaries alone.

Two points in the diagnosis are useful for answers. The Commission held that communal and inter-group riots are not merely law-and-order problems but manifestations of collective behavioural disorders. It also noted that the instability of elected governments, driven by opportunistic politics and unprincipled defections, carries high economic and administrative costs.1a9:T886,The Commission wanted the anti-discrimination rule in Articles 15 and 16 extended to ethnic or social origin, political or other opinion, property and birth. Article 19 would expressly cover freedom of the press and other media, and the freedom to hold opinions and to seek, receive and impart information.

It proposed several new Fundamental Rights, which are easiest to remember in a table.

| Proposed right | Core content |
|---|---|
| Against torture | Protection from torture, cruelty and inhuman treatment or punishment |
| Compensation | Compensation if a person is illegally deprived of life or liberty |
| Movement | Right to leave India and to return |
| Privacy | Right to privacy and family life |
| Work | Rural wage employment for at least 80 days in a year |
| Justice | Access to courts and tribunals, speedy justice, equal justice and free legal aid |
| Children | Right to care, assistance and protection |
| Environment | Safe drinking water, prevention of pollution, ecological conservation and sustainable development |

Other changes to Fundamental Rights were specific. Article 21A would require free education to age fourteen, and to age eighteen for girls and for members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Under Article 22, the maximum period of preventive detention would fall to six months, and advisory boards would consist of a chairman and two other members, all serving High Court judges. Sikhism, Jainism and Buddhism would be treated as religions separate from Hinduism, so that the Article 25 grouping would go. Protection under Article 31B for Ninth Schedule laws would be limited to agrarian reform, reservations and the implementation of the Directive Principles in clauses (b) and (c) of Article 39. During a national emergency, the Commission wanted Articles 17, 23, 24, 25 and 32 to be non-suspendable, in addition to Articles 20 and 21.

On property, Article 300A would be recast so that deprivation or acquisition requires authority of law and a public purpose, is not arbitrary, and, for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, requires a suitable rehabilitation scheme before possession of agricultural, forest or homestead land.1aa:T648,The Commission wanted the privileges of legislators defined and limited. Articles 105 and 194 would be amended so that parliamentary immunity does not cover corrupt acts done in connection with House duties, and so that no court takes cognisance of an offence arising from a member's House conduct without prior sanction of the Speaker or Chairman. The domicile requirement for contesting Rajya Sabha seats from a state would be kept, to protect its federal character. The MP local area development scheme would be discontinued.

On institutions, the Commission proposed a Standing Constitution Committee of both Houses to scrutinise constitutional amendment proposals in advance, a new Legislation Committee to plan and coordinate legislation, and a Nodal Standing Committee on National Economy. The Committees on Estimates, Public Undertakings and Subordinate Legislation would not be continued. A parliamentary ombudsman was proposed for public scrutiny of MPs, and a study group outside Parliament for procedural reform.

Sittings were a major concern. The Commission wanted a minimum of 100 days a year for the Rajya Sabha and 120 for the Lok Sabha. State legislatures with fewer than 70 members would sit at least 50 days, and others at least 90 days. The Election Commission would be empowered to declare which offices of profit disqualify a person from membership.

| Institution | Recommended minimum sittings |
|---|---|
| Rajya Sabha | 100 days a year |
| Lok Sabha | 120 days a year |
| State legislature with fewer than 70 members | 50 days a year |
| Other state legislatures | 90 days a year |1ab:T50f,If a Lok Sabha is hung, the House would elect its leader, who the President would then appoint as Prime Minister, with the same procedure at state level. The Commission favoured a constructive vote of no confidence: a motion against the Prime Minister must name an alternative leader to be voted on at the same time. It also wanted a no-confidence notice to require the support of at least 20 per cent of the House's members.

The size of government was to be limited. Council of Ministers would be capped at 10 per cent of the lower house's strength, and political offices carrying ministerial perks would be limited to 2 per cent. Lokpal would be created with the Prime Minister outside its purview, and lokayuktas would be set up in the states. Lateral entry above joint secretary level would be allowed. Article 311 would be amended to penalise dishonest public servants, not only protect honest ones. Personnel decisions such as postings and promotions would move to autonomous Civil Service Boards set up by statute.

On transparency, the Commission wanted the right to information guaranteed and an oath of transparency to replace the traditional oath of secrecy. Whistle-blower legislation and a law to forfeit benami property of corrupt public servants and others were also recommended.1ac:T48c,Several recommendations addressed Article 356 and the Governor. Article 356 should stay but be used sparingly, only as a last resort. The President should appoint a Governor only after consulting the Chief Minister of that state. A ministry's loss of majority should be tested only on the floor of the House, and a Governor should not dismiss a ministry that still commands the House. President's Rule could continue without an emergency if elections cannot be held, and a state assembly should not be dissolved before the Article 356 proclamation is laid before Parliament.

Other proposals covered federal institutions. Management of natural and man-made disasters would be moved to the Concurrent List. A statutory Inter-State Trade and Commerce Commission would be set up. The Inter-State Council Order of 1990 would specify the matters requiring consultation. River-water disputes would be heard by a bench of at least three Supreme Court judges and, if necessary, five, and the River Boards Act of 1956 would be replaced after consultation with all states. For bills reserved for the President, a time limit of about three months for a decision was proposed.1ad:T497,The most structural proposal was a National Judicial Commission under the Constitution to recommend Supreme Court appointments. Its members would be the Chief Justice of India as chairman, the two senior-most Supreme Court judges, the Union law minister and one person nominated by the President. A committee of this body would examine complaints about the conduct of Supreme Court and High Court judges.

Other recommendations concerned tenure, power and efficiency. Retirement ages would rise to 65 for High Court judges and 68 for Supreme Court judges. Only the Supreme Court and the High Courts would have contempt power over themselves, and only they could declare Acts of Parliament or state legislatures unconstitutional or beyond competence. A National Judicial Council and state Judicial Councils would prepare plans and budgets. Judgments should ordinarily be delivered within 90 days of the case concluding. Each High Court should prepare a time-bound plan to clear arrears, with no case pending more than a year. Plea bargaining was to be introduced as part of decriminalisation, and the subordinate judiciary was to be reduced to two tiers under each High Court.1ae:T951,On the criminal side, anyone charged with an offence carrying a maximum of five years or more would be disqualified from contesting, and anyone convicted of a heinous crime such as murder, rape, smuggling or dacoity would be permanently barred. Special courts would try cases against politicians, and election petitions would go to special courts or to special benches in High Courts.

On the electoral system, the Commission wanted a candidate to be barred from contesting from more than one constituency for the same office, and the model code of conduct to acquire the force of law. It asked the government and the Election Commission to examine a run-off system that requires 50 per cent plus one vote, in place of first-past-the-post. An independent candidate who loses three consecutive times would be barred from the same office. The forfeiture threshold for deposits would rise from 16.67 per cent to 25 per cent of valid votes. Whether citizens born outside India, or whose parents or grandparents were Indian citizens, should be eligible for high offices such as President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Chief Justice should be examined through a national dialogue. The Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners would be appointed on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, the Leaders of the Opposition in both Houses, the Speaker and the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

On parties, the Commission wanted a comprehensive law on registration and functioning. Parties would keep their doors open regardless of caste or community, keep proper accounts, require candidates to declare assets and liabilities, and refuse tickets to anyone convicted or charged with a criminal offence. Violations would lead to disqualification of the candidate and de-registration of the party. Funding should be regulated transparently, with audited accounts published yearly, and state funding deferred until regulation is in place.

The Commission also proposed changes to the Tenth Schedule. Defectors, whether individuals or groups, would have to resign their seats and contest afresh, and be barred from ministerial or other remunerative political posts for the rest of the term. A vote cast by a defector to topple a government would be invalid. The power to decide disqualification for defection would shift from the Speaker or Chairman to the Election Commission.1af:T4ca,For panchayats and municipalities, the Commission wanted the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules restructured to create a separate fiscal domain, and a state panchayat council chaired by the Chief Minister. Both would be declared institutions of self-government with exclusive functions, through amendments to Articles 243G and 243W. The Election Commission of India would be able to direct State Election Commissions, which would report to it and to the Governor. A panchayat should be heard before it is dissolved, and the CAG should audit panchayat accounts or lay down accounting standards for them. Delimitation, reservation and rotation of seats would go to a Delimitation Commission rather than the State Election Commission. Municipalities should have a distinct tax domain.

For the North East, the Commission proposed extending the 73rd and 74th Amendments with due regard to local political traditions, entrusting Sixth Schedule and Eleventh Schedule subjects to Autonomous District Councils, and associating traditional forms of governance with self-government. It also called for a National Immigration Council to review the Citizenship Act, the Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunal) Act and the Foreigners Act.1b0:T45a,- Set up in 2000 by a government resolution; eleven members; headed by M. N. Venkatachaliah; report submitted in 2002.

Two side points are worth remembering. In the Berubari reference (1960) the Court said that handing Indian territory to a foreign state needs an amendment under Article 368, not an ordinary law under Article 3, and added that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution; the 9th Amendment (1960) then implemented the transfer under the Nehru–Noon agreement. Second, Kesavananda is popularly called the Fundamental Rights case and Indira Gandhi's is the Election case.1b2:T5ba,In **A.K. Gopalan (1950)**, the preventive detention case, the Court read "personal liberty" as freedom from physical restraint, treated "law" as state-made statute, and held that "procedure established by law" is not the American "due process". Article 21 therefore protected only against the executive, not the legislature. Only Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 was struck down. This textualist view lasted until 1978.

The low point came in **A.D.M. Jabalpur (1976)**, the Habeas Corpus case, decided during the Emergency. The Court held that once a Presidential Order under Article 359 suspended Article 21, no detainee could move a High Court under Article 226 on any ground, and it upheld Section 16A(9) of MISA, 1971. The 44th Amendment (1978) later barred the suspension of Article 21 by a Presidential Order, leaving the ruling of academic interest only.

**Maneka Gandhi (1978)** overruled Gopalan. It reached a verdict on the Passport Act that favoured the government, but its reasoning transformed Article 21:

- Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not separate silos; a law touching personal liberty must pass all three, the so-called **golden triangle**.
- Personal liberty is of the widest amplitude, and life means a life of dignity, not bare existence.
- Procedure must be just, fair and reasonable, which brought the American idea of due process into Indian reading.
