The doctrine of severability, also called separability, says that only the offending portion is struck down if it can be cleanly detached; if it cannot, the whole Act goes. Its textual anchor is **Article 13**: clause (1) makes pre-Constitution laws void to the extent they conflict with fundamental rights, and clause (2) bars the state from making laws that take away or abridge those rights, with the same "to the extent" consequence.

The tests the Supreme Court laid down (in the Chamarbaugwalla case, 1957) can be compressed into a short list.

- The deciding factor is legislative intent: would the legislature have passed the valid part had it known the rest was invalid?
- If valid and invalid provisions are tangled together, the whole falls; if what remains is a complete and independent code, it stands.
- Even separate provisions fall together if they form one scheme meant to work as a whole.
- If what is left is so thin that it differs in substance from the original law, or can work only after being rewritten, it is rejected, since rewriting would be judicial legislation.
- Form does not matter (same section or different), only substance. The history, object, title and preamble of the Act can be consulted.

| Case | Outcome |
|---|---|
| A. K. Gopalan (1950) | Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act struck down for conflict with Article 22; rest of the Act upheld |
| F. N. Balsara (1951) | Eight sections of the Bombay Prohibition Act held invalid; Act as a whole survived |
| Chamarbaugwalla (1957) | Prize Competitions Act: provisions covering skill-based contests struck down while the gambling part stayed |
| Minerva Mills (1980) | Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment struck down as beyond amending power; rest valid |
| Kihoto Hollohan (1992) | Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule void for lacking ratification required under Article 368(2); remainder of the Schedule valid |1bc:T5ee,Article 13(1) operates prospectively, and that gave rise to the doctrine of eclipse. A pre-Constitution law that conflicts with a fundamental right is not dead from birth; it merely becomes inoperative from 26 January 1950, covered by the shadow of the right. It still governs past transactions, rights and liabilities that arose earlier, and the position of non-citizens who have no fundamental rights. If an amendment removes the conflict, the shadow lifts and the law revives.

The doctrine was stated in **Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955)**. A Motor Vehicles Act provision allowing the state to take over motor transport had become void under Article 19(1)(g) in 1950. After the First Amendment (1951) changed Article 19(6), the state issued its takeover notification, and the Court held that the old provision had only been eclipsed and became enforceable again.

The next question is whether eclipse also covers laws made after the Constitution under Article 13(2). The Court's position shifted:

| Case | Position |
|---|---|
| Deep Chand (1959) | Eclipse applies only to pre-Constitution laws; a post-Constitution law that violates a right is stillborn and cannot be revived by amendment |
| Mahendra Lal Jain (1962) | Repeated Deep Chand |
| Ambica Mills (1974) | Reversed course: a post-Constitution law violating Article 19 still works against non-citizens, who have no such right, and is void only against citizens |
| Dulare Lodh (1984) | Applied eclipse to a post-Constitution law even as against citizens |1bd:T5ee,Under **Article 245**, Parliament can legislate for all or any part of India and can also make extra-territorial laws, which follow Indian citizens and their property anywhere. A state legislature can legislate only for its own territory. The doctrine of territorial nexus supplies the exception: a state law with effect beyond its borders is valid if a **sufficient connection** exists between the state and the subject of the law.

Early applications came in income-tax cases before the Constitution: Raleigh (1944) and Wadia (1949) in the Federal Court, and Wallace (1948) in the Privy Council. After 1950 the Court applied it in Chamarbaugwalla (1957) on a tax on gambling, and in TISCO (1958) on sales tax, noting that the doctrine does not itself impose a tax but only shows when a tax can be enforced. Two conditions apply: the nexus must be real, not illusory, and the liability imposed must be relevant to that nexus. The NTPC case (2002) restated that only Parliament can ordinarily legislate extra-territorially, with a real nexus as the single exception for states.

The doctrine is not limited to tax. In Charusila Dasi (1959) a Bihar law on trusts was upheld even though some trust property lay in West Bengal, and in Shrikant (1994) Gujarat could count land held outside the state when fixing agricultural ceilings. It does not apply to a state scheme for inter-state routes under the Central Motor Vehicles Act, nor to trade the state itself carries on under Article 298 (both from Khazan Singh, 1973).1be:T712,**Article 246** divides subjects into the Union, State and Concurrent Lists. When a law strays into another list, the court looks at the Act as an organic whole, its main objects and the scope and effect of its provisions to find its true character. If the pith and substance falls within the enacting legislature's field, the law is valid even if it touches another field incidentally. The doctrine came from Privy Council rulings on Canada and Australia, and rests on the point that no list can be drawn so cleanly that overlap never occurs.

The leading statement is the Privy Council's ruling in **Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee (1947)**, where the Bengal Money Lenders Act was upheld as a law on money-lending (a provincial subject) though it incidentally touched promissory notes (a federal subject). Its principles: ask what the Act is in substance and in which list it belongs; the degree of invasion matters only to discover the true character; and where lists conflict, the Union list prevails over the Concurrent and State lists, and the Concurrent over the State list, but incidental effects do not strip a legislature of its own subject.

| Case | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Balsara (1951) | Bombay Prohibition Act upheld against a challenge that it entered the Union List |
| D. N. Banerji (1952) | Parliament's Industrial Disputes Act upheld despite touching municipalities |
| G. Chawla (1958) | Rajasthan law on sound amplifiers upheld against a broadcasting-based challenge |
| Shantilal Mangaldas (1969) | Doctrine decides competence only; irrelevant to whether a law infringes a fundamental right |
| Ismail Faruqui (1994) | Ayodhya land acquisition Act upheld as acquisition of property (Concurrent List), not public order |
| Zameer Ahmed (2010) | Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act upheld |1bf:T5f5,A law may look as if it lies within the legislature's competence while in reality it covers something the legislature cannot touch, either because the subject is not in its list or because the Constitution (including Part III) forbids it. Such a law is colourable and void. The maxim behind it is that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly, which is why it is also named the doctrine of **fraud on the Constitution**.

Key propositions:

- Substance, not form, decides. A disguise will not save the law.
- The court may study effect, object and design only to find the true character of the law, not to judge motives.
- The doctrine has nothing to do with good or bad faith; it is purely a question of competence.
- A set of Acts that individually look harmless can be struck down if together they evade a constitutional limit.

**Fraud on the Constitution** differs from **fraud on legislative power**. In the latter the legislature has the power but only pretends to exercise it, so the Act is no law at all. In the former the legislature lacks the power or is prohibited but enacts the law as if it had power.

| Case | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Kameshwar Singh (1952) | Bihar Land Reforms Act invalidated; the compensation provision was only a pretence |
| Moopil Nair (1960) | Travancore-Cochin Land Tax Act invalid for violating Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) and being confiscatory |
| M. R. Balaji (1962) | Mysore order reserving 68 per cent of seats void; violated Article 15(4), a fraud on the Constitution |1c0:T821,**Implied powers.** Whoever is granted something is taken to be granted whatever is needed to make the grant effective. A court will read in an auxiliary power only when a statutory duty or power could not otherwise be exercised at all, so that the provision would become a dead letter. Applications:

- Gopal Chandra Misra (1978): a High Court judge may withdraw a resignation even after the letter has been received (Article 217).
- Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002): the Supreme Court may reconsider final judgments through a curative petition after a review is dismissed (Article 137).
- Raja Ram Pal (2007): Parliament can expel members for contempt (Article 105).
- Salil Sabhlok (2013): the Governor's power to appoint State Public Service Commission members (Article 316) carries the power to lay down the procedure.

**Implied prohibition** is the reverse, built on the idea that mentioning one thing excludes another. It works in the United States and Australia, where only central powers are listed and residuary power rests with the states. It does not apply in India, where both levels have enumerated lists and Parliament also holds residuary power.

**Incidental and ancillary powers** are those required to make the express legislative power effective; the United States calls them "necessary and proper" powers. Entries in the lists are read broadly, so a power to tax includes provisions to check evasion, and a power over rent collection includes remission of rent. There are limits: a power to tax does not cover confiscating goods; betting and gambling (Entry 34, State List) does not cover taxing them, since that is a separate Entry 62; and the doctrine cannot protect a colourable law.

| Case | Holding |
|---|---|
| Rai Ramkrishna (1963) | Power over a subject includes enacting a valid retrospective law after an earlier one is struck down |
| Pathumma (1978) | Money-lending entry covers relief for debts already recovered by sale in execution |
| Godfrey Phillips (2005) | Taxing power covers all events concerning that tax unless an event sits in another list |1c1:T5fa,When Parliament legislates on a subject it occupies the field, leaving no room for a state law there. This doctrine, also called the covered field, matters chiefly for the **Concurrent List**: in the Union List the states are excluded anyway, and the State List is closed to Parliament in normal times. It stems from **Article 254**, which says that if a state law and a parliamentary law on a Concurrent subject conflict, the parliamentary law prevails and the state law is void to the extent of the repugnancy.

The Supreme Court identifies repugnancy by three questions: is there direct conflict, did Parliament intend an exhaustive code, and do both laws occupy the same field? The Karunanidhi case (1979) adds that:

- the laws must be inconsistent and irreconcilable so they cannot stand together;
- there is no repeal by implication unless the inconsistency is apparent on the face of the statutes;
- no repugnancy arises if both can operate without colliding, or if the later law creates distinct and separate offences.

**Exception.** A state law reserved for the President and given assent prevails in that state over the central law. Parliament may still override it later by enacting a fresh law on the same matter.

**Outside the Concurrent List.** If laws overlap between lists, the central law wins through the non-obstante clause in Article 246(1), not Article 254. Article 254(1) applies only where both laws occupy the same field in a Concurrent List matter and conflict directly (Hoechst Pharmaceuticals, 1983).1c2:T69a,An American idea, applied in India for the first time in **Golak Nath (1967)**. When a court replaces an earlier ruling, it may apply the new rule only to the future, leaving past transactions undisturbed. In Golak Nath the Court overruled Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1964), which had held that Parliament could amend fundamental rights, and decided that an amendment is "law" under Article 13(2) and cannot take away or abridge Part III rights. But it made the ruling prospective, so the First (1951), Fourth (1955) and Seventeenth (1964) Amendments stayed valid and only future curtailment was barred.

The Court rejected the claim that this is judicial legislation. It reasoned that nothing in the Constitution forbids it and that Articles 32, 141 and 142 are wide enough, and that the doctrine reconciles the view that judges find law with the view that they make it. It laid down three propositions: the doctrine can be invoked only in matters arising under the Constitution; only the Supreme Court may apply it; and how far retroactivity is limited is left to the Court's discretion. Its advantages are that it avoids reopened settled issues, uncertainty and multiplied litigation. Critics call it legislation by courts; the Court answered that a power to overrule includes a power to limit the ruling to the future.

Golak Nath itself was overruled by **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, but the doctrine of prospective overruling survived and was extended to ordinary statutes. The Mandal ruling (Indra Sawhney, 1992), which postponed its operation by five years, and B. Karunakar (1993), which gave benefit only to cases pending before authorities, are cited as instances.1c3:T517,If provisions of the Constitution seem to clash, courts should read the document as a whole, presume that the makers intended no conflict, and reconcile the provisions so that each has effect and none is rendered meaningless. It is also called the rule of avoidance of conflict. The Court has used it to reconcile fundamental rights with directive principles (the two supplement each other in aiming at a welfare state), different fundamental rights, rights and legislative privileges, rights and the amendment procedure, and competing entries in the Seventh Schedule, where the Union's overriding power operates only if reconciliation is impossible.

- Waiver: fundamental rights cannot be waived in India, unlike in the United States (Basheshar Nath, Olga Tellis).
- Eclipse: a pre-1950 law conflicting with a right is dormant, not dead; revives when the conflict is removed (Bhikaji, 1955).

### The American President

The election is indirect on paper, because voters choose electors who form an electoral college, but party conventions have made it nearly direct. The college has 538 members: 435 for the House, 100 for the Senate and three for the District of Columbia. A candidate needs 270. The electors are a temporary body, not members of Congress. If no one wins a majority, the House of Representatives elects the President from the top three candidates, as in 1800, 1824 and 1876.

A candidate must be a natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old and a resident for 14 years. The term begins on 20 January, and the 22nd Amendment (1951) limits any person to two elections, so ten years at most. For impeachment, the House brings the charge by simple majority and the Senate tries the case under the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court; a two-thirds vote convicts. No President has ever been removed, though Johnson (1868), Nixon (1974), Clinton (1998) and Trump (2019 and 2021) faced proceedings.

When Congress passes a bill, the President has three choices. He may sign it. He may return it within ten days, and Congress can override with a two-thirds majority; this is the **qualified veto**. Or he may sit on it; the bill becomes law after ten days, but if Congress adjourns first it dies, which is the **pocket veto**. Other powers include commanding the armed forces, appointing judges and ambassadors with Senate consent, granting pardons for federal offences except impeachment, preparing the budget, calling special sessions and issuing executive orders.1c6:Tb24,The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland took its present form in 1921; England and Wales were united in 1535 and Scotland joined in 1707 to form Great Britain. Britain is often called the mother of constitutions and the home of representative government.

**Unwritten and evolved.** Much of the British constitution is not codified. It rests on five sources:

| Source | Content |
|---|---|
| Conventions | Customary rules such as acting on the advice of the Cabinet, appointing the leader of the majority party in the Commons as Prime Minister, and dissolving the Commons on the Prime Minister's advice; not enforced by courts |
| Great charters | Magna Carta (1215), Petition of Right (1628), Bill of Rights (1689) |
| Statutes | Habeas Corpus Act 1679, Statute of Westminster 1931 and similar laws |
| Common law | Judge-made rules accepted and enforced by courts |
| Legal commentaries | Writings of Dicey, Bagehot and Blackstone |

**Flexible and unitary.** Parliament amends constitutional matters exactly as it makes ordinary laws, so no legal distinction exists between the two. Local bodies depend wholly on the Centre and can be abolished by it.

**Parliamentary government and sovereignty of Parliament.** The monarch is the nominal head and the Cabinet the real executive; ministers are in Parliament and responsible to the Commons. Parliament is supreme: it can make or unmake any law, and no court can strike down its statutes, so there is no judicial review. The constitutional monarchy follows the maxim that the sovereign reigns but does not rule, and the Crown, an institution, survives each individual monarch.

**Rule of law.** Dicey's *Law of the Constitution* (1885) gave three meanings: no punishment except for breach of law, equality of all before the ordinary courts, and rights that come from judicial decisions instead of a constitutional grant.

**Bicameral Parliament.** The House of Lords is the oldest second chamber and mainly hereditary or appointed; the House of Commons is elected on adult franchise and is the more powerful.

### The British Cabinet

The Cabinet is led by the Prime Minister with about twenty senior ministers. The Attorney-General, Solicitor-General, Lord Advocate and Paymaster-General are not Cabinet members. The Privy Council, a body dating from the fifteenth century, once advised the monarch; most of its power passed to the Cabinet as an inner committee, and it is presided over by the Lord President of the Council. The Prime Minister was once first among equals, but writers such as Crossman and Mackintosh describe the modern arrangement as **Prime Ministerial government**. The Opposition forms a **Shadow Cabinet**, in which each minister is matched by a critic, ready to take office; Ivor Jennings called the Leader of the Opposition the "alternative Prime Minister".1c7:Ta58,France has changed constitutions on average every twelve years since the Revolution of 1789–99: three monarchic, two dictatorial, three imperial and four republican. The present Constitution, which began the Fifth Republic in 1958, was prepared under General de Gaulle to give a strong and stable government. Originally it had a Preamble and 92 Articles in 15 chapters, and it declares France an indivisible, secular, democratic and social republic with the motto Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.

### The French President

The President wins by an absolute majority; if nobody does in the first round, the two leaders contest a second ballot. The Constitution sets no minimum age or other qualification. If the post falls vacant, the President of the Senate acts temporarily, but cannot call a referendum or dissolve the Assembly. Impeachment requires an absolute majority in both Houses for high treason, and the High Court of Justice conducts the trial.

He is the pivot of the system: he appoints the Prime Minister, names ministers on the PM's advice, presides over the Council of Ministers, commands the armed forces, negotiates treaties, appoints the President and three members of the Constitutional Council, promulgates laws within fifteen days (he may ask for reconsideration) and may put bills to a referendum. He can dissolve the National Assembly after consultation, though not more than once in twelve months and never during an emergency, and he is not bound by the advice he receives.1c8:T826,Modern Japan dates from the Meiji Restoration of 1868; the Meiji Constitution (1889–1947) rested on autocratic monarchy. After the Second World War the Allied Occupation, led by General MacArthur, produced a democratic Constitution adopted in 1946 and effective from 1947. It is known as the MacArthur or Showa Constitution, Showa meaning "radiant peace" after the era of Emperor Hirohito.

- **Written and rigid:** a Preamble and 103 Articles in 11 chapters. Amendment needs a two-thirds vote of the Diet and then approval by a majority of the people in a referendum, after which the Emperor promulgates it. It has never been amended.
- **Unitary:** all power rests with the central government at Tokyo; provinces exercise delegated powers.
- **Parliamentary:** the Emperor is nominal head and the Cabinet real executive. The Diet designates the Prime Minister, the Emperor appoints him, he selects and can remove ministers, a majority of whom must be Diet members, and the Cabinet resigns if the House of Representatives passes a no-confidence motion.
- **Constitutional monarchy:** the Emperor is only a symbol of the state, sovereignty lies with the people, and every act needs Cabinet advice and approval.
- **Judicial review:** the Supreme Court can strike down laws, and unlike the American Court it derives that power directly from the text.
- **Rights:** Articles 10 to 40, thirty-one in all, form a detailed chapter on rights and duties, described as eternal and inviolate.
- **Renunciation of war:** Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right and bars land, sea and air forces, which makes Japan unique; the country maintains "self-defence forces" justified on the right to defend itself.
- **Bicameral Diet:** House of Councillors (upper) and House of Representatives (lower), the latter stronger especially in finance.

Japan differs from Britain in four ways: the Diet chooses the Prime Minister while the Emperor only appoints; the Prime Minister, not the monarch, appoints ministers; he can dismiss them; and only a majority of ministers must sit in the legislature.1c9:T71b,The Soviet Union grew out of the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 under Lenin, and collapsed in 1989–91. It adopted constitutions in 1918, 1924, 1936 (the Stalin Constitution) and 1977 (the Brezhnev Constitution). It was the first socialist constitution in the world, built on Marxism–Leninism.

- **Rights and duties:** a broad list, but not to be exercised against the interests of the state, society or others; duties include paying taxes, military service and practising family planning.1cb:T7aa,Switzerland has had three constitutions: 1848, which created the federal state, 1874, and the present one adopted by the Federal Assembly on 18 December 1998, approved by people and cantons on 18 April 1999, and in force from 1 January 2000. Article 261 addresses this. The President therefore cannot choose a minister the Prime Minister has not recommended. Ministers usually come from either House of Parliament, but a person from outside can be appointed. Such a person must become a member of one House, by election or nomination, within six months, failing which the person ceases to be a minister. It became common in the twentieth century to describe judges who make law rather than simply apply it. Scholars also call it judicial dynamism, and it stands opposite to judicial restraint, the self-control a court exercises over its own power.\n\nIn substance, activism means a court that departs from precedent, or reads a law more broadly than its words suggest, in order to protect rights or advance social goals. Lawyers did not serve many groups with weak or dispersed interests, so public-spirited litigation was built to fill that gap. In India the concept grew close to judicial activism, and the Supreme Court's activist role is the main reason for its emergence. Put simply, PIL is an outcome of activism and its most popular form.\n\nThe Indian version began in the early 1980s. Its main drivers were the same judges who laid the foundations of activism, Krishna Iyer and Bhagwati. The chapter notes the three alternative labels, which are useful for recognising the concept in question paper options.","anchor":"origin-and-the-indian-introduction"},{"topicId":"polity.public-interest-litigation","topic":"Public Interest Litigation","title":"Meaning and the relaxed locus standi","text":"The traditional rule of locus standi allowed only a person whose own rights had been infringed to approach a court for a remedy. PIL is an exception to that rule. Any public-spirited citizen or social organisation may move the court to enforce the rights of persons who, because of poverty, ignorance or a disadvantaged social or economic position, cannot approach the court themselves. The test is whether the person has sufficient interest in the common grievance.\n\nThe Supreme Court describes PIL as legal action brought for the enforcement of public or general interest, in which the public or a class of the community has a stake that its legal rights or liabilities affect. The purposes it serves are three: upholding the rule of law, giving the weaker sections effective access to justice, and making fundamental rights meaningful in practice.","anchor":"meaning-and-the-relaxed-locus-standi"},{"topicId":"polity.public-interest-litigation","topic":"Public Interest Litigation","title":"How PIL differs from ordinary litigation","text":"$cf","anchor":"how-pil-differs-from-ordinary-litigation"},{"topicId":"polity.public-interest-litigation","topic":"Public Interest Litigation","title":"Which matters are entertained","text":"$d0","anchor":"which-matters-are-entertained"},{"topicId":"polity.public-interest-litigation","topic":"Public Interest Litigation","title":"Principles the Supreme Court evolved","text":"$d1","anchor":"principles-the-supreme-court-evolved"},{"topicId":"polity.public-interest-litigation","topic":"Public Interest Litigation","title":"Safeguards against misuse","text":"$d2","anchor":"safeguards-against-misuse"},{"topicId":"polity.public-interest-litigation","topic":"Public Interest Litigation","title":"Revise in 60 seconds","text":"- PIL: originated in the USA in the 1960s; introduced in India in the early 1980s. The oath of office binds the holder to the Constitution, the sovereignty and integrity of India, faithful discharge of duty, and fair treatment of all people. The term is not fixed. The Chief Minister holds office during the Governor's pleasure, but that does not let the Governor dismiss him at will. One-half of its total membership forms a quorum. Every decision needs a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes of members present and voting. The weights split the votes between the two sides of the table:\n\n| Voter | Weight in each vote |\n|---|---|\n| Central government | One-third of the total votes cast |\n| All state governments combined | Two-thirds of the total votes cast |\n\nThe weighting means the Union cannot carry a decision alone, and the states together cannot carry one without at least some Union support. It was created by an executive resolution of the Union Cabinet, not by the Constitution or by an Act of Parliament. That single fact decides a whole family of questions. NITI Aayog is therefore a non-constitutional and non-statutory body, and it can be reconstituted or reshaped by the executive alone.\n\nIts function is advisory and directional. It offers policy inputs and technical advice to the Centre and to the states, and it helps design long-term strategic programmes. Its stated aim was to serve people's needs better through a holistic approach to development that goes beyond the public sector alone. Three foundations were named: states as equal partners under cooperative federalism; a knowledge hub that doubles as a think tank; and a collaborative platform that tracks progress and brings ministries at the Centre and in the states together.\n\nThe shift is best summarised in a comparison of method. The old model moved policy one way, from the Centre to the states, and it relied on command and control. NITI Aayog replaces that with a continuing partnership, a collaborative setting in which many views are accepted, and a bottom-up way of shaping policy. Delimitation carried out under the law and accepted norms is what secures fair elections for the people. Since the system elects representatives from single-member constituencies, the boundaries must be redrawn at regular intervals to match changes on the ground. The principle of one person, one vote calls for equal value in every vote, but that ideal is hard to reach. When two constituencies each elect one member but have different populations, a voter in the smaller one carries more weight. The Supreme Court made this observation in R. C. Poudyal v. The state legislature names the body that prepares electoral rolls and runs the elections.\n\nA board may be superseded or kept under suspension only on specified grounds. These are persistent default, negligence in its duties, acts prejudicial to the society or its members, a deadlock in the board's constitution or functioning, and the election body's failure to hold elections under the state Act. No board may remain superseded or suspended for more than six months. For co-operative banks other than multi-state ones, the limit is one year. Social and historical reasons include the cultural and ethnic diversity of Indian society, the wish of some groups or areas to keep a separate identity rooted in history, the interests of deposed Maharajas and dispossessed zamindars, and the alienation of tribal groups. Caste and religion, too, shape politics in ways that a regional party can use.\n\nPolitical and economic reasons were equally important. Economic disparities and regional imbalances in development gave people reason to look for local champions. National parties often failed to meet regional aspirations, and the reorganisation of states on linguistic lines gave each language group a political unit to organise around. The centralising tendencies of the Congress, factional fights inside the big parties and the lack of a strong opposition at the Centre left room for regional alternatives. Charismatic regional leaders filled that room.","anchor":"why-regional-parties-emerged"},{"topicId":"polity.political-parties","topic":"Political Parties and Regional Parties","title":"Role of regional parties","text":"$180","anchor":"role-of-regional-parties"},{"topicId":"polity.political-parties","topic":"Political Parties and Regional Parties","title":"Dysfunctions of regional parties","text":"The same parties carry real costs. Their narrow approach puts regional interests above national ones, and they often neglect the wider consequences of their stance on national issues. They have encouraged regionalism, casteism, linguism, communalism and tribalism, which hinder national integration. Their stances have also made inter-state water and border disputes harder to resolve.\n\nPower has sometimes been misused for self-interest. Corruption, nepotism and favouritism have appeared, and populist schemes aimed at widening the electoral base have sometimes damaged the state economy. In politics it names an alliance between distinct parties. The working definition is this: when a set of parties pool their strength, take office together and govern by a shared plan, the system is called coalition politics or coalition government.\n\nCoalitions usually appear when no party wins enough seats on its own. If two or more parties together hold a majority, they can often draft a common agenda that asks little of each member's core beliefs, and then take office. Put simply, a coalition is a multi-party government assembled from smaller groups that set aside their wider differences in favour of one platform and one combined majority.","anchor":"what-a-coalition-is"},{"topicId":"polity.coalition-government","topic":"Coalition Government","title":"Features of coalition politics","text":"The features of coalition politics are easiest to remember as a short list of traits:\n\n| Feature | What it means in practice |\n|---|---|\n| Two or more partners | A coalition needs at least two parties; partners join for a reward, whether material or political |\n| Temporary tie | The alliance lasts only as long as the shared interest does, so partners split and regroup over time |\n| Compromise over doctrine | A minimum programme binds the partners, and it may not suit any one partner fully |\n| Pragmatism over ideology | Practical gains come first, and principles may be set aside when the arithmetic demands it |\n| Aim of power | The underlying purpose of any adjustment is to acquire and hold government |\n\nBecause the players and blocs keep changing, coalition politics is dynamic rather than fixed. In the United States a citizen can waive some constitutional rights, but **India follows the opposite rule: fundamental rights cannot be waived**. The Supreme Court (in Basheshar Nath, 1958) reasoned that these rights are obligations placed on the state in public interest, not merely personal benefits; a citizen cannot invite discrimination or accept conviction by giving up Articles 15, 20 or 21, and no line can be drawn between rights meant for the individual and those meant for the public.\n\n| Case | Holding |\n|---|---|\n| Behram Khurshid Pesikaka (1954) | An accused cannot waive fundamental rights to get convicted |\n| Basheshar Nath (1958) | Agreeing to pay tax did not waive the Article 14 right |\n| Olga Tellis (1985), the pavement dwellers case | No act of a person waives a fundamental right; there is no estoppel against the Constitution |\n| Nar Singh Pal (2000) | Fundamental rights cannot be bartered away or compromised |","anchor":"waiver"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Eclipse","text":"$1bc","anchor":"eclipse"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Territorial nexus","text":"$1bd","anchor":"territorial-nexus"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Pith and substance","text":"$1be","anchor":"pith-and-substance"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Colourable legislation","text":"$1bf","anchor":"colourable-legislation"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Implied powers and incidental powers","text":"$1c0","anchor":"implied-powers-and-incidental-powers"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Precedent","text":"Precedent, or *stare decisis*, is an English doctrine: lower courts follow higher courts, and settled rulings are not unsettled without strong reason. The aim is consistency and certainty. In India, **Article 141** gives it constitutional force: the law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts in the territory of India, so a High Court that refuses to follow a Supreme Court ruling, or revives a decision the Supreme Court set aside, passes a nullity. The Court has called this both judicial discipline and a constitutional mandate.\n\nThe Court has noted limited exceptions: a ruling may be revisited if the subject is of such fundamental national importance, or the earlier reasoning so plainly mistaken, that being right matters more than being consistent. Judgments, in the Court's phrase, are decisional between the parties but declaratory for the nation.","anchor":"precedent"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Occupied field and repugnancy","text":"$1c1","anchor":"occupied-field-and-repugnancy"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Prospective overruling","text":"$1c2","anchor":"prospective-overruling"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Harmonious construction","text":"$1c3","anchor":"harmonious-construction"},{"topicId":"polity.constitutional-doctrines","topic":"Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation","title":"Styles of interpretation","text":"| Approach | Core idea | Illustration |\n|---|---|---|\n| Liberal | The Constitution is a living instrument for making laws and must be read broadly, not in a narrow or pedantic way; list entries get their widest meaning | Fundamental rights not cut down by a restricted approach |\n| Literal (strict or positivist) | Plain, ordinary, grammatical meaning; nothing read in from a supposed spirit, policy or to fill omissions | Gopalan (1950), which refused to void a law on the basis of an unwritten spirit |\n| Purposive | Ask why a provision was included; the Preamble and Constituent Assembly debates reveal the makers' intent | Berubari Union case (1960): the Preamble as the key to the makers' minds |\n| Creative | Courts devise new concepts and procedures for changing needs | Golak Nath's prospective overruling;
